A book in thirteen chapters

Dams in Section

From a handful of sand to a dam you design

Soil holds only as well as its grains press on one another, and the water between them can take that press away.

A dam is a heap of earth and rock, or a block of concrete, that holds back water or mine waste. This book cuts dams open the way engineers draw them, in section, and asks of each one the two questions in the sentence above. It starts with a handful of sand on a beach and ends with a dam you design and test yourself. Most of the drawings are live. Drag them, play them, and try to break them.

Preface

Stand on the crest of an earth dam and look down the far side. A slope of grass, a gravel road along the top, a ditch at the bottom where a little clear water runs. Behind you is a lake, perhaps tens of metres deep and several kilometres long. Between the two is a heap of soil and broken rock, much of it dug from the hills nearby and rolled flat in layers. That a heap of loose grains can hold a lake back for a century, and the few ways it stops doing so, is what this book is about.

It is written for a curious adult with school arithmetic: someone who can work out a percentage, read a graph and is willing to meet a tangent. The toolkit after Plate 0 checks every piece of maths the book uses, and that is all of it. If you are an engineering student you will find here the ideas of a first course in soil mechanics and dam engineering, worked with real numbers, along with plain statements of where the models are simplified.

Dams hold back more than drinking water and the water that turns turbines. They protect towns from floods, and at mines they hold what is left of the ore once the metal is out, ground to sand and silt and mixed with water. That waste has to stay put long after the mine closes. When a dam of either kind fails, everything it held comes out at once.

Most of the examples come from British Columbia. More than 1,900 dams there are regulated under the province's Water Sustainability Act.BC Dam Safety (2026). Tailings dams at mines are not in that count; they are regulated under the Mines Act. Four dams from the province run through these pages. Mount Polley, whose night in August 2014 opens the book, is the one the whole book works toward. The W.A.C. Bennett Dam on the Peace River shows what each zone inside an embankment is for. Coquitlam shows that the way a dam was built can matter more than what it holds. Testalinden, a small dam near Oliver, shows that inspection and regulation are part of a dam as much as its soil is.

By the last chapter you will be able to read a dam's cross-section the way an engineer does, work out how hard the water pushes on it and where, follow water through and under it, and say why one soil is strong and another weak. You will be able to check whether a slope will stand, name the ways embankments fail, and design a small dam of your own. You will also be able to say what your own check cannot see.

One sentence holds the book together. It is on the title page: soil holds only as well as its grains press on one another, and the water between them can take that press away. The first chapters build it from a beach, a bucket and a block on a ramp; Chapter 4 proves it; every chapter after that applies it. It does not cover everything that brings a dam down. A flood that pours over the crest can wash a heap away however hard its grains press, and Chapter 6 deals with that separately.

The figures run in your browser, among them a seepage solver, a slope-stability solver and a box of simulated grains. Each number the text quotes from a figure is checked by a test that recomputes it from the code behind the figure, so the words and the drawings can't drift apart. Numbers from the literature carry a note in the margin that names their source. The seven narrated films were made separately; each is captioned, and each has a transcript.

How to read this book

This is a book to read and a set of instruments to play. A few habits get the most out of both, and each is shown here once, working.

Commit before you look

Some figures wait behind a question. Pick an answer before you open them. A wrong guess you committed to teaches more than a right answer you only nodded at, because it shows you exactly which picture in your head needs mending. Try this one:

A glass is filled to the brim with dry sand. Can you still pour water into it without spilling any?

About a third. Sand grains can't fill space: they touch at points and leave gaps between them, and in the sand this book uses the gaps make up 35% of the volume. Every drop of water in this book lives in gaps like those, and almost everything that goes wrong with a dam starts there.

Figures you can play with

Most figures are instruments. The strip across the top gives each one its number, and on the right says whether it is drawn to scale or simplified. Plate 0, on the next pages, is a still drawing; Fig. 2.1 is live, and its sliders move a sensor through a lake. Every caption opens with the figure's claim in bold, says how to read the drawing, gives the one number worth keeping and ends with a short list of things to try. On a phone, every figure wider than the text has an Expand button that opens it full screen; turn the phone sideways to read it.

Each chapter opens with a small drawing of a dam that grows a piece at a time. The Prologue starts with bare ground, and by Chapter 13 it is the whole section; the words under it say what that chapter adds.

Every number the text quotes from a figure is the figure's own. A test recomputes each one from the code that draws the figure, so when Chapter 12 says a dam's slope has a factor of safety of 1.12 (its strength divided by the push on it; the Prologue explains it), the workbench in the last chapter shows 1.12 for the same dam.

Worked examples, and Set the figure

Each chapter works two to five problems with real numbers, one step to a line, with the reason for each step beside it (under it, on a phone). Most end with a Set the figure button, which loads the example's numbers into the live figure and takes you there; a pill at the foot of the screen brings you back. Here is the smallest one in the book:

Example 0

How hard does the water press 10 m down?

Given
A sensor 10 m below the surface of still water. Water weighs 9.81 kN per cubic metre.
Find
The water pressure on the sensor.
The idea
Every square metre at that depth carries the weight of the column of water standing on it.
  1. column above one square metre: 10 m × 1 m² = 10 m³the water standing on the sensor's patch
  2. its weight: 10 × 9.81 = 98.1 kNeach cubic metre weighs 9.81 kN
  3. p = 98.1 kN ÷ 1 m² = 98.1 kPapressure is force per area; 1 kPa is 1 kN/m²

The water presses 98.1 kPa on the sensor.

Check. Set the figure: it rounds to whole kilopascals and shows 98. Double the depth and the column doubles, so at 20 m it shows 196 kPa; at the surface, with no column, zero.

What it means. Ten metres of water press about as hard as the whole height of the air above us. The size of the lake appears nowhere in the sum. Chapter 2 asks whether that can really be right.

Notes in the margin

Notes sit in the right-hand margin beside the line they belong to, and on a phone they fold away behind a small number or ⊕ that you tap to open.Like this one. Nothing the argument needs is ever in a note; you can skip every one and lose nothing but the pleasure. They come in four kinds. Source notes name where a number from the literature comes from, with the page or table when there is one; the Prologue has several. Units notes translate a unit into something you can feel.A kilopascal is a kilonewton spread over a square metre: about the weight of a 100 kg mass, 0.981 kN, resting on a square metre. History notes say who found something out, and when. For the curious notes hold a derivation or an aside for anyone who wants to go a step further.

Check yourself, and the questions at the end

Inside each chapter, a few one-line questions fold open to show their answer:

Check yourself A dam's crest is 24 m above the ground, and the lake behind it is 20.4 m deep. How far below the crest is the water?

3.6 m. That margin has a name, the freeboard, and Plate 0 shows it on this very dam.

Each chapter ends with a box of what to remember and then four to six questions. A tag says what kind each one is, and the dots say how hard:

  • Checkrecall what the chapter said
  • Reckonestimate on paper, with numbers
  • Exploreuse a figure to find out
  • Casereason about a real dam
  • Designchoose something and justify it
  • ●○○ to ●●●from a quick one to a long one

Every question has a hint under it, and the answers, with their working, are collected at the back of the book. After the questions come two or three readings, each marked gentle, serious or primary source, and a card that points to the next chapter.

Films

Seven narrated films, 58 minutes in all, retell the story with moving drawings. Each sits in the chapter it retells most closely, and several range over other chapters as well; the note before each film says where. Before it plays, a film asks its question. Under it, chapter marks jump to the part you want, each linked back to the figure it retells, and a transcript is there for reading instead of watching. Film 2.1 is the first you will meet.

Words, scale and typical values

A dotted underline marks a word defined in the Glossary at the back: hover over it, or tap it on a phone, to read the definition, as with crest. Plate 0 names the parts of a dam and gives the book's three conventions.

All drawings are simplified. Those marked "drawn to scale" are drawn to scale, from the code's own dimensions or from published ones; the rest are schematic, and say so. The soil properties are typical values for teaching, not design values: a real dam is designed from tests on its own soils.

Time, and a tutor

Plan on eight to ten hours for the whole book, more if you work the questions, plus the films. Each chapter's opening page says how long it takes to read, and the bar at the top of the screen shows where you are and opens the Contents. If you are reading on claude.ai, each live figure also has a Why did that happen? button that asks Claude about exactly what the figure is showing you; the standalone page does not have it.

Plate 0 · How to read a section

A section is what you would see if you cut a dam straight across with a very large knife, lifted one half away and looked at the cut face, the way you look at the layers in a slice of cake. Engineers draw dams this way because the things that decide whether a dam stands (how deep the water is against it, where water seeps through it, which slope might slide) all show in that one cut, and along most of a long dam one slice looks much like the next. So the book works per metre of dam: picture a slice one metre thick.

The plate names every part of a section the book uses, on the dam it keeps coming back to:

The toolkit: a self-check

The book uses arithmetic, a little trigonometry and no algebra beyond turning a formula round. These eight questions cover all of it, and each uses a number you will meet later. Answer in your head or on paper first, then open the answer.

1 · Powers of ten The workbench's rockfill has a permeability of 10⁻⁴ m/s; its clay, 10⁻⁹ m/s. How many times more easily does water pass through the rockfill?

10⁻⁴ ÷ 10⁻⁹ = 10−4 + 9 = 10⁵, a hundred thousand times. Dividing powers of ten subtracts their exponents: −4 − (−9) = 5.

2 · A slope as an angle Both faces of our dam slope at 2H:1V, two metres across for every metre up. What angle does each face make with the ground?

The tangent of the angle is rise over run: tan β = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5, so β = tan−1 0.5 = 26.6°. On a calculator, tan−1 is often marked atan or arctan, and it must be set to degrees.

3 · The area of a section Our dam is 24 m high, with a crest 6 m wide and both faces at 2H:1V. What is the area of its cross-section?

Split it into a rectangle under the crest and a triangle on each side. Each face runs 2 × 24 = 48 m across, so each triangle is ½ × 48 × 24 = 576 m². The rectangle is 6 × 24 = 144 m². In all, 1,296 m²: that many cubic metres of fill for every metre of dam, and the same 1,296 one-metre squares you will paint in the workbench at the end of the book.

4 · Mass and weight What does a 100 kg mass weigh, in kilonewtons?

Weight is mass times gravity: 100 kg × 9.81 m/s² = 981 newtons, or 0.981 kN. A tonne weighs 9.81 kN, and a cubic metre of water has a mass of one tonne, so it weighs 9.81 kN. That number turns up on almost every page.

5 · Pressure A tonne of water stands on one square metre. How hard does it press, in kilopascals?

9.81 kN spread over 1 m² is 9.81 kN/m², and a kilopascal (kPa) is exactly one kilonewton per square metre: 9.81 kPa. A column of water one metre deep presses that hard on its base; ten metres press 98.1 kPa.

6 · A log axis On an axis whose ticks read 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁴, what value sits exactly halfway between the first tick and the last?

10⁻⁵, the middle tick. On a logarithmic axis each step multiplies by the same factor, here ten, so halfway between 10⁻⁶ and 10⁻⁴ is the value ten times the first and a tenth of the last. The tempting answer, 5 × 10⁻⁵, sits much nearer the 10⁻⁴ end. The book needs one for permeability, which runs from 10⁻² m/s for gravel to 10⁻⁹ m/s for clay.

7 · Turning a formula round A formula says q = k · i · A. If q/A = 7.0 × 10⁻⁵ m/s and i = 0.70, what is k?

Divide both sides by i · A: k = (q/A) ÷ i = 7.0 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 0.70 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m/s. These are the numbers of the sand in Darcy's pipe in Chapter 3, and the formula is his law.

8 · Significant figures The seepage lab opens with 2,366 litres a day seeping past each metre of dam. Write that to two significant figures.

2,400. Keep the first two digits, 2 and 3, and let the next one, 6, round the 3 up. The lab works with typical soil properties, not measured ones, so two figures are as many as its answer deserves.

Missed two or more? Appendix A opens with a refresher on each of these.

Prologue

4 August 2014

How does a dam that passed its calculations fail in a night?

The dam, piece by piece so far, only the ground

1 figure · about 5 min to read

At half past ten on the night of 3 August 2014, the night shift's logbook at the Mount Polley mine, in the hills of central British Columbia, recorded three things about the tailings dam: "Good berm, good slope, no visible cracks." (A berm is a bank or ledge of earth.)Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), the timeline of the night, p. 10. The mine is about 65 km northeast of Williams Lake: Chief Inspector of Mines (2015), p. 1. At a quarter to twelve another worker drove along the top of the dam, across the stretch that was about to fail, and back again, and noticed nothing unusual.

At a quarter to one, the water in a small pond below the dam, which collects what seeps through it, began to rise. By one o'clock it was rising fast. At a quarter past one the lights went out in the electrical shop and the mill shut down. At five past two an operator found that the dam had been breached.The same timeline, p. 10, from the mine's reports and the panel's interviews.

What came out was more than water. A tailings dam holds back tailings: the rock that is left once the copper and gold have been taken out of it, ground to sand and silt and pumped in as a slurry. Over the next sixteen hours the gap kept widening, and between 21 and 25 million cubic metres of water and tailings came through it, about ten million of them water from the pond.Chief Inspector of Mines (2015), p. 13; the range is the mine owner's estimate. Spread a metre deep, that would cover 21 to 25 square kilometres.

It washed away a stand of forest and ran two ways. Some went into Polley Lake, where the debris plugged the lake's outlet and raised its level by about a metre. The rest went down Hazeltine Creek, a narrow stream, and scoured it into a mudflow 150 metres wide that ran 7 kilometres to Quesnel Lake, one of the deepest lakes in the province.Chief Inspector of Mines (2015), p. 13; on who was below the dam, p. 160. Nobody was at work below the dam that night, or out on the lake or the creek, and nobody was killed.

P.1 A dam that passed

The dam had been watched. Its first, low embankment, the starter dam, was built in 1996, and it had been raised in stages ever since, a few metres at a time, as the mine filled it; the ninth stage was being finished that summer. By that night it stood about 40 metres high where it failed, its crest 1 metre short of the height it was permitted to reach, and that evening the pond stood 2.3 metres below the crest (taken, as the review panel took it, at the top of the dam's core, the watertight zone inside it): its freeboard. Engineers designed each raise and checked it, the dam's engineers inspected it once a year, and the province's geotechnical inspectors, engineers who specialize in soil and rock, visited the site.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), pp. 5 and i; Chief Inspector of Mines (2015), pp. 3, 5 and 47.

The checks said it was safe. When the side of the dam that later failed was checked during the raise of 2007 to 2011, its calculated factor of safety was 1.7; its designers required 1.3.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), p. 64; for 2012, p. 79. A factor of safety is the strength holding a slope up divided by the push trying to bring it down, so 1.7 meant 70 per cent more strength than the slope needed. In 2012 its engineers judged the numbers high enough that the instruments measuring water pressure in that side needed no alarm levels.

Here is that side of the dam, cut across where it failed, drawn to scale from the panel's own section:

Notice that the pond is only a thin skin on top of the tailings, and how big the heap is that holds them: a bank of broken rock as tall as a twelve-storey building. Nothing in the drawing looks fragile.

So how does a dam that passed its calculations fail in a night? The province's Chief Inspector of Mines, in his own investigation, put the puzzle plainly: "The failure of the dam took place suddenly, without any warning signs."Chief Inspector of Mines (2015), p. 13. The province, with the Williams Lake and Soda Creek Indian Bands, set up a panel of three engineers to find out why. It was chaired by Norbert Morgenstern, whose name is on one of the standard methods of checking whether a slope will stand, and one of its members, Steven Vick, had written a standard textbook on tailings dams.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), pp. i and 1; the textbook is Vick (1990). They had the site drilled and sampled and the samples tested, read the design reports of eighteen years, and reported in January 2015.

Their answer is in the last chapter of this book, and by then you will be able to follow it: to see what they found, and why the calculations said the dam was safe. It takes nothing more exotic than the thing every chapter between here and there is about: grains, and the water between them. We start somewhere smaller, on a beach.

Chapter 1 · Part I · Ground

The beach

The same sand, and only the water has changed. Why does it behave three ways?

When the falling tide leaves the sand firm, as the foot falls on it the sand whitens, or appears momentarily to dry round the foot.

Osborne Reynolds, On the dilatancy of media composed of rigid particles in contact, 1885

So far. The Prologue left a dam that had passed its calculations and failed in a night. Following the engineers who worked out why takes a handful of ideas about soil and water, and the cheapest place to collect them is a beach.

After this chapter you can

  • describe the three ways one sand behaves, and name the one thing that changed between them;
  • measure an angle of repose, and write any slope both as an angle and as a ratio, across to up;
  • say why a damp sand wall stands 30 cm tall and never 30 m.

This chapter adds a heap of sand at its angle of repose

2 figures · about 15 min to read

Walk down a beach at low tide, from the dunes to the sea, and the sand changes under you three times. Up by the dunes it is dry. Your foot sinks in, the sand pours back round your ankle, and when you kick it, it runs.

Halfway down, where the sea was an hour ago, the sand is dark and firm. It takes a crisp footprint, and as your weight comes down a pale ring spreads round your foot for a moment, as if the sand had dried where you stood. Then the colour comes back.

At the edge, where every wave lays down a fresh sheet of sand and soaks it, you can stand quite happily as long as you keep still. Wiggle your feet and the sand goes soft. You sink to the ankles, and it takes a tug to get out.

Three steps, one sand. The grains are near enough the same all the way down the beach. What changes is the water in the gaps between them. At the top there is almost none. In the middle every gap is still full, but the water is held up in the sand by the pull of its own surface, the way a sponge lifted out of the bath stays full, and the grains there are packed tight. At the edge the gaps are full too, and the grains lie loose.

1.1 Three sands

Take those three sands home in buckets. On the way the middle sand drains a little, as sand lifted out of water does, and arrives damp: air in most of its gaps, and water clinging only where the grains touch. Then the three keep their characters.

Dry sand pours. Tip it out and it spreads into a low heap whose sides settle at one slope, however carefully you pour.

Damp sand stands. Pack it into the bucket, turn it out, and you get a castle with walls that go straight up.

Loose wet sand flows. Where every gap is full of water and the grains were laid down loosely, the sand bears you while you keep still and turns to something like soup when you shake it.

Ask people what water does to sand and most of them say it makes it slippery, the way water makes a tiled floor slippery. Keep that answer in mind, because the castle is already evidence against it. Damp sand has water in it, and it stands steeper than either of the others. Whatever the water is doing in the castle, it is not greasing the grains. Chapter 4 settles the question with a block on a ramp. For now, notice only that more water does not mean weaker sand, or stronger: the soup holds the most water and the castle the next most, and they are the weakest and the strongest of the three.

The three sands also differ in a second way, which the beach hides. Sand that a wave has just dropped lies loosely packed, with wide gaps. Sand that has been walked on, rained on and settled for a tide lies densely packed, each grain nestled into the hollows of its neighbours. Wet sand that is saturated (every gap full of water, no air at all) can be either.

Below, one heap of sand is drawn four ways: dry, damp, sitting under still water, and with water draining out through its faces. A switch sets how tightly it was packed. Pick a state, then press Jiggle to shake the ground:

Notice first that the heap never gains or loses a grain. When the castle goes dry it spreads out, and the drawing keeps the area of its slice exactly the same, so a lower heap must be a wider one.

Then notice the two wet states. Sand that is wet all through sounds as if it ought to slump flatter than dry sand; wet sand, after all, is supposed to be slippery. Pick Under still water and the heap stands about as steep as dry sand, at about 34°. Still water hardly changes its slope. Now pick Water draining out. This is the state of a beach face at low tide, where the water that soaked in at high tide seeps back out through the sand, and the heap slumps to about 19°. The water is the same water in both. In one it sits still; in the other it moves, and the moving water drags the grains downhill as it leaves. Why that drag costs about fifteen degrees is a sum of a few lines, worked in Example 4.5.

Last, notice the jiggle. Dry sand and damp sand barely change. Wet sand packed loosely flows flat and swallows the flag, which is the soup at the water's edge. The same wet sand packed densely holds. So saturation alone does not turn sand to soup; it takes loose sand as well. That is the water's edge and the firm middle of the beach in one experiment, and it is also the first hint about the pale ring round your foot, which Chapter 5 explains.The pale ring was described in 1885 by Osborne Reynolds, the Manchester engineer whose name is on the Reynolds number of fluid flow, in the paper that coined the word dilatancy. The epigraph to this chapter is his description of it.

1.2 The angle of repose

The slope a dry heap settles at has a name, the angle of repose, and you can watch it form. Pour dry sand from a funnel onto a table. Grains land on the top and roll down the sides until the sides reach the steepest slope on which a grain can rest without rolling. Pour more and the heap grows, but its sides keep that one slope, because any extra steepness slides off in small avalanches. The slope of its sides is set by how hard the grains grip one another, not by how much sand you pour.Charles-Augustin Coulomb spent 1764 to 1772 building a fort on Martinique for the French army. In 1773 he read the Paris Academy a memoir on walls, arches and the earth behind them. In its worked examples, earth that, left to itself, settles at a slope of 45° is taken to have friction equal to the press on it: the slope of a loose heap measures the friction of its grains (Coulomb (1776), pp. 361–362).

Dry sands settle in the low-to-mid thirties of degrees. Angular, rough grains stand a little steeper than round, polished ones, and the lee faces of dunes, where wind-blown sand piles up until it avalanches, stand at about 32–34°.Dune faces, measured by laser scanning: Pelletier et al. (2015), who give 32–33° for the faces they surveyed in Brazil and quote earlier surveys at 32° settled and 34° just before an avalanche. Grain shape and friction set the dry angle: Hornbaker et al. (1997). The sand drawn in Fig. 1.1 settles at 34°, near the top of that range. Every slope in the figure follows from that one angle and the weights of sand and water.

The figure draws its heap as a slice. Picture the castle as a long wall of sand running away from you, like a sea wall, and the drawing as one slice cut straight across it. When the wall slumps, each slice keeps its own sand, so what stays the same is the area of the slice, which engineers call the section. Every drawing in this book is a section of something long, and every force and every flow is counted per metre of its length. A dam is drawn the same way.

That gives a sum you can do. The castle in the figure is a slice of known area. Poured dry, the same sand makes a triangular heap with 34° sides. How tall?

Example 1.1

Same sand, new shape

Given
The damp castle's section, as the figure draws it: 20.4 cm across and 29.2 cm tall, less two notches between the battlements, each 3.2 cm wide and 3.6 cm deep. Its area is A = 20.4 × 29.2 − 2 × 3.2 × 3.6 = 572.64 cm². Dry, the sand stands at β = 34°.
Find
The height and width of a dry heap holding the same sand.
The idea
The dry heap's section is a triangle with 34° sides. Write its area in terms of its height, set it equal to the castle's, and solve for the height (Fig. 1.1).
  1. half-base = H ÷ tan βeach side climbs H over a run of H/tan β, the definition of the slope's tangent
  2. A = ½ × (2H ÷ tan β) × H = H² ÷ tan βa triangle's area is half its base times its height
  3. H = √(A · tan β)rearranged for the height
  4. tan 34° = 0.67451from a calculator; the steps below keep enough digits to come out the same on yours
  5. A · tan β = 572.64 × 0.67451 = 386.25 cm²the same sand, now on a 34° slope
  6. H = √386.25 = 19.653 cmthe height of the dry heap
  7. half-base = 19.653 ÷ 0.67451 = 29.137 cm, so the base is 58.27 cmback to step 1 with the height known

The dry heap stands 19.7 cm tall on a base 58.3 cm wide: 0.67 times the castle's height and 2.9 times its width.

Check. Put the area back together: ½ × 58.27 × 19.653 = 572.6 cm², the castle's area. And the limits behave: a gentler slope (smaller tan β) gives a lower, wider heap, and a slope near vertical gives a tall thin one, more like the castle.

What it means. The castle lost no sand when it dried; it lost the grip that held its walls up, and the same sand then needed about three times the ground. Soil that cannot hold a steep face has to be laid out wide. Most of the width of an earth dam is the price of its slopes.

You can measure an angle of repose at home with a funnel, a ruler and a cup of dry sand, sugar or rice. Pour a heap, measure its height and the width of its base, and the tangent of the angle is the height divided by half the base. The questions at the end of the chapter ask you to try.

1.3 A slope is a number

Angles are awkward on a building site. Nobody holds a protractor against a hillside of fill. Engineers write a slope as a ratio instead, how far across for each unit up, and they put the across first: a slope of 2H:1V (two across for every one up) climbs one metre for every two metres of ground it covers. This book writes it 2H:1V, or 2:1 for short. The bigger the first number, the flatter the slope.Road signs turn the same ratio upside down and give it as a percentage, rise over run: a 10% hill climbs 1 m for every 10 m across, which this book would write 10:1.

The ratio and the angle are tied by one piece of trigonometry. The tangent of a slope's angle β is the rise over the run, so for a slope written n:1, tan β = 1 ÷ n. A dam drawn at 2:1 and a heap at 34° can then be compared on the same footing:

Example 1.2

A slope as a number

Given
A dam face at 2:1. The dry heap's 34° and the draining face's 19.0° from Fig. 1.1.
Find
The angle of the 2:1 face, and the two heap slopes written as ratios.
The idea
tan β = rise ÷ run = 1 ÷ n, which works in both directions.
  1. tan β = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5one up for every two across
  2. β = arctan 0.5 = 26.6°the angle whose tangent is 0.5
  3. n = 1 ÷ tan 34° = 1 ÷ 0.6745 = 1.48across for one up, for the dry heap
  4. n = 1 ÷ tan 19.0° = 1 ÷ 0.344 = 2.9the same for the face with water seeping out

A 2:1 face slopes at 26.6°. The dry heap stands at 1.48:1, and the draining face at 2.9:1.

Check. A 1:1 slope is 45°, as steep as it is wide, and a 3:1 slope is arctan ⅓ = 18.4°. A 2:1 slope must lie between them, and 26.6° does.

What it means. A 2:1 face built of this beach's sand would stand dry, with room to spare, and would slump wherever water seeped out of it. Keeping water from coming out of the face of a dam, or catching it safely where it does, is much of Part III of this book.

Check yourself A road sign warns of a 10% hill. Write the slope as a ratio, and as an angle.

10:1, ten across for each one up. tan β = 0.1, so β = 5.7°: a hill that feels steep in a car is far flatter than any heap of sand.

1.4 Why a castle stays small

Look again at the close-up in Fig. 1.1 with the sand set to Damp. The water does not fill the gaps. It gathers in small rings where one grain touches the next, and the surface of each ring is curved and pulled tight, like the skin on a drop hanging from a tap. That skin pulls the two grains together. Every grain has several, and a handful of sand holds a great many grains, so together the rings give damp sand a grip that dry sand lacks, and that grip holds a wall up where dry grains would roll away.It takes remarkably little liquid. Films of oil less than 50 nanometres thick on plastic beads about 0.8 mm across raised the steepest slope a heap would hold sharply (Hornbaker et al. (1997)). Columns of beach sand were strongest with about 1% water by volume, and the tallest column that would stand grew as its base radius to the power ⅔ (Pakpour et al. (2012)).

But the grip is small, and it does not grow as the castle does. Each ring pulls with the same tiny force however much sand sits above it. The weight that the bottom of a wall must carry grows with every centimetre of height. A wall 30 cm tall puts a hundred times less weight on each square metre of its base than a wall 30 m tall of the same sand, and somewhere between the two the weight wins. Sand sculptors do build castles several metres high, but they build them on broad bases that lean on their own width.Sandcastles "of several meters high", and the rule that the safe height depends on the width of the base: Pakpour et al. (2012). Chapter 5 puts a number on the grip.

There is a second reason a dam engineer never counts on it. The rings exist only while the sand is damp. A week of rain fills the gaps, the rings vanish, and the grip goes with them; a drought dries them out and does the same. A castle slumps as the rising tide soaks it for the same reason, before the waves reach it. Dams are designed as if the grip were not there.

Check yourself Of the three beach sands, which holds the most water, and which stands steepest?

The soup at the water's edge holds the most, and it stands at nothing at all once shaken. The damp castle holds a little and stands vertical. Water can make sand stronger or weaker; what matters is where the water sits and what it is doing.

1.5 The beach inside a dam

Now scale the heap up to a hill, and lean a lake against one side of it. That is an earth dam. The water in the reservoir soaks into the soil and creeps slowly through it, so inside the dam there is a boundary between soil that is full of water and soil above it that is not. Engineers call that boundary the phreatic surface: the water line inside the dam. It starts at the reservoir level on the upstream face, the side the water comes from, and falls as it crosses toward the downstream face, the side the water is trying to reach. (Every section in this book is drawn with the water on the left, so it flows left to right.) Here is a dam with the three beach sands mapped onto it:

Notice where the water comes out. At the foot of the downstream face, the soil is in the state that slumped the heap in Fig. 1.1 from 34° to 19°, and the face there is 2:1, 26.6°. A dam of beach sand would crumble at its foot, grain by grain, and the slope above would follow. Real dams are built of better-chosen soils, and a well-designed one catches the water in drains and filters inside the dam before it can reach the face, and how they do it is the work of Chapters 9 and 11. But the danger is the beach's, at the scale of a hill.

Notice too that the upstream face, under the reservoir, is the heap under still water: soaked, and standing about as steep as it would dry. The water there is not quite still, since it is soaking slowly into the dam, and Chapter 3 follows where it goes. The damp soil above the water line has the castle's grip, and it is the grip a designer leaves out. Everything below the line is held up by grains pressing on grains, with water filling every gap between them.

1.6 One sentence for the whole book

All of this can be said in one sentence. It is printed on the title page, and every chapter after this one comes back to it:

Soil holds only as well as its grains press on one another, and the water between them can take that press away.

You can't prove it yet, and you shouldn't believe it yet. The castle seems to contradict it: there the water makes the grains press harder. By the end of Chapter 4 you will be able to prove it, castle included, with a block on a ramp and a column of soil. The sentence does not explain every way a dam can fail. Floods that pour over the top are a different story, told in Chapter 6. But it explains most of what this book asks of soil.

To get there you need two facts about water first. Its pressure grows with depth, which is Chapter 2. And it moves through the ground, slowly or very slowly depending on the ground, which is Chapter 3. Chapter 4 puts them together, and Chapter 5 comes back to this beach for the soup and the pale ring round your foot.

What to remember

  • One sand pours, stands or flows, and only the water between its grains changed.
  • Dry sand stands at its angle of repose, 34° here. Still water barely changes that; water seeping out of a face drags the grains downhill and the face slumps to about 19°.
  • Saturated sand turns to soup when shaken only if it is loosely packed.
  • A slope is written across to up, n:1, with tan β = 1 ÷ n; 2:1 is 26.6°.
  • Damp sand's grip is small and does not grow with height, so castles stay small and dams are designed without it.

It is also reprinted in the second volume of Reynolds's collected Papers on Mechanical and Physical Subjects (1901), free online.

A damp wall of sand stands 30 cm, and nothing you do makes it stand 30 m. A dam has to stand with a lake leaning on it. How hard does a lake lean, and does a bigger lake lean harder?

2

Chapter 2 · Part I · Ground

Depth, not size

Two dams hold water 50 m deep, one a long lake and one a narrow slot. Which has to be stronger?

So far. On the beach one sand behaved three ways, and only the water had changed. To say why, we need two facts about water first. This chapter is the first of them: how hard still water presses, and on what. Chapter 3 adds the second, what happens when it moves.

After this chapter you can

  • work out the water pressure at any depth, and the push of a reservoir on each metre of a dam;
  • say where that push acts, and why doubling the depth makes it four times bigger and its tipping effect eight times bigger;
  • explain why a concrete dam is a triangle, and why water on an embankment's sloping face presses it down harder than it pushes it sideways.

This chapter adds water against the left face, with the pressure triangle

4 figures · about 20 min to read · Film 2.1, 3 min 11 s

Stand on the crest of a big dam on a still day and look upstream. The reservoir runs back between the hills further than you can see, millions of tonnes of water, and it is hard not to feel all of it leaning on the wall under your feet. Somebody had to decide how strong to make that wall, so the feeling is worth testing. Make a guess before you read on:

Two dams each hold back water 50 m deep. One holds a lake 10 km long. The other holds a slot of water only 2 m wide, with solid rock behind it. Which dam has to be stronger?

The lake is the natural guess, and it is wrong. Water pressure depends only on how far below the surface you are. Fifty metres down it is the same in a slot as in an ocean, so the two dams feel exactly the same push. The big lake is far heavier, but its weight rests on the lake bed: cut the lake into upright columns, like slices of a cake still in its tin, and each column stands on the bed and presses straight down on it. Only the water touching the dam pushes on the dam. The size of a lake decides how much water escapes if the dam breaks. The depth decides the load on the dam.

To decide, start with what sets how hard water presses on anything at all. You have felt it. Swim down to the bottom of a deep pool and, a few metres down, your ears start to hurt. The water above you has weight, and the deeper you go, the more of it there is. That weight is where water pressure comes from. The rest of this chapter turns it into a number, and then into the push on a dam.

2.1 A tonne on every square metre

Picture a column of water one metre tall standing on one square metre of a pool floor. It holds one cubic metre of water, which is a tonne. On Earth a tonne weighs 9.81 kilonewtons (kN),Mass and weight are different things. A tonne is 1,000 kg of stuff; gravity pulls on it with 9.81 kN, and that pull is its weight. Turned round, a kilonewton is the weight of about 102 kg. This book uses tonnes for how much water there is and kilonewtons for how hard it pushes. so the floor under that column carries 9.81 kN on its square metre. A force of one kilonewton on each square metre is one kilopascal (kPa), the unit of pressure in this book. Stack a second metre of water on top and the floor carries two tonnes, 19.62 kPa. Every metre of depth adds the weight of one more tonne on every square metre:

p = ρ · g · h ≈ 9.81 kPa × depth in metres(2.1)

p pressure (kPa) · ρ density of water, 1,000 kg/m³ · g gravity, 9.81 m/s² · h depth below the water surface (m). With these units 1,000 × 9.81 × h comes out in pascals, newtons on each square metre; divide by 1,000 for kPa.

Notice what the rule leaves out. It names the depth and nothing else: not the width of the lake, not its length, not how much water lies beyond. Engineers call the pressure of still water hydrostatic, and in a moment we will see that it is also blind to direction.

Ten metres of water presses with about 98 kPa, roughly the pressure of the whole atmosphere above us.Galileo recorded that a suction pump could lift water no higher than about 18 braccia (Museo Galileo). A Florentine braccio, an arm's length, was a little under 60 cm (the museum gives two braccia as about 115 cm), so that is a little over 10 m; the museum's page rounds it to 11 m. In a letter of 11 June 1644 to Michelangelo Ricci, Evangelista Torricelli explained why: the air presses on the water outside the pipe, and that press can hold up a column only so tall. He showed it with mercury, which stood 1¼ braccia high, about three quarters of a metre; the museum's page rounds it to 70 cm (Museo Galileo). The standard atmosphere, 101.325 kPa, balances 10.3 m of water, or 76 cm of mercury, which is 13.6 times as dense. That raises a fair question. The air presses on the lake's surface too, so shouldn't every reading include it? A sensor that counted the air would read 396 kPa thirty metres down, not 294.Sea-level air: 101.325 kPa and 1.225 kg/m³, U.S. Standard Atmosphere (1976). But the air presses as hard on the dam's downstream face, on the rock, on everything, and equal pushes from two sides cancel. So engineers leave it out and measure pressure above the air's, as a tyre gauge does. That is gauge pressure, and this book uses it throughout: the surface of still water is at zero.

Check yourself A lake high in the mountains has thinner air above it than a lake at sea level. Does a gauge 30 m down read less there?

No. It reads 294.3 kPa in both, because a gauge measures the press of the water above the air's. The thinner air lowers the pressure on the surface and on the gauge's back alike.

Below, a sensor hangs on a cable in front of a concrete dam. Drag it up and down, or use the Sensor depth slider; the Water depth slider changes the depth of the water itself:

Notice that the sensor's reading depends on how far it hangs below the surface and on nothing else. Leave it 30 m down and make the water deeper: the reading stays at 294 kPa, though there is now more water beneath it and more water behind it. Notice too that the arrows on the face are the same pressures drawn as arrows, and they grow evenly, from nothing at the surface to the most at the foot.

Example 2.1

The sensor 30 m down

Given
A sensor 30 m below the surface of a reservoir 50 m deep. Water weighs 9.81 kN per cubic metre.
Find
The pressure on the sensor, in kPa and as tonnes on each square metre.
The idea
The pressure is the weight of the column of water standing on one square metre at the sensor's depth (Eq. 2.1).
  1. Column above 1 m²: 30 m × 1 m² × 1 t/m³ = 30 ta tonne for every metre of depth
  2. Its weight: 30 × 9.81 = 294.3 kNeach tonne weighs 9.81 kN
  3. p = 294.3 kN ÷ 1 m² = 294.3 kPaa kilonewton on each square metre is a kilopascal

The sensor feels 294.3 kPa, the weight of 30 tonnes on every square metre. The 20 m of water below it play no part.

Check. Ten metres adds about 98.1 kPa, so thirty metres should add three times that: 3 × 98.1 = 294.3.

What it means. A pressure in still water is a property of one number, the depth. A gauge lowered to the foot of the lake dam and one lowered to the foot of the slot dam would read the same.

2.2 Sideways too

The column explains why a pool floor feels the water above it. It doesn't yet explain your ears, which face sideways, or a dam, which stands beside the water and not under it. A stack of bricks presses down on the floor and hardly at all on the walls beside it, because each brick holds its shape. Water can't. A liquid is a material that flows when anything tries to change its shape, however gently.

So suppose that at some point in still water the push from above were harder than the push from the sides. The water there would be squeezed out sideways, the way toothpaste leaves a tube, and it would start to flow. Still water doesn't flow; that is what still means. Therefore at any point in still water the push is the same in every direction: down, up, sideways and slantwise.A tighter version of the argument. Take a tiny wedge of still water with one face level, one upright and one sloping. The pushes on its three faces must balance its weight. Now shrink the wedge: the pushes shrink with the faces' areas, the weight much faster, with its volume. In the limit the weight drops out, and the pushes balance only if the pressure on all three faces is the same, whatever the slope. At the foot of a 50 m dam the water presses as hard on the concrete beside it as on the rock beneath it, 490.5 kPa each way.

That settles the opening question, and in 1586 the Flemish engineer Simon Stevin found a way to see it without any algebra.Stevin published it in De Beghinselen des Waterwichts (Stevin (1586)), the first systematic treatise on hydrostatics since Archimedes. He explained the paradox, as in the figure, by imagining parts of the water set solid (Minnaert (1976)). Take the lake, at rest. Imagine that all of it except a slot 2 m wide against the dam sets solid, like jelly, without changing its weight or its shape. Nothing in the lake was moving before, and setting it solid gives nothing a reason to start, so every pressure stays what it was, including every pressure on the dam. But the dam now holds back a slot of liquid water 2 m wide with a solid block behind it. The slot must push exactly as hard as the lake did. The figure below draws the argument:

Notice that the two triangles of arrows are identical. The ten kilometres of lake behind the slot carry their own weight down into the lake bed and leave the dam alone.

Check yourself One diver is at the bottom of a flooded mine shaft 1 m across and 10 m deep. Another is at the bottom of a swimming pool 10 m deep. Whose ears hurt more?

They hurt the same. Both are 10 m down and both feel 98.1 kPa. The narrow shaft matters as little as the narrow slot.

2.3 The push on a whole dam

A sensor gives the pressure at one point. A dam has to hold the pressure over its whole face, and that pressure changes all the way down. Draw it as Fig. 2.1 does, as arrows: at the surface the arrow has no length, and it grows by 9.81 kPa for every metre down to its longest at the foot. Together the arrows fill a triangle, and the push on each metre length of dam is the area of that triangle: half its height times its width at the bottom, ½ × H × (9.81 × H). An area can be a push because of what its two sides measure. Cut one metre length of the face into strips a metre tall: each strip is one square metre, so the push on it in kilonewtons is the length of its arrow in kilopascals. Adding the strips adds up the arrows, and kilopascals times metres of height come out as kilonewtons on each metre of dam. The depth appears twice, once as the height of the wet face and once in the pressure at its foot. So the push grows with the square of the depth:

F = ½ · ρ · g · H²(2.2)

F push of the water on each metre length of dam (kN per m) · H depth of water at the dam (m)

Make the water twice as deep and the triangle is twice as tall and twice as wide at the bottom, so four copies of the first triangle fit inside it. A dam holding 100 m of water takes four times the push of one holding 50 m.

2.4 Where the push acts

A push on a dam does two things. It tries to slide the dam downstream, and it tries to tip it over about its toe, the downstream foot (Plate 0), the way you tip a bookcase by pushing near its top. For tipping, where the push acts matters as much as how big it is. Most of the triangle sits low down: the bottom third of the face carries 56% of the push.Why 56%: the push above any level grows with the square of its depth, so the top two thirds of the face carry (⅔)² = 4/9 of the whole, and the bottom third the other 5/9. Add up all the arrows and the whole push acts as though it were gathered at one point, the centre of the triangle. A triangle's area balances a third of the way in from its wide side, and the wide side of the pressure triangle is at the bottom, so the push acts H/3 up from the base. Its tipping effect about the toe, the moment, is the push times its lever arm, the distance from the pivot to the line the push acts along. For a sideways push that distance is its height above the base, H/3, wherever on the base the pivot is:

M = F · H/3 = ρ · g · H³ / 6(2.3)

M tipping moment about the toe, per metre length of dam (kN·m per m, or MN·m per m; 1 MN·m is 1,000 kN·m)

Double the depth and the push grows four times while the height it acts at doubles, so the tipping effect grows eight times. Here are all three numbers for the dams of the opening question:

Example 2.2

The push on a 50 m dam, and where it acts

Given
Still water H = 50 m deep against an upright face; each metre of depth adds 9.81 kPa.
Find
The pressure at the foot of the face; the push on each metre of dam, in kilonewtons and as tonnes; the height it acts at; its tipping moment about the toe.
The idea
The push is the area of the pressure triangle (Eq. 2.2) and acts at its centre, a third of the way up (Eq. 2.3).
  1. p at the foot = 9.81 × 50 = 490.5 kPathe width of the triangle at its base
  2. F = ½ × 490.5 × 50 = 12,262.5 kN per metrehalf the base times the height of the triangle
  3. 12,262.5 ÷ 9.81 = 1,250 tthe push, as the weight of so many tonnes
  4. Height of the push: 50 ÷ 3 = 16.67 m above the basethe triangle's centre, a third of the way up from its wide side
  5. M = 12,262.5 × 16.67 = 204.4 MN·m per metrepush times its lever arm; 1 MN·m is 1,000 kN·m
  6. At H = 100 m: F = 49,050 kN, M = 1,635 MN·mthe same steps with the depth doubled

Each metre of a 50 m dam carries a push as heavy as 1,250 tonnes, acting 16.7 m up. At 100 m the push is 4 times as big and the tipping moment 8 times.

Check. Water weighs a tonne per cubic metre, so for water the push in tonnes is ½ × H × H: ½ × 50 × 50 = 1,250, which is what the figure's readout says.

What it means. The height of the water is what a dam pays for. Each extra metre of depth costs more than the one before.

Now the slot, which looked as though it could never push that hard:

Example 2.3

A hundred tonnes that push like 1,250

Given
The slot of the opening question: water 2 m wide and 50 m deep, between a dam and solid rock. Water: a tonne per cubic metre.
Find
The weight of the water in the slot, per metre length of dam, and the push it puts on the dam.
The idea
The water's weight goes down into the slot's floor; its push on the dam depends only on the depth.
  1. Water per metre of dam: 2 m × 50 m × 1 m = 100 m³, so 100 ta tonne per cubic metre
  2. Push on the dam: 12,262.5 kN, as heavy as 1,250 tthe same as the lake's, from Example 2.2
  3. 1,250 ÷ 100 = 12.5push over the water's own weight

100 tonnes of water push on the dam with the weight of 1,250 tonnes, 12.5 times their own weight.

Check. Where can a sideways push bigger than the water's weight come from? Compare the areas the water presses on. Each metre of the slot's floor is 2 m² and carries the 100 tonnes: 50 tonnes on each square metre, the pressure at 50 m. Each metre of the dam's face is 50 m² and carries on average half that pressure, 25 tonnes on each square metre, so 50 × 25 = 1,250 tonnes. The same pressure acts on a big face and a small floor. Nothing moves, because the rock pushes back on the water as hard as the dam does, from the other side.

What it means. Pressure is not weight. A thin layer of water can carry an enormous push as long as it is deep, which is why a narrow crack under a dam, filled from the reservoir, matters so much in Chapter 7.

Check yourself A reservoir is raised from 50 m to 60 m deep. Does the tipping moment on the dam grow by more or less than the push?

By more. The push grows by (60/50)² = 1.44 times, the moment by (60/50)³ = 1.73 times.

2.5 Why a concrete dam is a triangle

Look at a concrete dam from the side and it is close to a triangle, narrow at the top and wide at the foot. One could assume the reason is that the pressure is greatest at the bottom, so the wall needs to be thickest there. That explains a thick foot, but not a thin top: a wall as thick as its foot all the way up would hold too. The full reason is about every level at once.

Cut the dam in your mind along a level line, z metres below the water's surface. Everything above the cut has to hold against the water above the cut, or it would slide or tip off along that line; so engineers check a concrete dam at levels all the way up, not only at its base. What holds it is its weight, pressing down on the concrete below (Chapter 4 shows how a press becomes a grip). The push of the water above the cut grows with z². For a triangle, the width at depth z is proportional to z, so the area above the cut, half its width times its height, grows with z² as well. Push and weight grow in step. The figure shows three cuts:

Notice that the green bar stays the same multiple of the red one at all three cuts, though both grow ninefold between the top cut and the bottom. Here is the arithmetic for any level:

Example 2.4

Why the triangle keeps step

Given
A concrete section with an upright upstream face, 0.8z wide at depth z, water to its top. Concrete weighs 23.5 kN/m³, water 9.81 kN/m³.
Find
At any depth z: the weight of concrete above that level, the push of water above it, and how they compare, for sliding and for tipping.
The idea
Both are areas of triangles whose sides grow with z, so both grow with z². Tipping adds one more factor of z to each, through the lever arms.
  1. Weight above z: ½ × 0.8z × z × 23.5 = 9.40 z² kNarea of the triangle above the cut, times concrete's unit weight
  2. Push above z: ½ × 9.81 × z² = 4.905 z² kNEq. 2.2 with the depth to the cut
  3. Weight ÷ push = 9.40 ÷ 4.905 = 1.92z² cancels: the same at every level
  4. Holding moment: 9.40z² × ⅔ × 0.8z = 5.013 z³a triangle balances a third of the way across from its tallest side; here that is the upright face, so the weight acts two thirds of the width from the toe
  5. Tipping moment: 4.905z² × z/3 = 1.635 z³the push acts a third of the way up, Eq. 2.3
  6. Holding ÷ tipping = 5.013 ÷ 1.635 = 3.07z³ cancels too

Above every level of the triangle the concrete weighs 1.92 times the push, and holds 3.07 times the tipping moment.

Check. At z = 30 m: weight 8,460 kN, push 4,414.5 kN, and 8,460 ÷ 4,414.5 = 1.92. At z = 45 m: 19,035 ÷ 9,932.6 = 1.92.

What it means. A triangle gives every level the same margin, so no level is weaker than the rest and none carries concrete it does not need. What this leaves out, water seeping under the dam and pushing it up, is the subject of Chapter 7.

To see what the shape buys, compare a wall with straight sides that uses the same concrete. Down to 50 m the triangle holds 1,000 m³ of concrete for every metre of dam, so the straight wall is 20 m thick. Its weight above a cut grows only in proportion to the depth, while the push grows with the depth squared. Ten metres down it weighs 9.6 times the push above, far more than it needs. At the foot its weight is the same 1.92 times the push as the triangle's, but against tipping it holds only 1.15 times the moment where the triangle holds 3.07, because its weight sits closer to the downstream toe. The triangle puts its concrete where the push is.

Dams that hold back their water by their own weight in this way are called gravity dams, and real ones are close to this shape. Revelstoke Dam on the Columbia River is 175 m high and 126 m thick at its base,Height: BC Hydro (2013). Base thickness, 126 m, and 9 m at the crest: BC Hydro (2016). a base 0.72 times its height, a little slimmer than the 0.8 used here. BC Hydro describes it as relying on its massive weight and the friction that weight produces to hold back the reservoir.

The first three minutes of the film Depth, not size retell the chapter up to this point, in pictures:

2.6 Water on a sloping face

Most of the dams in the rest of this book are embankments, heaps of earth and rock whose upstream face leans back at a gentle slope. The still-water argument holds on any face, at any angle: the water presses equally in every direction, so on a surface it presses straight at it, at right angles. On a sloping face the arrows tilt. They point down into the slope as well as across it. Here is a 24 m embankment whose upstream face slopes at 2H:1V (two across for every one up, as in Example 1.2), holding water 20.4 m deep, the dam of the seepage lab in Fig. 10.3:

Notice that you can split the push in two. Across, it is exactly the push on an upright wall of the same depth, because a sideways push only counts the face's height. Down, it is the weight of the wedge of water standing on the face.

Example 2.5

Water pressing an embankment down

Given
An upstream face at 2:1 holding still water H = 20.4 m deep; water weighs 9.81 kN/m³.
Find
The push of the water on each metre length of dam, across and down, and the whole push.
The idea
Across: the pressure triangle on the face's height, Eq. 2.2. Down: the weight of the water standing on the face.
  1. Run of the wet face: 2 × 20.4 = 40.8 mtwo across for every one up
  2. Across: ½ × 9.81 × 20.4² = 2,041.3 kNas on an upright wall 20.4 m tall
  3. Water on the face: ½ × 40.8 × 20.4 = 416.16 m³the hatched wedge, per metre of dam
  4. Down: 416.16 × 9.81 = 4,082.5 kNthe wedge's weight, which the face holds up
  5. Whole push: √(2,041.3² + 4,082.5²) = 4,564 kNthe two parts at right angles, Pythagoras

The water presses each metre of the embankment down with 4,083 kN and across with 2,041 kN: twice as hard down as across.

Check. Every arrow is at right angles to the face, so the whole push must be too. Its angle from the vertical has a tangent of 2,041 ÷ 4,083 = 0.50, which is 26.6°, the same as the face's angle from the horizontal, 26.6°. At the other extreme, an upright face has no water standing on it and the downward part vanishes, as on the concrete dam.

What it means. On an embankment the reservoir mostly presses the dam onto its foundation, which helps it grip. The picture is exact for a watertight face, such as a concrete skin on rockfill; in an earth dam the water also soaks into the face, and Chapter 10 follows it inside. Chapter 12 shows what happens when the reservoir is let down fast: the help on the face goes, while the water inside the dam stays.

2.7 Water in the ground has pressure too

Dig a hole in the sand near the sea and it fills with water from below. The water in the hole settles at a level, and below that level every gap between the grains is full of water. That level is the water table.

The water in those gaps is joined up from gap to gap, like the water in a soaked sponge, so while it is still it obeys the same rule as the water in a lake. A metre below the water table it presses at 9.81 kPa, ten metres down at 98.1 kPa, and at every point it presses equally in every direction, on every grain around the gap. The pressure of the water in the gaps between grains is called pore pressure, written u. It is the water half of this book's one sentence: Chapter 4 shows how it takes away the press of grain on grain that gives soil its strength.

The important word there is still. The water in a lake is still. The water in the ground under a dam almost never is: it creeps through the gaps from the reservoir toward the far side of the dam, and moving water does not keep to the rule of this chapter.

What to remember

  • Still water presses equally in every direction, and how hard depends only on the depth: 9.81 kPa for every metre. The size of the lake does not enter.
  • The push on each metre of dam is the area of the pressure triangle, ½·ρ·g·H², acting a third of the way up. Double the depth and the push grows four times, its tipping effect eight.
  • A gravity dam is a triangle because the weight above any level then grows with the square of the depth, as the push does, so every level is equally safe.
  • On a sloping face the water presses at right angles to the slope; on an embankment it presses the dam down harder than it pushes it across.
  • Water in the gaps of soaked ground follows the same rule while it is still. That pore pressure carries part of the load the grains would otherwise carry between them, so they press on one another less; Chapter 4 makes this exact as σ′ = σ − u.

Questions

  1. 2.1

    A reservoir is raised from 40 m deep to 60 m. By what factor does the push on each metre of its dam grow?

    Hint

    The push grows with the depth squared, so compare 60² with 40².

    Answer

  2. 2.2

    Predict the push on each metre of dam when the water is 70 m deep, then set the figure and check. How does it compare with the push at 50 m?

    Hint

    70² is close to 2 × 50².

    Answer

  3. 2.3

    Your ears hurt 3 m down in a pool, but not after a 30 m ride up a lift in a tall building. Why?

    Hint

    Both are the same rule, Eq. 2.1, with a different fluid. A cubic metre of sea-level air has a mass of about 1.2 kg; a cubic metre of water, 1,000 kg.

    Answer

  4. 2.4

    Where does the push on a dam holding 50 m of water act, and by what factor does its tipping moment grow if the water is twice as deep?

    Hint

    The push acts at the centre of the pressure triangle; the moment is push times height.

    Answer

  5. 2.5

    Is the water on an embankment's sloping upstream face a danger or a help to the dam's stability?

    Hint

    Split its push into the part across and the part down. What does each do?

    Answer

  6. 2.6

    Revelstoke Dam is 175 m high and 126 m thick at its base. Suppose water stood against it right to the top (a real reservoir is kept a little below the crest). What would the pressure be at its foot, and the push on each metre of dam? How does its base compare with the triangle of Example 2.4?

    Hint

    Use Eq. 2.1 and Eq. 2.2 with H = 175 m; in tonnes, the push is ½ × H².

Free from the Bureau of Reclamation.

All of this assumed the water was still. In a lake it is. In the ground under a dam it almost never is: it creeps through the gaps between the grains, and as it moves, its pressure stops following this chapter's neat rule. Which way does it go, and what makes it move?
