3

Chapter 3 · Part I · Ground

Which way the water goes

The sea is lower than the beach. What pushes the water out of the sand, and why does it take hours?

Thus, it appears that for an identical sand, it can be assumed that the volume discharged is (directly) proportional to the head and inversely proportional to the thickness of the sand layer that the water passes through.

Henry Darcy, Les fontaines publiques de la ville de Dijon, 1856, in English as quoted by Simmons

So far. Still water presses harder the deeper you go, 9.81 kPa for every metre, and Chapter 2 turned that into the push on a dam. Water in the ground is rarely still. Under a dam it creeps through the gaps between the grains. This chapter asks which way it goes, how fast, and what it does to the grains on the way.

After this chapter you can

  • find the total head at a point from a piezometer reading, and say which way the water there will flow;
  • use Darcy's law to estimate a flow, and how long a drop of water takes to cross a layer of soil;
  • explain why a thin layer of clay takes almost the whole drop in head, and how hard moving water pushes on the grains it passes.

This chapter adds the phreatic line through the heap and one standpipe (the straw)

3 figures · about 20 min to read

Go back to the beach an hour or two after high tide, while the sea is still going out. Near the bottom of the beach, where the sand flattens toward the water, it is dark and shining, and thin streams of water run out of it and braid their way down the last few metres to the sea. They keep running for hours. Nothing is raining on the beach and nobody is squeezing it, yet the water keeps coming.

It comes out because the beach is full of it. At high tide the sea soaked into the sand and filled the gaps between the grains. As the tide falls, the water inside the sand falls too, but far more slowly, and it is left standing higher inside the beach than the sea outside. Where that buried water surface meets the sloping sand, it leaks out, and the streams are the leak.On a falling tide the water table in a beach comes apart from the sea and leaks out over a seepage face: Turner (1993), who tracked it on a beach in North Queensland.

That leaves two questions, and they are the questions of this chapter. What pushes the water out of the sand, when the sea it came from has gone? And why does it take hours?

Most people say water flows from high pressure to low pressure, the way air rushes out of a punctured tyre. It sounds right for the beach. But the rule fails in the simplest place there is. In a still lake the water at the bottom is at a far higher pressure than the water at the top: Example 2.1 found 294.3 kPa thirty metres down, and zero at the surface. If water flowed from high pressure to low, the deep water would rise toward the surface and the lake would stir itself, forever. It lies still. So pressure alone does not decide where water goes. Whatever does decide it must be the same at every point of a still lake.

3.1 Head

To tell which way the water will go, engineers use a simple measure. Imagine pushing a clear straw down into wet ground and watching how high the water climbs inside it. The level the water reaches, measured from some fixed height such as sea level, is the total head at the bottom of the straw. Water in the ground creeps through the gaps between the grains, from where its head is high to where it is low.

The level in the straw adds two things. The first is how high the bottom of the straw is, its elevation head, z, measured from the fixed level, which is called the datum. The second is how far the water pressure at the bottom of the straw can push water up it, its pressure head. A pressure u holds up a column of water u ÷ γw tall, where γw = 9.81 kN/m³ is the weight of a cubic metre of water: one metre of column for every 9.81 kPa. Together:

h = z + u / γw(3.1)

h total head (m) · z elevation head, the height of the point above the datum (m) · u water pressure at the point (kPa) · γw unit weight of water, 9.81 kN/m³. The datum can be any level you like, as long as you keep it: only differences in head move water.

Now the still lake makes sense. Go one metre deeper and you lose a metre of elevation head, but the pressure grows by 9.81 kPa, which is exactly one more metre of pressure head. The two trade evenly, so the total head is the same everywhere in still water, and with no difference in head nothing flows. The figure puts straws into a still lake, and then into the beach as the tide goes out:

Notice that in panel A the three straws reach very different depths, and the water in all of them stops at exactly the lake's surface. The pressures at their tips differ, but the heads don't, and nothing moves. In panel B the straws step down: the head inside the beach is highest far from the sea and lowest where the water comes out. That difference in head is what pushes the water out of the sand. The beach's water is still higher than the sea, and so it runs downhill to it, through the sand.

Two consequences surprise people. Groundwater can flow uphill, as long as it is heading toward lower head; a spring that bubbles up out of a hillside is water rising toward a point of lower head. And water can flow from low pressure to high. Follow a drop in panel B from close under the water table down and along through the sand: it goes deeper, into higher pressure, and all the while toward lower head. The rule, every time, is head.

Check yourself The middle straw in panel A has its tip 4 m into the lake bed, 12 m below the lake's surface. What water pressure does the tip feel, and why does the water in the straw stop at the lake's level?

9.81 × 12 = 117.7 kPa, a pressure head of 12 m. The tip is 8 m above the datum, so its head is 20 m, the same as the lake's surface: a straw shows the head, and in still water that is the surface everywhere.

3.2 The straws are real

Engineers sink thin pipes into dams and the ground beneath them and measure the water level inside. They are called piezometers, and reading them, along with measuring the water that seeps out, is one of the main ways engineers know what the water inside a dam is doing.A real straw takes time to fill. Water has to flow in through the ground to raise the level, and in tight ground that can be slow. Juul Hvorslev worked out the delay in 1951. For one fine-grained soil, his estimates ran from 193 days for a 2-inch cased boring with soil in its foot to 0.4 seconds for a small pressure cell set in a pocket of sand, which reads the pressure directly without waiting for a column to fill.Hvorslev (1951), his figure 14 and p. 37. Each one gives the head at a single point, a pinprick of knowledge inside a mountain of earth, so a dam carries many of them and engineers read them for as long as it stands.

Inside an earth dam they show what panel B shows. The water line in Fig. 1.2 is a water table like the beach's: it starts at the reservoir's level on the upstream face and falls as it crosses the dam. A piezometer near the upstream face stands high, one near the downstream face stands low, and the water soaking into the dam runs between them, losing head as it goes. Chapter 10 maps that water through a whole dam. For a first look in three dimensions, the Dams Academy lesson Seepage in 3D lets you colour a model dam by total head and then by pressure head; only the first picture tells you where the water goes.

3.3 Some ground is a sieve, some is a wall

Head says which way the water goes. How fast it goes depends on the ground, and above all on the size of the gaps. Gravel has gaps you can see. Clay is made of flat flakes hundreds to thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand, and the gaps between them are tiny and twisting. The same difference in head that sends water racing through gravel barely moves it through clay. To say how much, engineers need a number for the ground, and that number comes from an experiment run in a hospital courtyard in Dijon.

3.4 Darcy's law

In 1855 and 1856 Henry Darcy, the engineer who had built the water supply of Dijon in France some fifteen years before, ran water down through sand packed in an upright column 2.5 m tall and measured how much came out at the bottom.Darcy's water reached Dijon's reservoir at the Porte Guillaume on 6 September 1840, and he waived the fees the town owed him for it. The sand experiments, 35 of them, were run with the engineer Charles Ritter, using sand from the river Saône, and the mercury in their gauge shook with the water hammer of the street fountains at the hospital: Darcy's own water supply, rattling his own experiment. He published them in 1856 as Note D, an appendix to his book on the fountains of Dijon (Darcy (1856); the story is told by Simmons (2008), pp. 1025 and 1030–1031).The column, 2.50 m tall by Darcy's text (his plate marks 3.5 m) and 0.35 m across, and the dates: Simmons (2008), pp. 1025 and 1030–1031. He found a simple rule. The flow grew in proportion to the difference in head between the top and the bottom of the sand, and shrank in proportion as the sand was made thicker: double the head difference and the flow doubles; double the thickness and it halves. What mattered was how steeply the head dropped along the way: the head lost for every metre the water travels. That slope is called the hydraulic gradient, written i. The flow through each square metre of ground is the gradient times a number that belongs to the soil, and that is Darcy's law:

q = k · i · A, so q / A = k · i, with i = Δh / L(3.2)

q flow (m³/s) · A area the water flows through (m²) · q/A flow through each square metre (m/s) · k permeability (m/s) · i gradient · Δh head lost (m) · L length of the path (m)

Read the second form with i = 1, a metre of head lost for every metre travelled, and it says what k is: the flow through each square metre of ground under that push. That is why it has the units of a speed, metres per second. Engineers call it the permeability of the soil.Strictly, k in m/s is the hydraulic conductivity, and permeability is a property of the gaps alone, in m² (Freeze & Cherry (1979), section 2.3). Dam engineers say permeability for both, and so does this book. k depends on the water too: at 5 °C water is half again as viscous as at 20 °C, 1.52 against 1.00 mPa·s (IAPWS (2008)), so the same sand passes cold water about two thirds as fast. The figures in this book use 10⁻² m/s for gravel, 10⁻⁴ for sand, 10⁻⁷ for silt and 10⁻⁹ for compacted clay.

Below, Darcy's column is laid on its side: a pipe full of sand joins two tanks, and each tank's water level is the head at that end of the pipe. Drag the water levels in the tanks, or use the sliders. The thin tubes along the pipe are piezometers:

Notice that the water in the tubes lines up in a straight slope from one tank to the other. The sand is the same all along the pipe, so every metre of it takes the same share of the head. Notice too that the readouts follow Darcy's rule: raise the left tank and the gradient and the flow grow together; lengthen the pipe and both shrink. Here is the arithmetic behind the readouts, and one more number the figure does not show:

Example 3.1

How fast does water move through sand?

Given
Darcy's pipe as the figure opens: sand with k = 10⁻⁴ m/s, whose gaps take up 0.35 of its volume; the left tank at 2.00 m, the right at 0.60 m; a pipe 2.0 m long.
Find
The gradient; the flow through each square metre of pipe; how fast a drop of water moves, and how long it takes to cross the pipe.
The idea
Darcy's law gives the flow through each square metre (Eq. 3.2). But the water can only travel through the gaps, so to carry that flow it has to move faster than q/A.
  1. Δh = 2.00 − 0.60 = 1.40 mthe head at each end is its tank's level
  2. i = 1.40 ÷ 2.0 = 0.70head lost for each metre of pipe
  3. q/A = 10⁻⁴ × 0.70 = 7.0 × 10⁻⁵ m/sDarcy's law: cubic metres a second through each square metre
  4. In litres: 0.070 L/s, and 0.070 × 60 = 4.2 L/mina cubic metre is 1,000 litres
  5. v = 7.0 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 0.35 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m/sthe same flow squeezed through the gaps, about a third of the area
  6. Time: 2.0 m ÷ 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m/s = 10,000 slength of the pipe over the drop's speed
  7. 10,000 ÷ 3,600 = 2.8 hours3,600 seconds in an hour

Each square metre of pipe passes 4.2 litres a minute. A drop moves at 0.2 mm a second and takes 2.8 hours to cross the 2 m of sand.

Check. Swap the sand for silt, whose k of 10⁻⁷ m/s is a thousand times smaller. The flow should fall a thousandfold, to 7.0 × 10⁻⁸ m/s, which is 6.0 litres a day through each square metre: what the figure's readout shows with Silt.

What it means. Even through clean sand, losing seven tenths of a metre of head for every metre it travels, the water moves only about 0.7 m an hour. Seepage is slow, and the soils a dam is made of are slower still.

The last lines of that example hold a distinction worth keeping. The flow through each square metre of ground, q/A, is what a dam engineer adds up to find a leak. The speed of the water itself, the seepage velocity, is that flow divided by the gap fraction, n (engineers call it the porosity), and it is what tells you how long water takes to get anywhere.Why does head leave out the speed of the water? For a river or a pipe, engineers add a third term, the height the water's speed could lift it, v²/2g. For the drop in the sand pipe that is (2.0 × 10⁻⁴)² ÷ (2 × 9.81) = 2 × 10⁻⁹ m, two millionths of a millimetre. In the ground it is always that small, so it is dropped.

3.5 Back to the beach

That is enough to answer the second question from the beach. The sand there is like the pipe's, but the beach slopes gently, so its water table does too. Take the water table to fall 1 m over 20 m of beach, an illustrative gradient of 0.05. Then each square metre passes 10⁻⁴ × 0.05 = 5 × 10⁻⁶ m/s, and the water itself moves at that divided by the gap fraction, 1.4 × 10⁻⁵ m/s: about 5 centimetres an hour. A drop that soaked in 20 m up the beach needs about 16 days to reach the sea. The beach cannot empty in one low tide, or anything like it. It leaks steadily through the hours the tide is out, and the sea comes back and fills it again long before it is drained.

3.6 A metre of clay

Sand is the fast end of a dam's materials. The slow end is clay, and a guess first:

A one-metre block of compacted clay has water pressing on one side, with the water level 1 m higher than on the other side. How long does a drop of water take to get through the metre?

About eleven years, 11.1 by the figures' numbers. Through gravel, the same push gets a drop across in about 30 seconds. The race below runs four materials side by side. Its clock has to speed up enormously before the clay moves at all.

To decide, the race below runs a metre of each of four materials under the same push, with the same arithmetic as the sand pipe:

Notice that the race is lopsided in a way no ordinary clock could show. Each tick on the time axis is ten times the one before, and still the four finishes are spread across almost the whole axis. The arithmetic is the sand pipe's, done four times:

Example 3.2

The race, by hand

Given
A metre of each material (L = 1 m) under a gradient of 1. Gravel: k = 10⁻² m/s, gap fraction 0.30. Sand: 10⁻⁴, 0.35. Silt: 10⁻⁷, 0.40. Clay: 10⁻⁹, 0.35.
Find
How long a drop of water takes to cross each metre.
The idea
The drop's speed is k · i ÷ n, as in Example 3.1, so the time is the length over that: t = n · L ÷ (k · i). With L and i both 1, it is the gap fraction over k.
  1. Gravel: 0.30 ÷ 10⁻² = 30 sdividing by 10⁻² multiplies by a hundred
  2. Sand: 0.35 ÷ 10⁻⁴ = 3,500 s, and 3,500 ÷ 60 = 58 minsixty seconds to a minute
  3. Silt: 0.40 ÷ 10⁻⁷ = 4.0 × 10⁶ s, or 46 days86,400 seconds to a day
  4. Clay: 0.35 ÷ 10⁻⁹ = 3.5 × 10⁸ s, or 11.1 yearsabout 3.16 × 10⁷ seconds to a year

Thirty seconds, 58 minutes, 46 days and 11.1 years, under the same push through the same metre.

Check. Clay's time over gravel's is 3.5 × 10⁸ ÷ 30 = 1.17 × 10⁷. If gravel's 30 seconds were drawn a millimetre long, clay's bar would be that many millimetres, 11.7 km: the figure caption's twelve kilometres.

What it means. The gap fractions hardly differ; the permeabilities differ ten million times, and they decide the race. In a dam it is the choice of soil, far more than its thickness, that decides where the water is held back.

That enormous range is what makes it possible to build a dam out of soil at all. A dam needs a part that water can barely get through, and parts that let water out quickly, side by side. Clay does the first job. Sand and gravel do the second.

3.7 Layers in a line

But a dam's clay is usually a narrow strip inside a much wider bank of sand and rock. How can a strip a few metres thick hold back the head of a whole reservoir? Darcy's pipe can show it. Go back to it and put a plug of clay in its middle:

The pipe is the same length and the tanks are at the same heights, but now nearly all the head is lost across the short piece of clay. The tubes in the sand on either side read almost the same as the tank next to them. The same flow has to pass through every part of the pipe, because water can't pile up anywhere in between. The tight clay needs a far steeper gradient than the sand to push that flow through, so the clay takes almost the whole drop. Each piece of the pipe needs head in proportion to its length divided by its k, which works like a resistance:

Example 3.3

The plug as resistances in a line

Given
The 2.0 m pipe with a clay plug 0.4 m long in its middle (k = 10⁻⁹ m/s) and sand on either side of it, 1.6 m in all (10⁻⁴ m/s); head difference 1.40 m.
Find
The share of the head the plug takes, and what it does to the flow.
The idea
The same flow passes every piece, and each piece needs head in proportion to L ÷ k, its resistance. Resistances in a line add.
  1. Sand: 1.6 ÷ 10⁻⁴ = 16,000 smetres over metres per second leaves seconds
  2. Clay: 0.4 ÷ 10⁻⁹ = 4.0 × 10⁸ sa fifth of the length, but a hundred thousand times tighter
  3. Together: 4.0 × 10⁸ + 16,000 = 4.00016 × 10⁸ sresistances in a line add
  4. Clay's share: 4.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 4.00016 × 10⁸ = 99.996%each piece takes head in proportion to its resistance
  5. k of the whole pipe: 2.0 ÷ 4.00016 × 10⁸ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ m/sits length over its total resistance
  6. q/A = 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 0.70 = 3.5 × 10⁻⁹ m/s, 110 L a yearDarcy's law for the pipe as a whole; the gradient is still 0.70
  7. 7.0 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 3.5 × 10⁻⁹ = 20,000the flow without the plug, from Example 3.1, over the flow with it

The plug takes 1.39994 m of the 1.40 m of head; all the sand together loses 0.056 mm. The flow falls 20,000-fold, to 110 litres a year through each square metre.

Check. The share depends only on the resistances, so a material nearer clay's k should take a bigger share of the drop. Silt's 1.6 m has a resistance of 1.6 ÷ 10⁻⁷ = 1.6 × 10⁷ s, a total of 4.16 × 10⁸ s, and the plug's share falls to 4.0 ÷ 4.16 = 0.9615, the figure's 96.15% with Silt.

What it means. In a line of layers, the tightest one sets the flow and takes almost all the head, however thin it is. The others are left with almost none.

This is how a dam with a clay core works. A core of clay, much narrower than the dam around it, takes almost the whole drop in head, from the reservoir level down to the downstream side. The sand and rock downstream of it carry almost none of the drop, so the water pressure in the downstream half of the dam stays low. Chapter 9 shows the zones that make this work.Water running along layers, instead of across them, meets them side by side, and then the most permeable layer carries most of the flow. Earth fill is spread and rolled in layers, and soil laid down by nature comes in beds, so both pass water more easily along their layers than across them. Hvorslev warned that because of such layering the horizontal permeability of a soil “often is many times greater than the vertical” (Hvorslev (1951), p. 37).

Check yourself Suppose the plug were moved from the middle of the pipe to its left end. Would the flow change? Would the tubes read differently?

The flow would not change: the resistances add the same way in any order, so it stays 110 litres a year. The tubes would: all the sand would now be downstream of the plug, so every tube in the sand would read almost the right tank's level.

A real core is thicker than the plug and holds back far more head, so here is a rough estimate for one:

Example 3.4

Through a real core

Given
An illustrative clay core 5 m thick, with the reservoir standing 30 m higher on its upstream side than the water on its downstream side. The figures' clay: k = 10⁻⁹ m/s, gap fraction 0.35.
Find
How long a drop takes to cross the core, and roughly how much water passes each metre of dam.
The idea
Darcy's law across the core, then the drop's speed through the gaps. For the leak, treat the whole 30 m height of the core as if it carried the full 30 m of head; nearer the top the head is less, so this overestimates.
  1. i = 30 ÷ 5 = 6steep: six metres of head lost for every metre of clay
  2. q/A = 10⁻⁹ × 6 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁹ m/sDarcy's law
  3. v = 6.0 × 10⁻⁹ ÷ 0.35 = 1.71 × 10⁻⁸ m/sthrough the gaps only
  4. t = 5 ÷ 1.71 × 10⁻⁸ = 2.92 × 10⁸ s, or 9.24 yearsthickness over speed
  5. Leak: 6.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 30 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁷ m³/s, which is 0.00018 L/sthrough a strip of core 30 m tall and 1 m long
  6. 0.00018 × 86,400 = 15.6 L a dayseconds in a day

A drop takes about 9 years to cross the core, and each metre of dam leaks about 16 litres a day through it.

Check. The race's clay took 11.09 years for a metre at a gradient of 1. Six times the gradient makes the drop six times faster, and five times the thickness makes the trip five times longer: 11.09 ÷ 6 × 5 = 9.24 years.

What it means. Even a good core leaks, about a bucket and a half a day for each metre of dam, and that water takes years to come through. Chapter 10 works out real leaks with the whole picture of the water in the dam.

Look again at the numbers for clay. A metre of it, under the push that sends water through gravel in half a minute, takes about a decade to pass a drop. The core of a dam is built on that slowness. Hold on to it. The last chapter needs it.

3.8 Water that pushes on grains

So far the water has been the thing that moves, and the grains have only been in its way. But every metre of head the water loses has gone somewhere. Water losing head is shoving its way past grains, and what it shoves, it pushes.

Take a slab of soaked sand one metre square and one metre thick, with water flowing straight up through it and losing 1 m of head on the way, a gradient of 1. If the water were still, the pressure under the slab would be higher than the pressure on top by the weight of the water between and no more, and the soaked sand would get only the lift of being under water. Flowing water needs a metre more head at the bottom to push itself through, so the pressure under the slab is higher than the still-water rule by another 9.81 kPa. That extra pressure, on one square metre, is an extra 9.81 kN pushing the slab up. The water does not rise any faster for it; it hands the push on to the grains, dragging on them as it squeezes past. In general, water that loses head at a gradient i pushes on the grains it passes, in the direction it flows, with a seepage force of

j = i · γw(3.3)

j seepage force on each cubic metre of soil (kN/m³) · i gradient · γw unit weight of water, 9.81 kN/m³

This is also where the pore pressure of Chapter 2 stops following its neat rule. Where water flows upward, the pressure grows faster with depth than 9.81 kPa per metre; where it flows downward, slower. The difference is the push on the grains. How big is it, set against what holds the grains down?

Example 3.5

Nearly enough to float it

Given
Soaked sand weighing 20 kN per cubic metre, grains and water together (the sand of Fig. 4.2); water at 9.81 kN/m³, flowing straight up through it at a gradient of 1.
Find
The seepage force on each cubic metre, and how it compares with the weight of the grains that is left once the water around them holds part of it up.
The idea
Under still water, soaked sand is buoyed up by the weight of the water it displaces, so the grains press down with the difference. Water flowing up pushes them up by i · γw on top of that (Eq. 3.3).
  1. j = 1 × 9.81 = 9.81 kN/m³upward, the way the water flows
  2. Grains' weight, under water: 20 − 9.81 = 10.19 kN/m³the soaked weight less the water's lift
  3. 9.81 ÷ 10.19 = 0.963the push up as a share of the weight down

Water flowing up through sand at a gradient of 1 pushes the grains up with 96% of the weight they have left under water. It nearly floats them.

Check. At a gradient of zero the water is still and the push is zero: the grains press down with their full 10.19 kN/m³. The push grows in step with the gradient, so it would match their weight at a gradient of 10.19 ÷ 9.81 = 1.04, only a little steeper than 1.

What it means. Grains that are pushed up nearly as hard as they weigh hardly press on one another at all. Chapter 4 shows why that matters: a grain's grip on its neighbours comes from that press.

The same push works in any direction. Water seeping down through the upstream part of a dam presses its grains together harder. Water seeping out of a slope drags its grains outward and down, and that is what the moving water does at the foot of the beach, where the streams come out. In Fig. 1.1 the heap with water draining out of its faces stood at 19° instead of 34°, and the drag is why. Example 4.5 does the sum.

Check yourself Water seeps straight down through a layer of sand at a gradient of 0.5. Does the seepage force make the grains press on one another harder or less, and by how much on each cubic metre?

Harder. The force acts the way the water flows, here downward, adding 0.5 × 9.81 = 4.9 kN to each cubic metre's press. Water flowing down presses soil together; water flowing up lifts it.

What to remember

  • Water flows from high total head to low, where head is elevation plus pressure head, h = z + u/γw. In still water the head is the same everywhere, so high pressure at depth moves nothing.
  • Darcy's law: the flow through each square metre is k · i. Permeability runs from 10⁻² m/s for gravel to 10⁻⁹ for compacted clay, and a drop moves faster than k · i, because only the gaps carry it.
  • In a line of layers the tightest takes almost all the head: a clay plug a fifth of the pipe's length takes 99.996%. A core holds back a reservoir the same way, and a metre of clay takes about a decade to pass a drop.
  • Moving water pushes on the grains it passes, i · γw on each cubic metre. Flowing up at a gradient of 1 it carries 96% of the weight the grains have left under water, so they hardly press on one another: the water has taken their press away.

Questions

  1. 3.1

    Piezometer A has its tip 10 m above the datum, and the water in it stands 25 m above the datum. Piezometer B has its tip 2 m above the datum, with water to 22 m. Which way does the water between them flow? Which tip feels the higher pressure?

    Hint

    The water level in each pipe is the head at its tip. The pressure head is the height of that level above the tip.

    Answer

  2. 3.2

    The pressure on the bed of a deep lake is far higher than at its surface. Why doesn't water flow up out of the lake bed toward the surface?

    Hint

    Push a straw into the lake bed. Where does its water stand?

    Answer

  3. 3.3

    With sand and the clay plug in Darcy's pipe, raise the right tank from 0.60 m to 1.80 m. What happens to the share of the head the plug takes, and to the flow?

    Hint

    The share depends only on the resistances of the pieces. The flow depends on the head difference too.

    Answer

  4. 3.4

    How long does a drop of water take to cross 2 m of the figures' silt under a gradient of 1?

    Hint

    Time is the gap fraction times the length, over k times the gradient. Silt: k = 10⁻⁷ m/s, gap fraction 0.40.

    Answer

  5. 3.5

    The core of Example 3.4 is built twice as thick, 10 m, holding back the same 30 m of head. How do the leak and the time a drop takes to cross it change?

    Hint

    Doubling the thickness halves the gradient. What does that do to the flow, and to the speed of a drop that also has twice as far to go?

    Answer

  • Freeze, R.A., Cherry, J.A. (1979). Groundwater. Englewood Cliffs: Prentice-Hall. https://gw-project.org/books/groundwater/ serious The classic groundwater textbook. Its second chapter sets out Darcy's law, hydraulic head and the difference between conductivity and permeability, with piezometers drawn exactly as this chapter's straws. Free to download from the Groundwater Project.

Water flowing up through sand at a gradient of 1 carries almost all the weight its grains have left. A grain that hardly presses on its neighbours can hardly grip them. How does a press become a grip, and how much of it can water take away, even when the water isn't moving at all?

4

Chapter 4 · Part I · Ground

Grip

If water doesn't grease the grains, what does it do to them?

All the measurable effects of a change of the stress, such as compression, distortion and a change of the shearing resistance are exclusively due to changes in the effective stresses.

Karl Terzaghi, The shearing resistance of saturated soils, 1936

So far. Still water presses harder the deeper you go, and water in the ground flows from high head to low, dragging on the grains it passes. Chapter 3 ended on a cubic metre of soaked sand that flowing water could nearly float. This chapter puts the water and the grains together.

After this chapter you can

  • work out the factor of safety of a block on a ramp, with and without water under it;
  • apply σ′ = σ − u to a column of soil, and say why a lake on top changes nothing;
  • derive the critical gradient, and the steepest face a sand can hold dry, under still water and with water seeping out of it.

This chapter adds small paired arrows under the slope: grains pressing (σ′)

4 figures · about 20 min to read

A wet floor is slippery. So is a wet road, a wet rock in a stream, a wet bar of soap. Everyone learns from the soles of their feet that water greases things. Most people say the same of sand: wet sand is slippery sand, and a bank that slumps after rain has been greased.

Chapter 1 asked you to keep that answer in mind, and it is already in trouble. The damp castle has water in it and stands with upright walls, steeper than the dry heap beside it. If water greased the grains, the castle would be the first to fall.

There is also a direct test. In 1962 two engineers, H. M. Horn and Don Deere, slid polished pieces of minerals over one another, first oven-dried and then soaked in water. Clear quartz, the commonest mineral in sand, gripped with a friction of 0.10 dry and 0.23 wet: more than twice as hard with water on it.Horn & Deere (1962), their friction coefficients for three surface-moisture conditions: clear quartz 0.10 oven-dried, 0.10 air-dried, 0.23 saturated.Not every mineral behaves like quartz. In the same tests the flaky sheet minerals went the other way: muscovite mica fell from about 0.43 dry to 0.23 soaked, and chlorite from 0.53 to 0.22 (Horn & Deere (1962)). Clay is made of flakes of this family, which is one reason clay comes back later in this book as a different kind of soil.

So water isn't greasing the grains. What it does instead was worked out by Karl Terzaghi, the engineer who founded soil mechanics in the 1920s, and the rest of this book stands on it. By the end of this chapter it explains why water can make the castle stronger, why a heap under still water keeps its slope, the 19° face that Chapter 1 left unexplained, and the number every later chapter uses to say whether a slope will stand. To see it, start with something simpler than sand.

4.1 Friction comes from pressing

Put a book on a plank and slowly tilt the plank. The book stays put until the slope gets steep, then it slides. Friction holds it, and friction comes from the book pressing on the plank. Press twice as hard and it takes twice the force to slide it. The friction on offer is always a fixed fraction of the press, and that fraction is what Horn and Deere measured.

The fraction sets a steepest angle for each pair of surfaces. Tilt beyond it and the book slides, whatever it weighs. Engineers call it the friction angle, written φ, and the fraction is its tangent, tan φ. For sand as a whole it is about 34°, the same angle as the dry heap in Fig. 1.1, because the surface of a heap is a ramp of sand resting on sand. Polished quartz grips far less than that: at Horn and Deere's dry 0.10, a polished block would slide off a polished ramp tilted past about 6°.Horn & Deere (1962), clear quartz oven-dried; the angle whose tangent is 0.10 is 5.7°.That dry 0.10 says as much about the surface as about the mineral. Later tests at MIT, in a vacuum chamber, found smooth quartz gripping with anything from about 0.1 to 1.0 depending on how clean its surface was, while rough surfaces varied much less (Bromwell (1966)). None of the tests found water making quartz slippery. Real grains are rougher than a polished block, and they also interlock: to move, they have to roll up and over one another. Both lift sand to its 34°.

The weight drops out of that angle, and a block on a ramp shows why. Put a block of weight W on a ramp tilted at an angle a. Gravity pulls it straight down, and the ramp feels that pull in two parts. The part pressing straight into the ramp is W cos a, and the part pulling the block down the slope is W sin a. Friction can offer up to the press times tan φ. So the block holds as long as W cos a · tan φ is at least W sin a. The weight is on both sides and cancels: the block holds while tan a is less than tan φ, and slides when the ramp passes φ, heavy or light. That is why the dry heap of Chapter 1 keeps one slope however much sand you pour on it.

A designer needs more than "holds" or "slides". The dam in the Prologue had been checked and found to hold; how comfortably it held was a number, and that number is the factor of safety, the friction available divided by the friction needed:

FS = N′ · tan φ ÷ (W · sin a) (4.1)

N′ the press left between the block and the ramp (kN) · tan φ the friction fraction · W sin a the pull down the ramp (kN). For a dry block N′ = W cos a, and the factor of safety is tan φ ÷ tan a.

Above 1 the block holds. Below 1 it slides. At 1.5 the ground could lose a third of its grip before anything moved, and about 1.5 is what dams are designed to, to leave room for everything nobody can measure exactly.1.5 is a convention, not a law of nature. The US Army Corps of Engineers asks a new embankment dam for 1.5 under steady seepage with the reservoir full, 1.3 at the end of construction, and 1.1 to 1.3 right after a fast drawdown of the reservoir; it says such values "continue to be based on experience" (USACE EM 1110-2-1902, p. 3-1 and its table of minimum factors on p. 3-2). The lower values are for conditions that last a short time. Every later chapter of this book uses the same definition, applied to a dam's slope instead of a block.

Now slip a thin cushion of water under the block's base. Make a guess before you see it:

A block rests on a ramp tilted to 25°, holding comfortably. A thin water cushion sits under its base. You pump up the water pressure in the cushion. The block's weight, shape and surface stay exactly the same. What happens?

It slides. The water carries part of the block's weight, so less weight is left pressing the block onto the ramp. Friction comes from that press, so it shrinks too, while gravity pulls the block down the slope as hard as ever. Try it below.

To decide, tilt the ramp and pump up the cushion in the figure below:

Start with the dry block, before any water. Notice that its two bars stand in the ratio of the factor of safety: 12.2 kN of friction available against 8.5 kN needed, so 1.45. Then notice what the water touches. As the cushion's pressure rises, the press left over falls and the friction bar shrinks with it, kilonewton for kilonewton times tan 34°. The bar for the friction needed doesn't move at all, because the water pushes straight up from the ramp and has no part along it. The block slides when the two bars meet, though its weight, its shape and its surface never changed. Here are the readouts by hand:

Example 4.1

How much water slides the block?

Given
A block weighing W = 20 kN on a base of 1 m², on a ramp at a = 25°. Friction angle φ = 34°, so tan φ = 0.6745.
Find
The factor of safety with no water, and the cushion pressure that slides the block.
The idea
Friction works only with the press left over; the water takes its pressure, times the base area, off the press and leaves the pull alone (Eq. 4.1).
  1. N = 20 × cos 25° = 20 × 0.9063 = 18.13 kNthe part of the weight pressing into the ramp
  2. Pull = 20 × sin 25° = 20 × 0.4226 = 8.45 kNthe part pulling it down the slope
  3. Friction available = 18.13 × 0.6745 = 12.23 kNthe press times the friction fraction
  4. FS = 12.23 ÷ 8.45 = 1.45available over needed, with no water
  5. Press that barely holds: 8.45 ÷ 0.6745 = 12.53 kNat FS = 1 the friction available equals the pull
  6. Water must carry 18.13 − 12.53 = 5.60 kN, so u = 5.60 kPaspread over the 1 m² base, a kilonewton per square metre is a kilopascal
  7. 5.60 ÷ 18.13 = 0.309that pressure as a share of the press

Dry, the block holds with FS = 1.45. It slides when the cushion reaches 5.6 kPa, when the water carries 30.9% of its press: a little under a third.

Check. There is a shortcut. The block slides when the press left is the pull divided by tan 34°, so the share the water must take is 1 − tan 25° ÷ tan 34° = 1 − 0.4663 ÷ 0.6745 = 0.309, the same. On a gentler ramp the water needs more: at 10° the share is 1 − 0.1763 ÷ 0.6745 = 0.7386 of a press of 20 × 0.9848 = 19.70 kN, and 0.7386 × 19.70 = 14.55 kPa.

What it means. Nothing about the block got weaker. The water took a third of its press away and left the pull alone, and a third was all the margin the block had. The steeper the ramp, the less water it takes.

Check yourself Two dry blocks sit on the same 25° ramp, one twice as heavy as the other. Which has the larger factor of safety?

Neither. Doubling the weight doubles the press and the pull alike, and a dry block's factor of safety, tan 34° ÷ tan 25° = 1.45, has no weight in it.

4.2 Soil is thousands of little blocks

Now shrink the block down to a grain of sand. A handful of soil is a crowd of grains, each resting on its neighbours at a few points of contact. Every contact is a tiny block on a tiny ramp, held by friction, and that friction comes from how hard the grains press on each other. The strength of soil is the friction of all those contacts added up.The press is not shared evenly. In experiments with a layer of plastic disks that glow between polarizing filters where they are squeezed, the load travels along branching chains of disks while their neighbours carry much less, and when the pile is sheared the chains line up with the push (Majmudar & Behringer (2005)). Soil mechanics works with the average over many grains, which is what σ′ is.

But fill the gaps with water and something has to carry the water's pressure. To see where it goes, picture a level surface one metre square, deep in soaked sand, that threads its way through the gaps and crosses the grains only where they touch. Everything above that surface, grains and water together, presses down across it. That is the total stress, written σ. The contacts between grains are tiny, so the water in the gaps meets almost all of the surface, and it presses on all of it with its own pore pressure, u. The water therefore carries u of each square metre's σ, and only the rest is left for the grains to carry, through their contacts, by pressing on one another. Terzaghi called that rest the effective stress:Karl Terzaghi, an Austrian engineer, worked the idea out while teaching at Robert College in Constantinople (now Istanbul), in a laboratory he built partly from cigar boxes and kitchenware, and published it in Erdbaumechanik in 1925 (Bennett (2023); Terzaghi (1925)). At the first international conference on soil mechanics, at Harvard in 1936, he put it in the sentence that heads this chapter (Terzaghi (1936), p. 54).

σ′ = σ − u(4.2)

Friction comes from pressing, so the most shear stress the grains can resist, their strength, is that press times the friction fraction:

τ = σ′ · tan φ′(4.3)

σ total stress, the weight of everything above, per square metre (kPa) · u pore pressure (kPa) · σ′ effective stress, how hard the grains press on one another (kPa) · τ shear strength, the most shear stress the soil can carry on a plane (kPa) · φ′ the soil's friction angle, with a prime because it goes with the effective stress; 34° for this sand, tan φ′ = 0.6745

The water does to the grains exactly what the cushion did to the block: it takes over part of the load they would otherwise carry by pressing on one another, and it adds no grip of its own.

To use the rule you need σ at a depth, the weight of everything above it, and for that you need the soil's unit weight, the weight of one cubic metre. Damp sand weighs about 18 kN per cubic metre. Soaked, it weighs about 20, because water has filled the gaps that air held. Below the water table the water in the gaps joins up like a lake, so in still groundwater u grows by 9.81 kPa for every metre below the water table, the rule of Eq. 2.1. The figure below stacks ten metres of this sand and lets you move the water table, from below the column to three metres above the ground:

Notice first what happens as the water table rises from below the column to the ground. The sand gets heavier, because water is replacing air in its gaps, yet the effective stress at 10 m falls from 180 to about 102 kPa. That is 43% of the soil's strength gone, and no grain had to move. Below the water table each extra metre of sand adds 20 kPa to the total stress and 9.81 to the pore pressure, so the grains feel only the difference, 10.19 kPa a metre: the sand's buoyant unit weight, written γ′. Above the water table they feel all 18.

Notice second what happens once the water rises above the ground. Every extra metre of lake adds the same 9.81 kPa to the total stress and to the pore pressure, so the effective-stress line stops moving. A lake sitting on soil doesn't press its grains together any harder, however deep it is. Here are the numbers:

Example 4.2

Ten metres of sand, three water tables

Given
A column of sand 10 m deep: 18 kN/m³ above the water table, 20 kN/m³ below it; water 9.81 kN/m³.
Find
σ, u and σ′ at the foot with the water table 4 m down, at the ground, and under 3 m of lake.
The idea
σ is the weight of everything above; u is the depth below the water surface times 9.81; the grains get the difference (Eq. 4.2).
  1. 4 m down: σ = 18 × 4 + 20 × 6 = 192 kPa4 m of damp sand on 6 m of soaked
  2. u = 9.81 × 6 = 58.86 kPathe foot is 6 m below the water table
  3. σ′ = 192 − 58.86 = 133.14 kPawhat the grains press with
  4. At the ground: σ = 20 × 10 = 200, u = 9.81 × 10 = 98.1, σ′ = 101.9 kPaall ten metres soaked
  5. 101.9 ÷ 180 = 0.566against 18 × 10 = 180 kPa with the water table below the column
  6. 3 m of lake: σ = 9.81 × 3 + 200 = 229.43, u = 9.81 × 13 = 127.53 kPathe lake's weight is added to both; the foot is now 13 m below the water's surface
  7. σ′ = 229.43 − 127.53 = 101.9 kPaunchanged by the lake

With the water table 4 m down the grains at the foot press with 133.1 kPa. Flooded to the ground they press with 101.9 kPa, 43% less than with the water table below the column, and 3 m of lake on top leaves that at 101.9.

Check. Count the grains' press metre by metre: 18 kPa for each damp metre and the buoyant 10.19 for each soaked one. With the water table 4 m down, 72 + 6 × 10.19 = 133.14 kPa, the same as step 3.

What it means. Water in the ground weakens soil by taking over part of the grains' press. Raising a reservoir over a sand bed adds to σ and u alike and leaves the bed's grains exactly as they were; what does change the press is water that flows, which comes next.

Check yourself Wells pump the water table down from the ground surface to 4 m below it. Is the sand at 10 m now heavier or lighter, and stronger or weaker?

Lighter and stronger. σ falls from 200 to 192 kPa, but u falls further, from 98.1 to 58.9, so the grains press with 133.1 kPa instead of 101.9.

4.3 One line for the strength

Every strength in this chapter so far has been a press times the same fraction. So if you plot strength against effective stress, every state of this sand, wet or dry, deep or shallow, lands on one straight line through zero, rising at the friction angle:

Notice that the water never moves the line. Flooding slides the column's point down along it, to a smaller press and so a smaller strength; the sand's friction angle is the same throughout. That is the whole effect of still water on sand. Engineers call this line the strength envelope. Some soils, clays among them, keep a little strength even when the grains are barely pressed, called cohesion and written c′; their line starts at c′ instead of zero, τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′. Clean sand has none.

Example 4.3

Reading strength off the line

Given
The effective stress at the column's foot from Example 4.2: 180 kPa with the water table below the column, 133.14 kPa with it 4 m down, 101.9 kPa flooded. tan φ′ = 0.6745.
Find
The shear strength of the sand at the foot in each case.
The idea
Strength is the press times the friction fraction (Eq. 4.3).
  1. Below the column: 180 × 0.6745 = 121.41 kPathe most strength the foot has
  2. 4 m down: 133.14 × 0.6745 = 89.80 kPathe figure's opening state
  3. Flooded: 101.9 × 0.6745 = 68.73 kPathe same line, further down it

The foot can resist 121.4, 89.8 and 68.7 kPa of shear in the three cases.

Check. The flooded strength over the dry one should be the flooded press over the dry press, since the fraction is the same: 68.73 ÷ 121.41 = 0.566, as in Example 4.2.

What it means. These are strengths, not loads: the grains at the foot of a level column are not being sheared at all. A slope shears them, and Chapter 12 sets the shear a slope asks for against this line, all along a curved slip surface.

4.4 Water that flows up

Still water, however deep, only takes away the press that its own pressure accounts for. But Chapter 3 ended with water that flows, and flowing water drags on the grains it passes: water losing i metres of head for every metre it travels pushes on the grains in each cubic metre with i × 9.81 kN, in the direction it flows.

Turn that flow upward, as it does where water that has passed under a dam comes up again on the far side. Soaked sand presses down with its buoyant unit weight, 10.19 kN per cubic metre. The water flowing up through it pushes up with i × 9.81. Raise the gradient and the upward drag eats into the downward press, until at one gradient they cancel. There the grains still touch but no longer press on one another, the effective stress is zero, and the sand has no grip at all. That gradient is the critical gradient:

ic = γ′ ÷ γw = (γsat − γw) ÷ γw (4.4)

γsat unit weight of the soaked soil (kN/m³) · γw unit weight of water, 9.81 kN/m³ · γ′ buoyant unit weight, γsat − γw

Example 4.4

The gradient that floats the grains

Given
Soaked sand of 20 kN/m³, the column's; water 9.81 kN/m³, flowing straight up through it. For the second route, typical quartz sand: grains 2.65 times as heavy as water, and 0.65 m³ of gap for every cubic metre of grain.
Find
The upward gradient at which the grains stop pressing on one another.
The idea
The water's upward drag, i × 9.81 per cubic metre, against the grains' buoyant weight (Eq. 4.4).
  1. γ′ = 20 − 9.81 = 10.19 kN/m³the press of each soaked cubic metre on the grains below
  2. ic = 10.19 ÷ 9.81 = 1.04upward drag equals that press
  3. From the grains: γsat = 3.30 ÷ 1.65 × 9.81 = 19.62 kN/m³a cubic metre of grain weighs as much as 2.65 m³ of water, and its gaps hold 0.65 m³ more: 2.65 + 0.65 = 3.30 cubic metres' worth of water's weight in 1.65 m³
  4. ic = (2.65 − 1) ÷ (1 + 0.65) = 1.65 ÷ 1.65 = 1.00the same rule, γ′ ÷ γw, written with the grains' numbers

Sand floats when the water flowing up through it loses about a metre of head for every metre it climbs: 1.04 for the column's sand, 1.00 for the typical one.

Check. The two routes differ only because the second sand is a little lighter, 19.62 kN/m³ against 20. A soaked sand weighs about twice as much as water, so its buoyant weight is about one water's worth, and a gradient of about 1 lifts it.

What it means. No sand anywhere is much stronger than this against water rising through it. Where seepage comes up at the downstream foot of a dam, a gradient near 1 makes the ground heave or boil, and Chapter 11 follows what happens next.

4.5 The beach face, worked out

Everything so far has been level ground. A slope adds a pull, and that brings back the two wet heaps of Fig. 1.1. A heap under still water stands about as steep as a dry one. The water carries part of each grain's weight, so the grains press on each other less, but the same buoyancy lightens their pull down the slope by the same share, and the angle depends only on the ratio of the two. The heap slumps to about 19° only where water drains out through its face, because the flowing water drags the grains downhill as well, the drag of Chapter 3. Chapter 1 promised the sum that turns that drag into degrees.

It needs one more idea. A beach face, or the long face of a dam, is so long and even that every patch of it is like every other. Engineers call it an infinite slope, and its great convenience is that one grain on the face, or one cubic metre of it, stands for the whole. Take that grain as a block on a ramp of sand and draw its forces in the three states:

Notice that panels A and B have the same shape. Under still water every arrow shrinks by the same share, because buoyancy takes the same fraction off the grain's weight wherever it points, and so the angle stays at 34°. Notice then what is new in C. The grain weighs what it did in B, and its press into the face is no bigger, but a second arrow has joined the pull: the drag of the water flowing past it. Friction comes only from the press, so the face must flatten until the press's friction catches up. Here is the sum Chapter 1 promised:

tan β = (γ′ ÷ γsat) · tan φ′ (4.5)

β the steepest angle of a face with water seeping out of it, parallel to the face, in sand with no cohesion · γ′ buoyant unit weight · γsat soaked unit weight · φ′ the sand's friction angle. Dry or under still water, tan β = tan φ′.

Example 4.5

Why the draining face stands at 19°

Given
The beach sand of Fig. 1.1: soaked, γsat = 20 kN/m³; water 9.81 kN/m³; φ′ = 34°, tan φ′ = 0.6745. Water seeps out through the face, flowing parallel to it.
Find
The steepest angle β the face can stand at.
The idea
Treat one cubic metre of the face as the block on its ramp (Example 4.1), and add the drag of the flowing water to its pull.
  1. Press into the face: 10.19 cos β kNthe grains' weight in water, 20 − 9.81, split as on the ramp
  2. Gradient along the flow: i = sin βflowing parallel to the face, the water stays at one depth and one pressure, so the head it loses equals the height it drops: sin β per metre
  3. Pull: 10.19 sin β + 9.81 sin β = 20 sin β kNthe weight's pull plus the drag, i × 9.81
  4. On the point of sliding: 20 sin β = 10.19 cos β × tan 34°friction available equals the pull, FS = 1; dividing by cos β gives Eq. 4.5
  5. 10.19 ÷ 20 = 0.5095γ′ ÷ γsat
  6. tan β = 0.5095 × 0.6745 = 0.3437a little over half of tan 34°
  7. β = arctan 0.3437 = 19.0°the angle whose tangent that is

The face stands at 19.0°, 15.0° flatter than the dry heap's 34°.

Check. Take the drag away and the pull is 10.19 sin β, the same weight as the press: the 10.19 cancels and tan β = tan 34°, the heap under still water. And at 19.0° the face is in balance: the press is 9.637 kN, which gives 9.637 × 0.6745 = 6.500 kN of friction, against a pull of 3.312 + 3.188 = 6.500 kN.

What it means. The 19° in Fig. 1.1 was right; Chapter 1 only couldn't say why yet. Soaked sand weighs about twice as much as water, so water seeping out of a face roughly doubles the pull on its grains and roughly halves the tangent of the steepest slope. The downstream face of an earth dam, where seepage comes out, is this face at the scale of a hill, and the drains of Chapter 9 are there to keep the water from reaching it.

Check yourself Water seeps out of the face of a sand with heavier grains, soaked at 22 kN/m³ instead of 20, with the same friction angle. Does its face stand steeper or flatter than 19°?

Steeper. Its buoyant weight is a larger share of its soaked weight: γ′ ÷ γsat = 12.19 ÷ 22 = 0.554, so tan β = 0.554 × 0.6745 = 0.374 and β = 20.5°. The heavier the grains against the water, the less the water's drag counts.

4.6 The sentence, proved

Turn back to the title page and read the sentence there. You can now prove it:

Soil holds only as well as its grains press on one another, and the water between them can take that press away.

The first half is Eq. 4.3: strength is the grains' press times a fixed fraction, and nothing else. The second half is Eq. 4.2: whatever pressure the water has, it subtracts from that press. Every result in this chapter is one of the two halves at work. Water in the cushion took 31% of the block's press and slid it. Flooding the column took 43% of the grains' press. Water flowing up at a gradient of about 1 takes all of it. Water seeping out of a face adds a pull and no press, and the face falls from 34° to 19°.

The castle of Chapter 1 seemed to contradict the sentence, because there the water makes the sand stronger. It obeys it too. In damp sand the water hangs in small rings between the grains, and the curved skin of each ring pulls, so the water's pressure is below the air's: u is negative. Subtract a negative and σ′ = σ − u is larger than σ. The water adds to the press instead of taking it away, by the same rule with the sign turned over (in damp sand only part of that pull counts, because the water touches only part of each grain). Chapter 5 puts a number on that pull and shows why it can hold up a wall a few tens of centimetres tall and never a 30 m one.

The sentence doesn't cover everything. Water that pours over the top of a dam washes it away whatever its grains are doing, and Chapter 6 takes up that story. But for what soil does with the water inside it, this is the rule the rest of the book applies.

What to remember

  • Friction comes from pressing: the grains' strength is their press times tan φ′, and the factor of safety is the friction available over the friction needed. A dry block, or a dry heap, slides at φ whatever it weighs.
  • Water pressure takes part of the grains' press and none of the pull: σ′ = σ − u. Under the 25° block, 31% was enough to slide it.
  • A rising water table makes soil heavier and its grains press less; a lake on top adds to σ and u alike and changes nothing.
  • Water flowing up at the critical gradient, about 1, takes the grains' whole press away.
  • Water seeping out of a face adds a pull and no press, so the steepest face falls to tan β = (γ′/γsat) tan φ′: 19.0° for the beach.

Questions

  1. 4.1

    Set the ramp in Fig. 4.1 to 30°, with no water. What is the block's factor of safety, and what cushion pressure slides it?

    A block twice as heavy as the one in Fig. 4.1, with the same base, sits on the same 25° ramp with the same 5 kPa of water in its cushion. Is it more or less likely to slide than the lighter block?

    Hint

    The water carries the same number of kilonewtons under each block. What share of each block's press is that?

    Answer

  3. 4.3

    Put the water table in Fig. 4.2 2 m below the ground. What are σ, u and σ′ at 10 m, and how much of the strength is left?

    Hint

    Two metres of damp sand on eight of soaked; the foot is 8 m below the water table.

  4. 4.4

  5. 4.5

    Below the downstream foot of a dam, water rises through the sand of the column (20 kN/m³), losing 0.6 m of head for every metre it climbs. What share of the grains' press is left?

    Hint

    Each cubic metre presses down with its buoyant weight and is pushed up by i × 9.81.

  6. 4.6
