Everything in this chapter let the water come and go as it pleased: it rose in the column, seeped out of the face, flowed up through the sand. What happens to the grains' press when the water in the gaps can't get out in time?

Next · Chapter 5 · When the water can't get out

Previous · Chapter 3 · Which way the water goes

5

Chapter 5 · Part I · Ground

When the water can't get out

Why does firm wet sand go pale under one foot, while the sand at the water's edge swallows the other?

So far. A soil grips only as hard as its grains press on one another, and water pressure in the gaps takes part of that press away: σ′ = σ − u. A lake standing on top changes nothing, because it adds to the weight and to the water pressure alike. All of that assumed the water could come and go as it pleased.

After this chapter you can

  • put a number on the grip of damp sand, and say why a sand wall stands a quarter of a metre and never thirty;
  • predict from how sand is packed whether shearing makes it swell or shrink, and so explain the pale footprint, the sinking foot and liquefaction;
  • estimate how long water takes to leave a layer of sand or clay, and so tell a drained loading from an undrained one.

This chapter adds the soaked zone below the phreatic line shaded (water carrying load)

3 figures · about 20 min to read · Film 5.1, 8 min 45 s

Go back to the beach at low tide and walk down to the firm sand in the middle, where the sea was an hour ago. Put your weight on one foot. A pale ring spreads round it, as if the sand had dried where you stood, and fades in a second or two. Lift the foot and the print turns dark and shiny for a moment, wetter than the sand around it.

Now step down to the edge, where each wave lays a fresh sheet of sand. Stand still and it holds you. Wiggle your feet and it goes soft and swallows them to the ankle.

Both sands are saturated: every gap between the grains is full of water. Chapter 4 showed that water pressure in the gaps takes part of the grains' press away, and that still water standing on top changes nothing. By that account two wet sands pressed by the same foot ought to behave alike. They behave as opposites. Most people, asked what a foot does to wet sand, say it squeezes the water out, so the sand round the foot should look wetter. On the firm beach it looks drier.

Chapter 1 left a clue. When its heap of wet sand was jiggled, the densely packed heap held and the loosely packed one flowed, so packing matters. Time matters too. Every sum in Chapter 4 let the water flow in or out as fast as it liked, and under a moving foot it can't, not quickly enough. This chapter is about what water does when it is trapped. It starts with the simplest case, the damp castle, where the water pulls.

5.1 Water that pulls

The damp castle has only a little water in it, and that water gathers in tiny rings where the grains touch (the close-up in Fig. 1.1 draws them). The surface of each ring is curved and stretched, like the skin of a soap bubble, and it pulls the two grains toward each other. So the water in a ring is at less than the pressure of the air around it: a negative pore pressure, which engineers call suction.

Put a negative u into Eq. 4.2 and the effective stress goes up: σ − u is more than σ when u is below zero. The grains press together harder than their own weight could make them, and by Eq. 4.3 more press means more grip. That extra grip does not depend on how much sand lies above, so it can hold grains on a vertical face, where weight alone would roll them off.

How much grip? Nobody can put a pressure gauge inside a ring of water a fraction of a millimetre across, but the grip can be measured whole. Shear damp sand in a box with nothing pressing on it and it still resists, with about 0.6 kPa for a sand of fine, angular grains.Richefeu, El Youssoufi & Radjaï (2006): sand of angular grains 0.1–0.4 mm across, sheared in a box; its cohesion rose with the water content and levelled off at about 600 Pa once the water was about 3% of the weight of the grains. Grip that is there with no press at all is called cohesion, written c. In damp sand it is borrowed from the water, so engineers call it apparent cohesion. It is the grip a suction of 0.6 ÷ tan 34° = 0.89 kPa would give if it pressed on every grain, the weight of about 5 cm of damp sand. Whether that matters depends on what it is set against.

A wall of soil with cohesion fails when a wedge of it slides off along a sloping crack: the block on the ramp of Fig. 4.1, with a little glue on the ramp. Try every angle of crack and every shape of wedge, and the worst one gives the tallest vertical wall the soil can hold:The factor 3.83, the best upper bound for a vertical cut whatever the friction angle: Salençon (2024), p. 273. Chapter 12 does the same kind of search for slopes.

H ≈ 3.83 · (c ⁄ γ) · tan(45° + φ′⁄2) (5.1)

H tallest vertical wall (m) · c cohesion (kPa) · γ unit weight of the soil (kN/m³) · φ′ its friction angle

Notice that the height grows with the cohesion and shrinks with the weight. The ratio c/γ is the cohesion written as a height of soil, and the wall can stand a few times taller than that.

Example 5.1

How tall can a damp wall stand?

Given
Damp sand weighing γ = 18 kN/m³ (the stress column's damp sand, Fig. 4.2), friction angle φ′ = 34° (the dry heap's), and the measured apparent cohesion c = 0.6 kPa. The castle in Fig. 1.1 is about 0.3 m tall.
Find
The press at the foot of the castle from its own weight, the tallest wall this sand can hold, and the cohesion a 30 m wall would need.
The idea
The weight presses harder the taller the wall grows; the cohesion stays the same. Eq. 5.1 says where the two balance.
  1. σ = 18 × 0.3 = 5.4 kPathe weight on each square metre at the foot of a 30 cm wall
  2. tan(45° + 17°) = tan 62° = 1.8807half the friction angle, added to 45°
  3. H = 3.83 × 0.6 ÷ 18 × 1.8807 = 0.24 mEq. 5.1: the tallest wall
  4. σ = 18 × 30 = 540 kPathe press at the foot of a 30 m wall
  5. 3.83 × 1.8807 = 7.203the two numbers in the formula that don't change
  6. c = 540 ÷ 7.203 = 75.0 kPathe same formula turned round: c = γH ÷ (3.83 tan 62°)
  7. 75 ÷ 0.6 = 125how many times the grip the water rings supply

This sand holds a vertical wall about 0.24 m tall. A wall 30 m tall would need 75 kPa of cohesion, 125 times what the water supplies.

Check. The answer falls a little short of the 0.3 m castle, and the gap is fair: 0.6 kPa was measured on one sand, prepared one way. Finer sand has more contacts in each square metre, each with its own ring, so it grips harder, and a round tower is braced by its own curve. What the sum settles is the size: tens of centimetres, never tens of metres. And with no cohesion at all, dry sand, H = 0: no vertical face, only the 34° heap.

What it means. At the foot of the castle the weight already presses with 5.4 kPa, six times the 0.89 kPa the suction adds, so suction matters most near the top, where the grains carry almost no weight. At the base of a dam the grains press with hundreds of kilopascals. Designers leave suction out, as Chapter 1 said, and a week of rain or drought would take it away in any case.

Dry the sand and the rings evaporate; flood it and they merge into one body of water at ordinary positive pressure. Either way the suction goes and the wall slumps.Treating suction as a negative u slightly overstates it. The rings wet only part of each grain, so only part of the suction presses the grains together. Alan Bishop wrote the effective stress of a damp soil with a factor χ between 0 (dry) and 1 (saturated) in front of the suction (Bishop (1959)). The measured cohesion used here already includes that factor. Suction needs air in the gaps. But the firm sand under your foot has no air in its gaps. It is saturated, and it stiffens anyway.

5.2 Loose and dense

The answer lies in how the grains are packed. Push on a heap of grains so that they must slide past one another, and what happens next depends on how they sat. Densely packed grains sit in each other's hollows. To slide, each must ride up over the one in front, so the heap swells as it shears. Loosely packed grains have hollows below them, and shearing drops them in, so the heap shrinks. Engineers call the first kind dilative and the second contractive.Osborne Reynolds named the swelling dilatancy in 1885. He filled a rubber bag with lead shot and water and sealed it, and the bag went rigid in whatever shape it had: to change shape the shot had to spread apart, and there was no more water to fill the room. Connected to a measuring vessel, the bag drew water in as he squeezed it out of shape. He explained the pale footprint in the same paper (Reynolds (1885), p. 475).

Here are both, in close-up, with every gap full of water:

Notice that in both drawings the water is the wrong amount for the new arrangement. The dense stack has grown more gap than it has water to fill. More water can only flow in through the narrow gaps from the sand around, which takes time. Until it arrives, the water already there is stretched to fill the larger space, and its pressure falls below what still water at that depth would have. Engineers call the difference from the still-water pressure the excess pore pressure, Δu; here it is negative. A negative Δu works like suction: by Eq. 4.2 the grains press harder, and the sand under your foot stiffens.

The water the sheared sand pulls in has to come from somewhere, and the nearest supply is the water among the top grains. So the water surface is drawn down below the top grains and leaves them looking dry: that is the pale ring. Reynolds saw both supplies, the surface and the sand around, and saw why the surface wins at first: drawing water through the sand "requires time to accomplish".Reynolds (1885), p. 475 (p. 209 of the 1901 reprint). A second or two later the water from below arrives, the surface rises, and the ring darkens again.

Keep the words apart. Suction is the pull in damp sand, where air fills most of each gap. Negative excess pore pressure is the pull in saturated sand that is trying to swell faster than water can follow. Both make the grains press harder.

Check yourself You lift your foot out of the pale ring and the print turns dark and shiny for a moment. Why?

With the foot gone, the swollen sand settles back into its dense arrangement and shrinks. It now holds more water than its gaps need, and the extra is pushed up to the surface until it drains away.

The loose sand at the water's edge does the opposite. Each wiggle of your foot shears it, and its grains start to drop into the hollows below them. For the pack to shrink, water has to leave it, and water leaves sand only through the same narrow gaps. So the pack can't shrink yet. The water, squeezed between grains that are trying to close on it, rises in pressure: a positive Δu. It now carries part of the weight the grains were carrying, so they press on one another less, and grip less, and your foot sinks. Stand still for a few seconds and the water seeps away upward, the grains settle and press again, and the sand holds you once more.

A house on the same sand is a much bigger foot, and an earthquake shakes it for longer than you can wiggle. Make a prediction before reading on:

A house stands on loose sand that is full of water. An earthquake shakes the ground for a few seconds, too fast for the water to drain away. What happens to the house?

It sinks and tilts. Each shake lets loose grains drop toward the gaps below them; the water in those gaps can't escape in time, so its pressure rises and it takes the weight the grains were carrying. Grains that hardly press can hardly grip. Experiment 3 in the grain sandbox, Fig. 5.3, lets you watch it.

The question turns on its last words: too fast for the water to drain away. How fast is that?

5.3 A matter of time

Whether the water keeps up is a race between two clocks: how long the load takes to come on, and how long the water needs to move. If the water wins, its pressure stays at the still-water value while the grains rearrange, and engineers call the loading drained. If the load wins, the water is trapped, the soil can't change its volume, and the water pressure changes instead; that is undrained. The same sand can be either; what decides is how fast.

The water's clock can be worked out from things you already have. Picture a saturated layer L thick, with free-draining gravel at its top, and a load put on it suddenly. At first the water carries the whole of the new load as an excess pressure Δu. To hand it on to the grains, the layer must squeeze out enough water to let it shorten, and how far it shortens depends on its stiffness against squeezing, M, in kPa: a press of Δu shortens it by the fraction Δu/M of its thickness. That is a volume of water Δu·L/M under each square metre. Darcy's law, Eq. 3.2, says how fast it leaves: the excess is a head of Δu/γw spread over a path of length L, so each square metre passes k·Δu/(γw·L) cubic metres a second. Divide the volume by the rate. Δu cancels, and what is left is a time:Karl Terzaghi published the theory of how excess water pressure drains out of a layer of clay in 1923 (Terzaghi (1923)), two years before the book Chapter 4 credits with effective stress. The rough sum here gives the form of his answer; his full solution adds a factor close to 1 for most of the pressure to drain.

t ≈ L² ⁄ cv (5.2)
cv = k · M ⁄ γw (5.3)

t time for most of the excess pressure to drain (s) · L the longest path the water must travel to a free-draining face (m) · cv the coefficient of consolidation (m²/s) · k permeability (m/s) · M the soil's stiffness against squeezing (kPa) · γw = 9.81 kN/m³

Notice the square. A layer twice as thick has twice the water to lose along a path twice as long, so it takes four times as long. And notice the k. Sand lets water through a hundred thousand times more easily than clay, so for the same stiffness its water leaves a hundred thousand times sooner. The slow squeezing out of water under a new load is called consolidation.

Example 5.2

How long does a layer take to drain?

Given
Sand with k = 10⁻⁴ m/s and clay with k = 10⁻⁹ m/s, the permeabilities of Fig. 3.3. Stiffnesses, illustrative round numbers (real soils vary widely, and stiffen with depth): M = 20,000 kPa for the sand and 10,000 kPa for the clay. Layers 2 m and 10 m thick, each draining through one face.
Find
How long each layer takes to drain.
The idea
Work out cv from Eq. 5.3, then the time from Eq. 5.2.
  1. M ÷ γw = 20,000 ÷ 9.81 = 2,038.7 mthe sand's stiffness written as a height of water
  2. cv = 10⁻⁴ × 2,038.7 = 0.20387 m²/spermeability times that height
  3. t = 2² ÷ 0.20387 = 19.6 s2 m of sand
  4. t = 10² ÷ 0.20387 = 490.5 s10 m of sand: about 8.2 minutes
  5. M ÷ γw = 10,000 ÷ 9.81 = 1,019.4 mthe clay's stiffness as a height of water
  6. cv = 10⁻⁹ × 1,019.4 = 1.0194 × 10⁻⁶ m²/stimes 86,400 seconds in a day, 0.08807 m² a day
  7. t = 2² ÷ 0.08807 = 45.4 days2 m of clay
  8. t = 10² ÷ 0.08807 = 1,135 days10 m of clay
  9. 1,135 ÷ 365.25 = 3.11 yearsin years

The sand drains in 20 seconds (2 m) to about 8 minutes (10 m). The clay takes 45 days to 3.1 years.

Check. For the same 2 m layer the clay should take longer than the sand by the factor of 100,000 in k times the factor of 2 in M, so 200,000 times. In seconds the clay takes 45.4 × 86,400, and that divided by 19.6 s is about 200,000. The 10 m layers take 25 times as long as the 2 m ones, as the square says.

What it means. Sand is drained under anything slower than a few minutes and undrained under anything quicker: a footstep, an earthquake. Clay is undrained under almost everything except the slow work of months and years.

Laid on one line beside the loads a soil meets, those four times sort themselves. The strong shaking of the 1971 earthquake at Lower San Fernando Dam, which comes back below, lasted about 15 seconds:Strong shaking at the dam for about 15 s: ASDSO, Lower San Fernando Dam.

Notice where the bar for 2 m of sand ends: a little past the earthquake's line. The sand's water has barely started to leave when the shaking stops, and each swing of the ground, a small fraction of the whole, is far quicker still: the shaking is undrained. The clay bars run past the earthquake and the footstep by a long way, and the thickest runs past a year. A dam raised over clay a few metres at a time loads it undrained at first, and the clay hands the load from its water to its grains over the months that follow.

Check yourself A 4 m layer of clay has sand above it and sand below it, and water can leave through both faces. Does it drain faster or slower than a 2 m layer that drains through one face?

The same. Water in the middle of the 4 m layer has 2 m to go either way, so L is 2 m and t = 2² ÷ 0.08807 = 45.4 days. Drained through one face only, it would take four times as long.

5.4 The sandbox as a laboratory

The two clocks are hard to watch in real sand: the grains are small and the water is hidden. The sandbox below shows both. Every grain in it is simulated as a disc that pushes, rubs and rolls on its neighbours, and the water in the gaps is a pressure that rises when the pack is squeezed and falls when it swells. To shear the grains is to push the top sideways so that they slide past one another. The Drain switch sets the race: Open lets water flow in and out of the box freely, which is drained; Shut traps it, which is undrained.

The four experiments are this chapter's four cases: the damp castle, dense and loose sand sheared, the house on loose wet sand shaken, and dense wet sand sheared with its water trapped, which is the firm beach under your foot. Pick one, or set the box up yourself:

Notice two things the sandbox does that the rest of this chapter has only described. In Experiment 2 the dense sample's strength rises to a peak and then falls as it keeps swelling: once its grains have climbed out of each other's hollows, the pack is no longer dense, and it grips like loose sand. And in Experiment 4 the extra water pressure falls and then stops falling, near −100 kPa*. Water can be pulled only so hard before it boils into bubbles of vapour, which is called cavitation, and the model stops it there.Why about −100? Pressures in this book are gauge pressures, counted from the air's 101 kPa (U.S. Standard Atmosphere (1976)). Lower the water's pressure to near zero absolute, which is about −100 kPa gauge (strictly, to its vapour pressure, a little above zero absolute), and dissolved air and vapour come out of it as bubbles. So a dense sand sheared with its water trapped can gain only so much strength. Laboratory tests meet the same ceiling, which is why they are run with the water under raised pressure, and the sandbox copies it.

5.5 Liquefaction

Push Experiment 3 to its end and the loose sand's trapped water carries nearly all the load. The grains still touch, but they hardly press, the effective stress falls toward zero, and the grip goes with it. The sand flows like a heavy liquid. That is liquefaction, and your wiggling feet do a small version of it at the water's edge. It needs three things at once: loose grains, every gap full of water, and a load that comes faster than the water can leave. An earthquake supplies the speed, but any load that comes on fast enough will do, even a small slip that sets the grains moving. Liquefaction with no earthquake is called static liquefaction, and Chapter 8 meets it.

Water dams are not immune. Lower San Fernando Dam, north of Los Angeles, was begun in 1912 largely as hydraulic fill: soil sluiced into place with water, which settles loose and stays saturated. Early on 9 February 1971 an earthquake of magnitude 6.6 shook it hard for about 15 seconds. Within about 12 of them, the water pressure in the sandy fill near the base of the upstream slope had climbed so high that much of that fill had liquefied, and most of the upstream slope slid into the reservoir. What was left of the embankment stood about 1.5 m above the water, and that was with the water kept, since 1966, at least 2.9 m below its old maximum level. Some 80,000 people below the dam were evacuated for four days while the reservoir was pumped down, and nobody was killed at the dam.The slide and its cause: Seed et al. (1975). The date, magnitude, about 15 s of strong shaking with high water pressures after about 12 s, the 5 ft (1.5 m) of freeboard left, the 80,000 evacuated for four days and the 9.6 ft (2.9 m) cut in the maximum operating level in 1966: ASDSO, Lower San Fernando Dam.

Dense sand behaves differently. Once its grains start to slide they must climb over one another, the pack must swell, its water is pulled thin, and the grains press harder. That is why the densely packed heap of Fig. 1.1 held when it was jiggled. Engineers who want an embankment that will not liquefy compact its fill densely, layer by layer, as Chapter 9 describes.In 1936 Arthur Casagrande sheared loose and dense samples of sand side by side and found that both ended at the same density, which he called the critical void ratio: sand looser than that shrinks as it shears, and sand denser swells (Casagrande (1936)). Two years later the upstream slope of Fort Peck Dam in Montana, a hydraulic fill dam, slid during construction and killed eight men. The board that investigated blamed weak shale and bentonite under the dam, and thought liquefaction of the fill may have carried the slide further (ASDSO, Fort Peck Dam).

This is why mine waste worries engineers so much. The ground-up rock a mine pumps out as slurry, called tailings, often settles loose and stays saturated for decades, and Chapters 6 and 8 follow what that means for a dam that holds it back, or stands on it.

5.6 Clay, the slow soil

Everything so far was sand. Clay, the soil of the cores that Chapter 3 made watertight, follows the same rule, σ′ = σ − u, on a far slower clock. Its flakes are so small that its water needs about a decade to cross a metre of it (11 years in Fig. 3.3), and by Example 5.2 a 2 m layer takes weeks to drain and a 10 m layer years. So almost any load on clay starts undrained.

Clay also grips less than sand. Its flat flakes slide on one another more easily than rounded quartz grains climb over each other: the workbench of Chapter 13 gives its clay a friction angle of 26°, against 34° for the beach sand. Loaded slowly, so that its water keeps pace, a clay grips as Eq. 4.3 says, with σ′ · tan φ′.

Loaded fast, it is another matter, and the reason is the loose sand's. A soft clay that has never carried more load than it carries now is loosely packed for its load, and when it is sheared it tries to contract. Its water can't leave in time, so the water pressure rises, σ′ falls, and the grip falls with it. The strength a clay shows when it is sheared too fast for its water to move is its undrained strength, su. Engineers who worked back from failures of soft clay under embankments, footings and excavations found the average strength the clay had actually supplied along the slip, and Gholamreza Mesri showed in 1989 that laboratory tests give the same answer:Mesri (1989): su = 0.22 times the largest effective stress the clay has ever carried, which for a clay never loaded more than now is its present σ′; first from field failures, then confirmed from laboratory tests.

su ≈ 0.22 · σ′ (5.4)

su undrained strength of a soft clay never loaded more than now (kPa) · σ′ its effective stress before the fast loading began (kPa)

Example 5.3

The same clay, slow and fast

Given
A soft clay whose grains press with σ′ = 150 kPa (an illustrative value, about what 15 m of soil and water above might give) and friction angle φ′ = 26°, with no cohesion.
Find
The grip it offers when sheared slowly, and when sheared fast.
The idea
Slowly, the water keeps pace and the grip is σ′ · tan φ′ (Eq. 4.3). Fast, the clay tries to contract, its trapped water takes part of the press, and the grip is su (Eq. 5.4).
  1. tan 26° = 0.4877the clay's grip per kilopascal of press
  2. grip, slow = 150 × 0.4877 = 73.2 kPadrained: the water keeps up, σ′ stays at 150
  3. grip, fast = 0.22 × 150 = 33 kPaundrained: the trapped water takes part of the press
  4. 33 ÷ 73.2 = 0.45the fast grip as a share of the slow

Sheared slowly the clay grips with about 73 kPa; sheared fast, with about 33 kPa, less than half.

Check. The undrained grip is what the slow formula gives for a smaller press: 33 ÷ 0.4877 = 67.7 kPa. So the fast shear behaves as if the trapped water had taken about 80 of the grains' 150 kPa of press. That is a rough reading: the two strengths act on surfaces at different angles, and real clays scatter around 0.22, but the size of the gap is real.

What it means. The same clay, in the same place, has two strengths, and which one counts depends on how fast it is asked for.

Clay, loaded fast, can be weaker than the same clay loaded slowly. Of everything in this chapter, that is the sentence the last chapter of the book needs most.

Undrained isn't always weaker. A clay that was once pressed harder than it is now, by ice or by soil since worn away, is densely packed for its load, and behaves like dense sand: sheared fast, it tries to swell, its water pressure falls, and for a while it is stronger. The danger then comes later, as water seeps in and the extra strength seeps away. And any clay that has slid a long way along one surface loses more still, because its flakes line up along the slip; the grip left is its residual strength.

Check yourself A dam is raised over a 2 m layer of the example's clay, with sand beneath it, by one metre every month. Is each raise drained or undrained for the clay?

Each raise goes on in days, far quicker than the 45 days the layer needs, so each starts undrained. But a month is not much shorter than 45 days, so most of each raise's water pressure has seeped away before the next. Over the life of the dam the clay is largely drained; for any one fast event, such as a slip, it is undrained.

The film The same sand, three ways retells Part I, from the beach to this chapter's sandbox, in under nine minutes:

5.7 Where Part I comes back

Soil holds as well as its grains press on one another, and water in the gaps, pushing or pulling, changes that press. Every later chapter leans on that pair:

  • Chapter 6 · A lake can't lose strength. Tailings can. A water dam holds a liquid; a tailings dam holds a loose, saturated deposit that can liquefy.
  • Chapter 7 · A concrete dam is the block on the cushion. Water under its base carries part of its weight, and the friction that stops it sliding goes with it.
  • Chapter 8 · An upstream raise stands on tailings. If the tailings under it liquefy, the raise has nothing left to stand on.
  • Chapter 9 · The core takes the head so the downstream shell keeps its grip. Low water pressure behind the core means a high effective stress and a strong downstream slope. The upstream shell stays soaked, so it relies on draining freely.
  • Chapter 10 · Drains put the press back. Lowering the water inside a dam lowers the pore pressure, so the grains press harder.
  • Chapter 11 · Sand boils: water flowing up can lift the grains. When its push on them equals their weight under water, the effective stress is zero and the sand boils.
  • Chapter 12 · A slope's water can't always leave as fast as the reservoir does. Let a reservoir down quickly and the upstream shell's water pressure lags behind, with nothing outside to balance it.
  • Chapter 13 · Your design is judged on this. The stability check weighs the friction the grains can supply against what's needed, using the water pressures from the seepage calculation.

What to remember

  • Water can pull as well as push. In damp sand its rings press the grains together, but only with a fraction of a kilopascal: enough for a wall a quarter of a metre tall, never one of thirty.
  • Sheared, densely packed grains must swell and loosely packed grains must shrink. Where the water can't follow, the dense sand's water is pulled thin and its grains press harder; the loose sand's water takes their weight and they press less.
  • Whether the water follows is a race between the load and the drainage time, t ≈ L²/cv: seconds to minutes for sand, months to years for clay. Drained if the water wins, undrained if the load does.
  • Liquefaction is the loose case taken to its end: loose, saturated and loaded faster than it can drain, the grains stop pressing on one another and the soil flows.
  • Clay, loaded fast, can be weaker than the same clay loaded slowly.

Questions

  1. 5.1

    Explain, in the terms of this chapter, why the firm sand goes pale under one foot while the sand at the water's edge swallows the other.

    Hint

    Which sand is dense and which loose? What must each do when it is sheared, and what does the water do meanwhile?

    Answer

  2. 5.2

    Run Experiment 4: dense, saturated sand, drain shut, sheared. Why does the grain stress rise with the drain shut, and stay level when you run it again with the drain open? And why does the extra water pressure stop falling where it does?

    Hint

    Dense sand must swell to shear. Where does the water to fill the new space come from in each case? Then read the model's lowest allowed water pressure in the caption.

  3. 5.3

    Run Experiment 3, the house on loose saturated sand with the drain shut. On the chart, does the grain stress fall all at once or a little with each shake? Then open the drain and shake again: what changes, and does the house still settle?

    Hint

    Each shake lets a few grains drop toward the gaps. With the drain shut, where does the water they displace go? With it open?

    Answer

  4. 5.4

    Using the illustrative soils of Example 5.2: is a 3 m layer of sand, draining through one face, drained during 15 seconds of earthquake shaking? Is a 5 m layer of clay drained under a dam raised 5 m in a year?

    t = L² ÷ cv, with cv = 0.20387 m²/s for the sand and 0.08807 m² a day for the clay.

    Answer

  5. 5.5

    Lower San Fernando was a water dam, yet in 1971 its upstream slope failed the way loose mine waste fails. What did it have in common with tailings, and why did 15 seconds of shaking matter?

Department of Civil Engineering, University of Washington. https://depts.washington.edu/liquefy/html/main.html gentle A plain-language tour of liquefaction: what it is, the earthquakes that taught engineers about it, why loose saturated sand is the culprit (with Casagrande's critical void ratio), and what can be done about it.
  • Terzaghi, K., Peck, R.B., Mesri, G. (1996). Soil Mechanics in Engineering Practice, 3rd ed. New York: Wiley. serious The working engineer's textbook, begun by the man who founded the subject. Read its treatment of consolidation, and of the strength of sands and clays under drained and undrained loading, for the full versions of this chapter's two rough sums.
  • Reynolds, O. (1885). On the dilatancy of media composed of rigid particles in contact. With experimental illustrations. Philosophical Magazine, Series 5, 20(127): 469–481. doi:10.1080/14786448508627791 primary source Thirteen pages that named dilatancy: the sealed rubber bag of shot and water that goes rigid, and the pale footprint on p. 475 (p. 209 of the 1901 reprint, free online), where "the sand is full of water".

A reservoir of water has no strength to lose: it is a liquid already. Some dams hold back loose, saturated, ground-up rock that does have strength, and can lose it in seconds. What changes when the thing behind the dam can lose its own strength?

Chapter 6 · Part II · Two kinds of dam

Two dams, two jobs

What changes when the thing behind the dam can lose its own strength?

So far. Part I built one idea from a beach, a bucket and a block on a ramp: soil holds only as well as its grains press on one another, and the water between them can take that press away, all at once when it cannot get out in time (Chapter 5). Part II puts the idea to work on real dams, starting with two that look alike in section and do opposite jobs.

After this chapter you can

  • set a water dam beside a tailings dam and say how they differ in what they hold, how long they must last and how they have failed;
  • work out the power of a hydro plant and the load on its dam, and tell the depth that loads a dam from the head that drives its turbines;
  • explain why a tailings beach sorts its own grains, and why every dam must pass its flood with metres to spare.

This chapter adds freeboard mark and a spillway notch at the crest

2 figures · about 20 min to read

At 12:28 in the afternoon on 25 January 2019, a video camera above an iron mine near Brumadinho, in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais, was looking across the valley at the face of a dam. Dam I held about 12.7 million cubic metres of waste from the mine, the Córrego do Feijão, and nothing had been added to it for two and a half years. A drone had filmed it seven days before and seen nothing wrong. Its instruments had recorded nothing that mattered either: survey markers on the crest, tubes that measure movement deep inside it, radar watching the face, and gauges reading the water pressure within it.Robertson et al. (2019), pp. i–ii (the time, the drone, the instruments, deposition ending July 2016), p. 5 (the camera) and p. 12 (the volume stored).

In the footage the crest sags first, along most of the dam's length. A fifth of a second later the face bulges outward, low down, just above the toe. Five seconds in, water spurts out near the toe. In under ten seconds the whole slope has collapsed, and what was a slope is a heavy liquid, moving. Within five minutes 9.7 million m³ of tailings, three quarters of everything the dam held, had poured out. The flow ran through the mine's canteen and offices, through houses and farms, and on down the valley to the Paraopeba River. It killed 270 people; 11 of them were never found.The sequence, the volume and the flow's path: Robertson et al. (2019), pp. i, 3, 5–6. The toll, 259 deaths and 11 people missing: Franks et al. (2021), p. 1.

When a water dam fails, water escapes. Here the dam itself went liquid. The ground-up rock behind its face had stood as a slope for decades, firm enough to walk on, and in seconds it had no grip left. A lake has no grip to lose; it is a liquid already. That difference is this chapter's question: what changes when the thing behind the dam can lose its own strength?

6.1 Two jobs

A hydroelectric dam holds back water, and the water is the product. Its height above the turbines is stored energy, released on demand. A tailings dam holds back mine waste, called tailings: rock ground to sand, silt and finer, pumped out of the mill as a slurry with the water used to process it. Nobody wants it back. The job is to keep it in place, forever.

There is a great deal of it. In April 2019, after Brumadinho, a group of investors asked the world's listed mining companies to describe their tailings facilities. The 107 companies that replied listed 1,743 of them, holding 44.5 billion m³; spread evenly over Manhattan, the authors worked out, that would stand 750 m deep. The same companies expected to add about 2.5 billion m³ a year.Franks et al. (2021), pp. 1–2.

Both kinds of dam face the physics of Chapters 2 and 3. Water pressure grows by 9.81 kPa for every metre of depth, which comes to nearly 1,000 kPa, or 1 MPa, at the foot of a 100 m reservoir, and water seeps through anything that isn't perfectly tight. Below, one of each is drawn in section, side by side:

Notice that on the left the dimension H stops at the tailwater, while the pressure triangle on the dam's face runs on down to the heel. Notice too, on the right, that the pond lies at the far end of the beach, as far from the dam as the deposit allows. The rest of the chapter takes those two details in turn.

6.2 Head drives the turbines, depth loads the dam

Start with the water dam, because its sums are short. A cubic metre of water weighs 9.81 kN. Let it fall H metres and gravity does 9.81 × H kilojoules of work on it, since a kilojoule is a kilonewton moved through a metre. The turbine catches as much of that as it can. Send Q cubic metres through every second and the power is the energy each cubic metre gives up, times the cubic metres per second, less what the machines lose:

P = η · ρ · g · Q · H(6.1)

P power (W, watts; a megawatt, MW, is a million watts) · η efficiency, the share of the falling water's energy that the turbine and generator turn into electricity · ρ 1,000 kg/m³ · g 9.81 m/s² · Q flow through the turbines (m³/s) · H head, the drop from the reservoir surface to the tailwater, strictly the gross head (m)

The figure takes η = 0.90 for the turbine and generator together.H here is the gross head, surface to surface. Part of it is spent pushing the water through the intake and the penstock, so the turbine itself works on a little less, the net head. The figure uses the gross head, and folds the losses on the way into one efficiency. At its opening settings:

Example 6.1

The power of a drop

Given
A turbine flow Q = 150 m³/s falling a head H = 84.8 m (the figure rounds it to 85); efficiency η = 0.90; water weighs 9.81 kN/m³. At the highest reservoir level the head is 92 m.
Find
The power, and the flow that would give 200 MW at the highest level.
The idea
Energy per cubic metre, times cubic metres per second, times the share the machines keep (Eq. 6.1).
  1. Each m³: 9.81 × 84.8 = 831.888 kJits weight times the drop; a kilonewton through a metre is a kilojoule
  2. Each second: 831.888 × 150 = 124,783 kW150 cubic metres every second; a kilojoule each second is a kilowatt
  3. Kept: 0.9 × 124,783 = 112,305 kW = 112.3 MWthe turbine and generator keep 90%; a megawatt is 1,000 kW
  4. At 92 m, per m³/s: 0.9 × 9.81 × 92 = 812.268 kWthe same three steps with one cubic metre a second
  5. Q = 200,000 ÷ 812.268 = 246.2 m³/s200 MW is 200,000 kW

The plant makes 112 MW, the figure's readout. With the reservoir at its highest, 200 MW takes 246 m³/s, inside the Turbine flow slider's range.

Check. Power is proportional to flow, so each cubic metre a second is worth 112,305 ÷ 150 = 748.7 kW at this head, and doubling the flow to 300 m³/s should double the power: the figure gives 224.6 MW.

What it means. A hydro plant sells head and flow in equal measure. The height of its water is what it earns from, and, as the next example shows, it is also what the dam has to hold.

The turbine in the figure turns at the same speed whatever the flow, and that is deliberate.Every generator on a grid has to keep step with the grid's alternating current, 60 cycles a second in North America, so it turns at one fixed speed; the rotors at Mica and Revelstoke turn at 112.5 revolutions a minute (BC Hydro (2016)). Open the gates wider and the water pushes the runner harder, so the generator delivers more power at the same speed. More flow means more push on the runner at the same speed.

One could assume that the H that drives the turbines is also the depth that loads the dam. But look at the left drawing again: H ends at the tailwater, and the dam's upstream face goes on below it, down to the heel on the rock. The water against the dam is deeper than the drop it makes past it. The figure's readouts use the depth, and a reader who checks them with H gets the wrong answer:

Example 6.2

Depth, not head

Given
The figure at its opening settings: the water is 88.8 m deep at the heel and the head is 84.8 m. Water weighs 9.81 kN/m³.
Find
The pressure at the heel, the push of the water on each metre of dam and the height it acts at; then the same two numbers worked, wrongly, from H.
The idea
The load is the pressure triangle on the whole wet face (Eqs. 2.1 and 2.2), and the face is wet all the way down to the heel.
  1. p = 9.81 × 88.8 = 871.1 kPa = 0.87 MPathe pressure at the bottom of the wet face
  2. F = ½ × 9.81 × 88.8² = 38,678 kNthe area of the triangle, per metre length of dam
  3. Height: 88.8 ÷ 3 = 29.6 m above the basethe triangle's centre, a third of the way up
  4. From H: 9.81 × 84.8 = 831.9 kPaa pressure taken at the tailwater, 4 m too high
  5. ½ × 9.81 × 84.8² = 35,272 kNthe push on a face that stopped at the tailwater

The heel feels 0.87 MPa and each metre of dam carries 38.7 MN, acting 29.6 m up: the figure's 0.87 MPa and 39 MN. Worked from H, the load comes out 8.8% short.

Check. The two depths differ by 4 m, the tailwater over the base, so the two pressures should differ by 9.81 × 4 = 39.24 kPa, and 871.1 − 831.9 = 39.2.

What it means. The depth of water at the dam sets its load; the drop to the tailwater sets its power. The tailwater also pushes back on the downstream face, a push this figure leaves out; Chapter 7 adds it, and the water underneath the dam.

Check yourself With the reservoir held where it is, the turbines are opened from 150 to 300 m³/s. What happens to the water load on the dam?

Nothing. The load comes from the depth at the heel, still 88.8 m. Only the power changes: it doubles, to 224.6 MW.

The drawing shows a concrete dam, but a water dam need not be concrete, and in British Columbia most of the big ones are not. Mica, on the Columbia, is an earthfill dam 244 m high, the tallest in the province, and W.A.C. Bennett on the Peace, the dam Chapter 9 opens with, is earthfill 183 m high. Revelstoke, downstream of Mica, has the concrete dam Chapter 2 measured.Mica and Revelstoke: BC Hydro (2016). Bennett: BC Hydro (2020). A dam is a water dam because of what it holds back.

6.3 A beach that sorts itself

The other half of the figure works differently. The mill sends its tailings out as slurry, and from the spigots along the crest it pours onto the deposit and runs downhill toward the pond. As the flow spreads and slows it drops what it carries, and it drops the biggest grains first. The coarse sand settles close to the spigots and builds the tailings beach, sloping gently away from the dam. The finest grains stay in suspension far longer and settle in the pond at the far end. A mine builds a beach, as the sea does, and sorts it the way a river sorts its bed. Why the sizes part so cleanly takes one new fact, about how grains sink; why it matters to the dam takes Darcy's law from Chapter 3. The numbers below are illustrative, chosen to be typical:

Example 6.3

Why the beach sorts, and why that helps

Given
Illustrative grains: fine sand 0.1 mm across, slime 0.01 mm. For grains this small, the speed at which a grain sinks through still water grows with the square of its size. Permeability: tailings sand 10⁻⁵ m/s (the workbench's, in Chapter 13), slimes an illustrative 10⁻⁸ m/s; gap fraction 0.4 for both.
Find
How much faster the sand settles out, and how long water takes to cross a metre of each.
The idea
Settling sorts the grains; Darcy's law then says how fast each kind drains. The crossing time is Fig. 3.3's: gap fraction ÷ (k × gradient), here with a gradient of 1.
  1. Size: 0.1 ÷ 0.01 = 10the sand grain is ten times wider
  2. Sinking speed: 10 × 10 = 100speed grows with the square of the size
  3. Permeability: 10⁻⁵ ÷ 10⁻⁸ = 1,000how much more easily water passes the sand
  4. Sand: 0.4 ÷ 10⁻⁵ = 40,000 s = 11.1 ha metre of sand, at a gradient of 1
  5. Slimes: 0.4 ÷ 10⁻⁸ = 4 × 10⁷ s = 463 daysthe same metre of slimes

The sand sinks out of the slurry about 100 times faster than the slimes, so it settles by the dam, and it passes water 1,000 times as easily: water crosses a metre of it in about half a day, and a metre of slimes in more than a year.

Check. Fig. 3.3 gave 46.3 days for silt with k = 10⁻⁷ m/s and the same gap fraction. A k ten times smaller should take ten times as long: 10 × 46.3 = 463 days.

What it means. The sorting does the dam a favour. It puts coarse sand that drains in hours next to the dam, where the deposit must be firm, and keeps the wet, slow slimes far away. The favour holds only while the pond stays at the far end of the beach.

Check yourself A mine lets its pond spread until the water lies against the crest. What now sits against the dam?

Water, and the slimes that settle out of it: the finest, wettest, slowest-draining tailings, where the dam most needs firm, drained ground. That is why tailings rules keep the pond far from the crest (Chapter 8).

6.4 What differs is almost everything else

The physics of the two dams is the same: pressure that grows with depth, and water that seeps from high head to low. Almost everything else about them differs:

Notice the two rows that decide most of what follows. A water dam is built once and then watched; a tailings dam is raised for as long as the mine runs and then has to stand indefinitely after it, earning nothing.The Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management was published in August 2020 by a review that the International Council on Mining and Metals, the United Nations Environment Programme and the Principles for Responsible Investment set up after Brumadinho (GISTM (2020)). It is the first standard meant to apply to tailings facilities anywhere, new or old. And when a water dam fails it lets out water, while a tailings dam lets out a deposit that may itself have turned to liquid.

6.5 Why tailings dams fail differently

Water has no strength to lose. A deposit of loose, saturated tailings has some, and can lose nearly all of it at once: it is the liquid beach from Chapter 5 at the scale of a mine. Sheared, the loose grains try to pack tighter, the trapped water takes over their load, and the deposit flows like a heavy fluid. That is liquefaction. An earthquake can set it off. So can something much quieter, with no shaking at all (static liquefaction): a rising water table, slow creep, or a small movement of the slope. It does not lose quite all: a liquefied deposit keeps a small residual strength, and what is left of its grip decides how far it runs before it stops.

Six failures show the range. For each, the table gives what the mine produced, how the dam was raised, what set it off, and what happened:

Notice that every dam in the table that killed people was raised the same way. Upstream means that each new wall was built out over the tailings already in place, so that the dam stands partly on its own loose, wet waste; Chapter 8 shows what that means and why some countries now forbid it. Notice too the trigger column. At Stava and at Brumadinho nothing came from outside at all, and at Fundão three small tremors only hastened a failure already well under way. A deposit that is loose and saturated can be brought down by a small push, or by none that anyone saw.

Two rows do not fit. Mount Polley, in British Columbia, the dam of the Prologue, was raised by a variant of the centreline method that Chapter 8 describes, and nobody died. It was not a liquefaction of the tailings. Its cause is the subject of Chapter 13, and the chapters between here and there collect what you need to follow it.

Merriespruit is the other. Its tailings probably did liquefy, as a later study argued, but only after water had poured over the crest for an hour or two and washed away the wall in front of them. What failed first was not the grip between grains at all. That failure belongs to a different story from the one this book mostly tells, and it is the commonest single way an embankment dam dies.

6.6 Every dam needs a door

Most people picture a dam failing because the water pushes it over or bursts through it. For embankment dams the commonest single way is simpler: the water goes over the top, which engineers call overtopping. Foster, Fell and Spannagle went through the record of large embankment dams built up to 1986 and sorted the failures that happened in service by how each one began:

Notice that the shares add to more than 100%. Of the 124 failures, 117 have a known cause, and the counts in the main rows add to 119, because two failures were filed under two headings. Statistics like these are counts of messy events sorted into boxes that overlap, and nobody should read the decimals as exact. Two things are plain all the same. About a third of these failures began with water over the crest, and about half did once the failed spillways and gates are added. Most of the other half is water inside the dam carrying its soil away, which Chapter 11 takes up.Foster, Fell & Spannagle (2000), failures in operation; the counts as reproduced in Adamo et al. (2020), which also gives the size of the record, 11,192 dams.

The sentence on this book's title page does not reach those overtopping failures. A flood pouring over an embankment does not need water in the gaps to take the grains' press away. It runs down the outer face fast, drags the grains off the surface and carries them away, and each grain it takes uncovers the next. A heap of earth can be cut through in a few hours; at Merriespruit an hour or two of water over the crest was enough. A concrete gravity dam can be built with its own crest as the spillway; an embankment cannot.Merriespruit: Fourie, Blight & Papageorgiou (2001), p. 708. An overflow crest "may make up an entire gravity dam": USBR (1987), §9.8(c). So every dam needs a door, a way to let a flood past that is not over the crest.

The door is a spillway: a channel past the dam, usually at one end of it, with a crest, the sill the water pours over, set lower than the crest of the dam. In ordinary times the lake is kept at or below the spillway's crest. When a flood comes in faster than the turbines and outlets can pass it, the lake rises and begins to pour over the sill, and the higher it rises, the faster it pours. It goes on rising until the spillway passes water as fast as the flood brings it. The designer's job is to make sure that happens with the lake still below the dam's crest, by a margin called the freeboard. Here are both, to scale, for an illustrative embankment 30 m high:

Notice that the freeboard is measured from the flood level, not from the normal one. The 5 m between the lake's everyday level and the crest is not all margin: the flood spends 3 m of it just to make the spillway pass the water.

How much a spillway passes depends on how deep the lake stands over its crest. The sheet of water pouring over is a fixed share of that height, h, deep (about two thirds of it, over a broad crest), and it moves at a speed that grows with the square root of h, so the flow over each metre of crest grows as h × √h, which is h to the power 3/2:

Q = C · L · h3/2(6.2)

Q flow over the spillway (m³/s) · L length of its crest, across the flow (m) · h height of the lake above the crest, measured upstream where the water is still level (m) · C a coefficient set by the shape of the crest (m½/s)

For a flat, broad crest, theory gives C = (2/3)3/2 × √g = 1.70 m½/s, which is the 3.087 that the Bureau of Reclamation's Design of Small Dams gives in feet. A rounded crest shaped to fit the falling water, over a deep approach, does better: the same book takes 4.0 in feet, 2.21 m½/s.USBR (1987), §9.10, equation (3) (p. 365), §9.12(a) for 3.087 (p. 369) and §9.12(d) for 4.0 (p. 370). A coefficient in feet becomes one in metres on multiplying by √0.3048: 3.087 gives 1.70. The example takes a round value between the two:

Example 6.4

The flood a spillway passes

Given
The illustrative dam of Fig. 6.2: spillway crest, and normal level, at 25 m; dam crest at 30 m. A design flood raises the lake to 28 m, so h = 3 m. The spillway's crest is L = 50 m long with C = 2.0 m½/s.
Find
The flow the spillway passes at that level, and the freeboard left.
The idea
Eq. 6.2, then the crest minus the flood level.
  1. √3 = 1.732the square root of the height over the crest
  2. h3/2 = 3 × 1.732 = 5.196depth times the square root of depth
  3. Q = 2.0 × 50 × 5.196 = 519.6 m³/stimes the coefficient and the length of crest
  4. Freeboard: 30 − 28 = 2 mwhat is left between the flood and the crest

The spillway passes about 520 m³/s with the lake 3 m over its crest, leaving 2 m of freeboard.

Check. The units come out right: m½/s × m × m3/2 is m³/s. And each metre of crest carries 519.6 ÷ 50 = 10.4 m³/s, about what a sheet of water a couple of metres deep carries at five metres a second.

What it means. The margin is counted in metres of water, and every metre of flood rise is a metre of freeboard spent. Because the flow grows faster than the rise, a bigger flood costs less extra height than you might fear; a flood the spillway was never designed for can still spend the rest.

Check yourself The flood turns out 10% bigger than the one the spillway was designed for. Does the lake rise 10% higher over the crest?

Less. With Q growing as h3/2, h grows as Q2/3: 1.12/3 = 1.066, so h goes from 3 m to 3.20 m, only 6.6% higher, and 1.80 m of freeboard is left.

Spillways can fail too, and when one does, the freeboard is tested in earnest.On 7 February 2017 the concrete chute of the main spillway at Oroville Dam, California, broke up while carrying a flood: water forced through cracks and joints lifted a section of the slab, and the weak rock beneath it washed out. With the main spillway damaged, the lake rose over the emergency spillway's weir for the first time in the dam's history, and the ground below the weir eroded so fast that about 188,000 people downstream were ordered to leave. The dam itself, an embankment 770 feet (235 m) high and the tallest in the United States, held (Oroville Independent Forensic Team (2018), pp. S-1, 7 and 26). Why water under a slab lifts it is a subject of Chapter 7. A tailings dam usually has no spillway at all. It stores the flood in its pond and pumps the water back to the mill, which works only if the pond has room. Suppose, for illustration, that a design flood brings 3 million m³ into a pond of 2 km²: the pond rises 3,000,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 1.5 m. That 1.5 m, plus room for waves, has to be kept empty below the crest all year round, and kept while the dam is raised and the deposit climbs. Merriespruit's history records too little freeboard and often poor control of its pond.Fourie, Blight & Papageorgiou (2001), p. 707: "insufficient freeboard provision and often poor pool control". Water over the top of a tailings dam does what it does to any embankment, and then it uncovers what lies behind the wall: tailings that may be loose, saturated, and ready to flow.

What to remember

  • A water dam holds a liquid, which has no grip to lose. A tailings dam holds loose, saturated ground rock whose grains grip only while they press on one another, and the water in its gaps can take that press away in seconds.
  • The head H, reservoir to tailwater, drives the turbines: P = η·ρ·g·Q·H, 112 MW in the figure. The depth of water at the heel, a few metres more, sets the load on the dam: 38.7 MN on each metre.
  • Slurry sorts itself: coarse sand settles by the dam and drains fast, so its grains press firmly on one another; the slimes settle by the pond and drain about a thousand times more slowly. The sorting helps only while the pond is kept away from the dam.
  • Every deadly failure in the case table was of a dam raised upstream, standing partly on its own loose, wet waste, and twice nothing from outside set it off at all.
  • Water over the crest, with failed spillways and gates, began about half the failures of large embankment dams, and it washes grains away however hard they press. Every dam needs a spillway, and freeboard above the flood.

Questions

    At a turbine flow of 150 m³/s, drag Reservoir level from its lowest to its highest. By what factor does the power grow, and by what factor the water load on the dam? Why are they different?

    Hint

    The power follows the head H; the load follows the square of the depth at the heel.

Before we watch a tailings dam grow, look at the simplest dam of all, the left half of this chapter's figure: a block of concrete that holds its lake by weight alone, pressing on the rock. Chapter 4 showed what water underneath a block on a ramp does to that press. Can the lake get under a concrete dam, and what is left of its grip when it does?
