7

Chapter 7 · Part II · Two kinds of dam

A block on a cushion of water

A concrete dam weighs more than twice the push of the water on it. Why isn't that the end of the story?

The danger peculiar to high dams, as they have been built until now, abroad as much as in France, comes from the uplift, or upward pressure, that water produces in them when it gets into the masonry through cracks over a large enough extent.

Maurice Lévy, Quelques considérations sur la construction des grands barrages, 1895 (translated)

So far. Chapter 2 worked out the push of a lake on a dam, and why a concrete dam is a triangle. Chapter 4 put a block on a ramp and showed that water under it takes away the press its grip depends on. Chapter 6 set the water dam, whose water is the product, beside the tailings dam. This chapter takes the simplest water dam of all, a block of concrete that holds its lake by weight alone, and finds the block's weakness in it.

After this chapter you can

  • work out the weight, the push, the uplift and the factor of safety against sliding of a concrete gravity dam, with its drains working and clogged;
  • explain how a grout curtain and a line of drains spend the water's head before it reaches the base, and why the grip of the rock matters as much as the weight;
  • find where the resultant crosses the base, apply the middle-third rule, and say what Lévy asked for after Bouzey and why.

This chapter adds a small concrete block beside the dam, with uplift arrows under it

3 figures · about 20 min to read · Film 7.1, 5 min 13 s

On 14 March 1884 the reservoir behind the new dam at Bouzey, in the Vosges hills of eastern France, was filling for the first time. The dam was a wall of stone masonry 22 m high, built to store water for the Canal de l'Est, and it stood on sandstone laid down in flat beds.Height, foundation and the events of 1884 and 1895: USBR (1998), pp. 16–17. The canal: Bordes (2010), p. 104. With the water a little over 3 m below the crest, a 135 m length of the wall slid as much as 34 cm downstream on its foundation. It sheared off the key that anchored its heel in the rock, and the leaks below the dam jumped to 230 litres a second.

The wall moved no further. In 1888 and 1889 the engineers thickened its lower third with a buttress of new masonry on the downstream side and sealed the crack along the heel; a drainage gallery was proposed and turned down.The buttress: USBR (1998), p. 16; the 4 m crest, its Fig. BF-1. The gallery that was proposed and set aside: Bordes (2010), p. 104. The upper two thirds kept their thin original section, 4 m thick at the crest.

On 27 April 1895, with the reservoir 55 cm below the crest, the upper wall broke away along 170 m of its length. The break ran almost level through the masonry about 10.5 m below the crest, well above the foundation, which this time did not move. The water went down the valley of the Avière through Bouzey and the villages below it. Accounts of the dead differ; the figure most often given is 87.The break: USBR (1998), pp. 16–17. The toll of 87: Bordes (2010), p. 76; the same article gives 70 on p. 104, and USBR (1998), p. 17, "more than 100".

Engineers argued over the cause: the mortar, the thin upper wall. But masonry cannot lose its strength the way the loose wet sand of Chapter 1 did, and nothing had shaken it. So what pushed the wall along its foundation in 1884, and what broke it in two in 1895? The answer that came out of Bouzey is the cushion of water from Chapter 4, at the base of a dam and in the cracks inside one.

7.1 The block, grown into a dam

Take the triangle of Fig. 2.3, 50 m tall and 40 m wide at its base, and lean it against a wall of concrete 8 m thick and 60 m tall, whose top carries a road. That makes the gravity dam of this chapter, 48 m wide at its base, drawn to scale in Fig. 7.1. Fill its reservoir to 57 m, 3 m below the crest, and let the river below it, the tailwater, run 5 m deep.Not every big water dam is concrete. British Columbia's tallest, Mica on the Columbia, is earthfill, 244 m high and nearly a kilometre thick at its base. Revelstoke, downstream, is a concrete gravity dam 175 m high (BC Hydro (2016), slides 7 and 8; BC Hydro (2013)).

Each metre of the dam is a slab of concrete 1,480 m² in section, and concrete weighs 23.5 kN/m³, so each metre of dam weighs 23.5 × 1,480 = 34,780 kN, or 34.78 MN. The reservoir pushes on its upright face with ½ × 9.81 × 57² = 15,936 kN (Eq. 2.2), and the river pushes back on the toe with 123 kN. The net push, F, is 15,814 kN, or 15.81 MN.

Weight holds a gravity dam the way it held the block in Fig. 4.1, by pressing on what is underneath: the dam is that block on level ground. The push F tries to slide it downstream; the rock grips back with the press times tan φ, where φ is the friction angle between concrete and rock. Take φ = 45°, so tan φ = 1, and count no glue. The factor of safety against sliding, the grip on offer divided by the grip needed, is then 34,780 ÷ 15,814 = 2.20: the opening question's dam, more than twice as heavy as the push on it.

But the block in Fig. 4.1 also had a thin cushion of water under its base, and the question about the cushion showed what that does to a grip. The dam stands on rock, and rock is cracked.

Check yourself With only 30 m of water behind it, is the same dam about twice as safe against sliding?

Far safer than that. The push grows with the square of the depth, so at 30 m it is only ½ × 9.81 × (30² − 5²) = 4,292 kN, and the weight is 8.10 times that. A gravity dam is in most danger in its last few metres of water.

7.2 Water under the base

One could assume a dam this heavy would hardly notice water under it. Concrete is 2.4 times as heavy as water, and the water in a crack is a film millimetres thick. To test the idea, go back to the hole in the sand of §2.7, which fills from below because the water in the gaps is joined to the sea. The rock under a dam is cracked by joints and by the partings between its beds, and the reservoir fills them in the same way. At the heel, where the base meets the reservoir, the water in the cracks has the full pressure of the 57 m above it, 9.81 × 57 = 559 kPa. The film holds almost no water, but Example 2.3 showed that a thin layer of water presses as hard as the depth it hangs from.

At the toe the water in the cracks is at the river's pressure, 49 kPa. In between it creeps from high head to low, and if the rock is the same all the way across, it loses its head evenly with distance, as the water did in the uniform sand of Fig. 3.2. So the pressure under the base falls in a straight line from heel to toe, pushing up on every square metre of the base. That push from below is called uplift, U. Before the numbers, a guess:

Nothing is done to stop the water: no drains, no seal. What share of the 60 m dam's weight does the uplift take away?

About two fifths, 42%. The comparison that matters is per square metre of base. The dam is on average only 30.8 m of concrete deep over its 48 m base, pressing the rock with 725 kPa. The water under it presses up with 304 kPa on average, the mean of 559 and 49. The next figure draws it to scale.

To decide, compare the two per square metre of base: how hard the concrete presses down on the rock, and how hard the water presses up. Here is the dam with its forces, drawn to scale:

Notice that the uplift arrow is nearly as long as the push, although the cracks hold very little water: the uplift is pressure spread over 48 m of base. The wedge under the base does in the dam what the cushion did in Fig. 4.1. It carries part of the weight, so the dam presses on the rock with less, and the grip shrinks with the press. The factor of safety becomes

FS = (W − U) · tan φ ÷ F (7.1)

W weight of the dam · U uplift on its base · F net push of the water, all per metre of dam (kN or MN) · φ friction angle between dam and rock. This is Eq. 4.1 on level ground, with W − U the press left.

Example 7.1

Water under the base, with nothing done about it

Given
The 60 m dam: weight 34,780 kN and net push 15,814 kN per metre, base 48 m, reservoir 57 m and river 5 m above the base, tan φ = 1. Water weighs 9.81 kN/m³.
Find
The uplift with no drains, its share of the weight, and the factor of safety against sliding.
The idea
The pressure under the base falls in a straight line from the reservoir's at the heel to the river's at the toe, and a straight-line wedge pushes as hard as its average all the way across.
  1. Mean head under the base: halfway between 57 and 5 m = 31 ma wedge that falls evenly averages its two ends
  2. U = 9.81 × 31 × 48 = 14,597 kNthe mean pressure times the base, a metre long
  3. 14,597 ÷ 34,780 = 0.420the share of the weight the water carries
  4. Press left: 34,780 − 14,597 = 20,183 kNW − U, what the grip works with
  5. FS = 20,183 ÷ 15,814 = 1.276Eq. 7.1 with tan 45° = 1

With no drains the water lifts 14.60 MN off each metre of dam, 42% of its weight, and the factor of safety falls from 2.20 to 1.28.

Check. Compare pressures instead of forces. Spread over its base, the section is 30.833 m of concrete deep on average, pressing with 23.5 × 30.833 = 724.6 kPa. The water under it averages 9.81 × 31 = 304.1 kPa, and 304.1 ÷ 724.6 = 0.420, the same share.

What it means. Nothing about the concrete changed. Water in the rock took away two fifths of the press that gives the dam its grip, and with it most of the margin the weight seemed to promise.

7.3 Drains, and what happens when they clog

The weight is fixed, and so is the lake. What an engineer can change is the water under the base, with two rows of holes. Near the heel runs a grout curtain: holes drilled deep into the rock in a line along the dam and pumped full of cement grout, to seal as many cracks as they can reach. A few metres downstream runs a line of drains, drilled into the rock from a gallery, a tunnel along the dam inside it, close to the base. Water that reaches a drain rises into the gallery and is led away, so the pressure at the drain line can be little more than the gallery's own.Foundation drains as 3-inch (76 mm) holes on 10-foot (3 m) centres, the rule below taken as conservative when they reach 40 to 50 per cent of the dam's height: USBR (1987), §8.10, p. 321.

How much do drains take off? Nobody can see into the rock, and the answer depends on which cracks the holes happen to cross. Designers start from a rule. The US Bureau of Reclamation's rule assumes that the head at the drain line is the tailwater's, plus a third of the difference between the reservoir and the tailwater:

hd = ht + (hr − ht) ÷ 3 (7.2)

hd head at the drain line · ht head of the tailwater · hr head of the reservoir, all in metres above the base. On either side of the drain line the pressure is taken to fall in a straight line.

In the language of Chapter 3, the water reaches the heel with 52 m of head to lose before it gets out at the toe. Uniform rock would spend it evenly; the curtain and the drains make it spend two thirds of it in the first 6 m.The one-third rule: USBR (1987), §8.10, pp. 320–321. The US Army Corps of Engineers is more cautious: its drains remove 25 to 50 per cent of the straight-line pressure above the tailwater's at the drain line, up to 67 per cent with tests to justify it (USACE EM 1110-2-2200, para. 3-3.d(1)(c)). The figure below draws the dam with its curtain, gallery and drains. Switch Foundation drains between Working and Clogged, and move the Reservoir slider:

Notice that the pressure at the heel never changes when you switch the drains: the heel touches the reservoir, which sets it. What the drains change comes after the heel. The wedge drops steeply to the drain line and runs gently on to the toe, and its area, the uplift, shrinks to a little over half:

Example 7.2

The same dam with its drains working

Given
The dam of Example 7.1, with a line of drains 6 m from the heel. Reservoir 57 m, river 5 m.
Find
The head at the drain line, the uplift, and the factor of safety against sliding.
The idea
Eq. 7.2 sets the head at the drains; the wedge is then two straight-line pieces, each pushing as hard as its own average.
  1. hd = 5 + 52 ÷ 3 = 22.33 mthe river's head plus a third of the 52 m difference
  2. Heel to drains: 39.667 × 6 = 238.0 m²the mean of 57 and 22.33 m of head, over 6 m
  3. Drains to toe: 13.667 × 42 = 574.0 m²the mean of 22.33 and 5 m, over the other 42 m
  4. U = 9.81 × 812.0 = 7,966 kNthe two pieces together, a metre of head being 9.81 kPa
  5. Press left: 34,780 − 7,966 = 26,814 kNW − U
  6. FS = 26,814 ÷ 15,814 = 1.696Eq. 7.1

With its drains working the dam carries 7.97 MN of uplift, 23% of its weight, and its factor of safety is 1.70. Clog the drains and the uplift grows 14,597 ÷ 7,966 = 1.83 times.

Check. The uplift is the area of the head wedge times 9.81, so the two states should compare as their areas: 812 m² against the straight line's 31 × 48 = 1,488 m², and 1,488 ÷ 812 = 1.83.

What it means. The drains act on one line, 6 m from the heel, but the saving is felt over the 42 m beyond it, where the head now falls from 22.3 m to the river's 5 instead of from 50.5 m.

With no glue counted, a common target for this check is a factor of safety of 1.5 under the worst ordinary loads, a convention that leaves room for what nobody can measure, such as the real head in the cracks.1.5 for the worst static case when no cohesion is counted, 1.3 for the probable maximum flood: FERC (2016), p. 3-27, the table of factors for a no-cohesion analysis. The dam passes with its drains working and fails with them clogged.

But drains clog. Water seeping through rock and grout dissolves calcium out of them, and in the drain holes the calcium comes out again as a crust, like the scale in a kettle; silt and bacterial slime add to it.Drains are usually "plugged with calcium deposits, sediment, or biological growth": Campbell, Rivett & Walpole (2022). Watching drain efficiency for clogging: FERC (2016), §3-2.4.3.2. A drain that passes no water lowers no pressure, and the wedge creeps back toward the straight line. That is what the gallery is for: engineers walk it to measure what each drain gives, read gauges set in some of the holes, and clean or redrill the holes that have gone quiet. A falling flow from a drain is as much a warning as a rising one.Uplift lifts more than dams. On 7 February 2017 the fast flow down the concrete chute of Oroville Dam's main spillway, in California, drove water through cracks and joints into the ground under a slab, probably faster than the drains there could carry it away. The forensic team concluded that the uplift most likely beat what the slab's weight, its anchors and the water on top could hold; the slab lifted out, and the flow tore into the poor rock beneath (Oroville Independent Forensic Team (2018), pp. S-1 and 33).

Check yourself Drains clog and a grout curtain needs no cleaning. Why not seal the rock with grout and leave out the drains?

Grout seals only the cracks it reaches, and a curtain ages. Water that finds a way past it arrives under the base with nearly the reservoir's head, and with no drains the wedge is the straight line again. The US federal regulator of hydropower dams allows no reduction in uplift for grouting alone.FERC (2016), §3-2.4.3.2.

Clogged drains matter most when the reservoir is high:

Example 7.3

How fast the margin goes as the lake rises

Given
The dam with its drains clogged, the reservoir at 50 m and at 57 m, the river at 5 m. Weight 34,780 kN per metre.
Find
The factor of safety at 50 m, and the level at which it falls to 1.5.
The idea
The push grows with the square of the depth (Eq. 2.2). The uplift grows only with the depth itself, through the head at the heel.
  1. F = ½ × 9.81 × 2,475 = 12,140 kN2,475 is 50² − 5², the reservoir's push less the river's
  2. U = 9.81 × 27.5 × 48 = 12,949 kNthe mean of 50 and 5 m of head, over the base
  3. FS = 21,831 ÷ 12,140 = 1.8034,780 − 12,949 = 21,831 kN left pressing
  4. FS = 1.5 at h = 53.6 mread from Fig. 7.2, and checked below

With its drains clogged the dam has a factor of safety of 1.80 with 50 m of water, 1.5 at 53.6 m and 1.28 at 57 m. The last 7 m take away more than half of its margin above 1.

Check. For a reservoir h metres deep, U = 235.44(h + 5) and F = 4.905(h² − 25), in kN. Setting W − U = 1.5F gives 7.3575h² + 235.44h − 33,787 = 0, whose positive root is h = 53.6 m.

What it means. One more metre of water at 57 m adds about 559 kN of push and only 235 kN of uplift. So a flood that lifts a full reservoir a few metres costs far more margin than the same rise lower down.

7.4 How hard concrete grips rock

Every number so far leaned on tan φ = 1, as the figure's readout says. The Bureau of Reclamation's guide gives a friction coefficient of 1 for concrete in a first design, and a federal regulator's worked example of a gravity dam uses 45°.Coefficient of internal friction 1.0 for concrete, for preliminary designs: USBR (1987), §8.6, p. 316. A worked example with φ = 45°: FERC (2016), Appendix C. But a dam can also slide on a joint or a bedding plane a few metres down in the rock, which is only as rough as the rock's own partings, and those may be polished smooth or filled with soft material.

With its drains working and a grip of 45°, the 60 m dam has a factor of safety of 1.70. If the rock under it grips at only 35°, the dam:

It holds, below 1.5: the factor of safety falls to 1.19. Ten degrees off the friction angle costs more margin than clogging the drains did. With the drains clogged as well it would slide.

To decide, look at where tan φ sits in Eq. 7.1. It multiplies everything else.

Example 7.4

The friction angle decides it

Given
The factors of safety at tan φ = 1: 1.696 with the drains working, 1.276 with them clogged (Examples 7.1 and 7.2).
Find
Both at φ = 35°, and the friction angle at which each would slide.
The idea
The factor of safety is proportional to tan φ; the dam slides where it reaches 1.
  1. tan 35° = 0.7002from a calculator
  2. Drains working: 1.696 × 0.7002 = 1.19the factor scales with tan φ
  3. Drains clogged: 1.276 × 0.7002 = 0.89below 1: it slides
  4. Working, slides at tan φ = 1 ÷ 1.696 = 0.590, φ = 30.5°the tan φ that brings the factor to 1
  5. Clogged, slides at tan φ = 1 ÷ 1.276 = 0.784, φ = 38.1°the same, with the bigger uplift

At 35° the dam holds with its drains working, at 1.19, and slides with them clogged, at 0.89. With working drains it is safe down to 30.5°; with clogged drains, only down to 38.1°.

Check. Work the clogged case from Eq. 7.1 directly: 20,183 × 0.7002 ÷ 15,814 = 0.894, as step 3 found by scaling.

What it means. Weight is easy to know and friction is hard. That is why the rock under a gravity dam is dug down to sound material, cleaned and grouted before any concrete is placed on it.

Site C, the newest dam on the Peace River in British Columbia, stands on bedded shale.BC Hydro's 1978 preliminary design for Site C was already an earthfill dam, because a concrete gravity dam was not feasible on that rock. The powerhouse and spillways sit on a concrete buttress keyed down through one bedding plane; in 2018 a deeper plane moved about 5 mm. The remedy chosen in 2020 sets up to 125 piles through that plane and adds drainage to lower the water pressure in the rock, the two levers of Eq. 7.1 (BC Hydro (2021), pp. 3, 4 and 6). During its construction a bedding plane under the concrete that carries its powerhouse and spillways turned out to grip at about 11°, below the 16° its contingency design had allowed for.BC Hydro (2021), Appendix A (Technical Advisory Board), pp. 3–4: "≈11º" against the contingency case's 16º.

7.5 The middle third

Sliding is one way for the push to win. The other is tipping: the push turns the dam about its toe with a moment, as Chapter 2 showed. Engineers check it by adding the weight, the push and the uplift into one force, the resultant, and asking where its line crosses the base.

Where the resultant crosses the middle of the base, the rock is pressed evenly. Move it downstream and the toe is pressed harder and the heel less, until the heel is not pressed at all: the pressure under the base, taken to change in a straight line, is then a triangle with its point at the heel, which balances a third of the way in from its tallest side (§2.4). So while the resultant stays between a third and two thirds of the base from the heel, in the middle third, the whole base stays pressed onto the rock. For the 60 m dam that is 16 to 32 m from the heel; the readout of Fig. 7.2 puts the resultant at 0.56 B, 26.7 m, with the drains working and 0.62 B with them clogged. The same straight-line picture gives the pressure at the heel:

pheel = (V ÷ B) · (4 − 6x ÷ B) (7.3)

pheel pressure of the dam on the rock at its heel (kPa) · V the downward force on the base (kN per metre) · B base width (m) · x where the resultant crosses the base, from the heel (m). At x = B/2 it gives an even press, V/B; at x = 2B/3, zero.

The middle third was the rule of the day at Bouzey. Lévy pointed out that it only keeps the joints from tending to open at their upstream ends, which is not enough: a crack can open anyway, from heat or a bad joint, and the reservoir fills it. A crack no thicker than a sheet of paper carries the full pressure of its depth (Example 2.3), which pushes its faces apart so that it grows.Lévy, an engineer and member of the Academy of Sciences, read his note on 5 August 1895. He compared the danger to a boiler without a safety valve, and proposed a valve: a guard wall on the upstream face with wells behind it, so that any crack opened into a well and drained instead of holding pressure. The wells would empty into a drain along the dam, whose flow would warn of what was happening inside (Lévy (1895), pp. 288–289). Drains in the body of the dam later did the same job (Bordes (2010), p. 104). So Lévy asked for more: at the upstream end of every joint, the masonry must press harder than the water presses there, and then water that finds a crack is squeezed back out.The usual condition and Lévy's new one: Lévy (1895), p. 289. Here is his test at the base of the 60 m dam, with no water inside the joint, as he posed it:

Example 7.5

Does the heel press harder than the water?

Given
The 60 m dam, reservoir at 57 m: weight 34,780 kN per metre, acting 15.71 m from the heel; pushes of 15,936 kN from the reservoir, 19 m up, and 122.6 kN from the river, 5/3 m up; base 48 m.
Find
Where weight and push together cross the base, and the pressure at the heel against the water's.
The idea
The push moves the resultant downstream of the weight by its moment ÷ the weight; Eq. 7.3 does the rest.
  1. Moment of the push: 15,936.345 × 19 = 302,790.6 kN·mthe reservoir's push times its height, H/3
  2. Less the river's: 302,790.6 − 204.4 = 302,586.2 kN·mthe river pushes the other way, 122.6 kN at 5/3 m
  3. Shift: 302,586.2 ÷ 34,780 = 8.700 mhow far downstream of the weight the resultant crosses the base
  4. x = 15.712 + 8.700 = 24.412 ma little past the middle, 24 m; well inside the middle third
  5. 6 × 24.412 ÷ 48 = 3.0515, and 4 − 3.0515 = 0.9485the bracket of Eq. 7.3
  6. pheel = 724.58 × 0.9485 = 687.3 kPaV/B = 34,780 ÷ 48, times the bracket
  7. Water at the heel: 9.81 × 57 = 559.2 kPa, and 687.3 ÷ 559.2 = 1.23Lévy's comparison

At its base the dam presses the rock at the heel with 687 kPa, 1.23 times the water's 559 kPa, so it passes Lévy's test there.

Check. With no push the resultant would sit under the weight, 15.71 m from the heel, pressing the heel harder than the toe. The push moves it 8.7 m downstream, almost to the middle, so the heel pressure should be close to the even press, 725 kPa, and it is.

What it means. The section puts its weight upstream of the middle, where the push needs it. A thinner wall, or one with its weight further downstream, leaves less press at the heel for the water to beat.

Bouzey's upper wall had no such margin. Here is its section as it stood in 1895, from the published drawing:

Notice how high the swept-away part sits. The lower wall, thickened and keyed, held; the upper wall took the push of a full reservoir on a section hardly thicker than a road.

After Bouzey, a ministerial decision of 10 March 1896 had every masonry dam in France checked again,Bordes (2010), p. 104. and gravity dams since have been built thicker, with drains in their bodies and their foundations. Lévy's condition survives in design manuals in a gentler form, with an allowance for drains.In the Bureau of Reclamation's version, the face must be pressed harder than four tenths of the water's pressure there when drains work and harder than all of it when they do not, less an allowance for the concrete's strength in tension (USBR (1987), sec. 8.19(b)(2), p. 329).

The second half of the film Depth, not size retells this chapter in five minutes and answers a question it left open:

What to remember

  • A gravity dam is the block on the ramp, on level ground: its weight presses it onto the rock, and the rock's grip, (W − U) · tan φ, holds it against the water's push.
  • Water in the cracks under the base presses up with the reservoir's pressure at the heel and the river's at the toe. With nothing to stop it, it carried 42% of the 60 m dam's weight and cut its factor of safety from 2.20 to 1.28.
  • A grout curtain and a line of drains make the water spend most of its head near the heel; working drains raised the factor to 1.70. Drains clog, and the gallery is there so they can be measured and cleaned.
  • The friction angle multiplies everything: at 35° the same dam fell to 1.19.
  • The resultant must cross the base inside the middle third, or the heel stops being pressed. Lévy asked for more after Bouzey: the masonry at every joint's upstream end must press harder than the water there, so that water is squeezed out of a crack instead of into it.

Questions

  1. 7.1

    In one sentence, say how the uplift under a gravity dam is the water cushion under the block of Fig. 4.1.

    Hint

    What did the cushion take away from the block, and what does the friction depend on?

    Answer

  2. 7.2

    By hand: the reservoir behind the 60 m dam stands at 50 m and the drains are working. What are the head at the drain line, the uplift and the factor of safety against sliding?

    Hint

    Use Eq. 7.2 with 50 and 5 m, then the two straight-line pieces of Example 7.2. The push at 50 m is in Example 7.3.

    Answer

  3. 7.3

    With the drains working, slide the reservoir from 30 m up to 59 m, a metre below the crest. Does the factor of safety ever fall below 1.5? Why does it fall faster near the top?

    Hint

    Compare how the push and the uplift grow with depth (Example 7.3).

    Answer

  4. 7.4

    Clog the drains and raise the reservoir to 59 m. Where does the resultant cross the base, and is the heel still pressed?

    The middle third runs from 0.33 B to 0.67 B. What happens to the heel pressure in Eq. 7.3 as x approaches 2B/3?

  5. 7.5

    The US Army Corps of Engineers assumes that drains remove only 25 to 50 per cent of the straight-line pressure above the tailwater's at the drain line. With the reservoir at 57 m, what does the 60 m dam's factor of safety come to at each end of that range, and would you accept the Bureau of Reclamation's one-third rule for this dam without measurements?

    Hint

    With no drains the straight line stands at 50.5 m at the drain line; take 50 or 25 per cent of its height above the river's 5 m away.

  6. 7.6

    Lévy said that the masonry at the upstream end of every joint must press harder than the reservoir's water presses there. What does that prevent, and why is the middle-third rule alone not enough to prevent it?

Further reading

  • U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (1987). Design of Small Dams, 3rd ed. Denver. https://www.usbr.gov/tsc/techreferences/mands/mands-pdfs/SmallDams.pdf serious Its chapter on concrete gravity dams sets out the loads of this chapter (uplift with and without drains, the one-third rule), the stress check at the upstream face that descends from Lévy's, and the sliding check. Free from the Bureau of Reclamation.
  • Anderson, C., Mohorovic, C., Mogck, L., Cohen, B., Scott, G. (1998). Concrete Dams: Case Histories of Failures and Nonfailures with Back Calculations. Report DSO-98-05. Denver: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Dam Safety Office, December 1998. https://www.usbr.gov/ssle/damsafety/TechDev/DSOTechDev/DSO-98-05.pdf serious Case histories of concrete and masonry dams that slid, cracked or failed, Bouzey among them, each with the Bureau's own back-calculation of the forces. A good place to see this chapter's checks applied to real failures.
  • Lévy, M. (1895). Quelques considérations sur la construction des grands barrages. Comptes rendus hebdomadaires des séances de l'Académie des sciences 121(6): 288–300 (séance du 5 août 1895). https://archive.org/details/mobot31753002064894 primary source Lévy's note, in French. The first two pages hold the boiler, the drained wells and the new condition; the rest works out the stresses inside a dam.

Concrete keeps its strength whatever the water does; only the press on its base changes. The waste behind a mine's dam is different. It is ground rock, sand and silt pumped in wet, and it can lose its strength altogether. What happens when a dam has to be built up, a few metres at a time, on top of the very waste it holds?

8

Chapter 8 · Part II · Two kinds of dam

Never finished

Why would a country write the word “upstream” into its laws?

So far. Chapter 6 set a tailings dam beside a water dam: what it holds can lose its strength, and the dam keeps growing for as long as the mine runs. Chapter 7 looked at a dam that is built once, of a material that never goes soft. This chapter watches a tailings dam grow, and asks why the direction it grows in matters so much.

After this chapter you can

  • sketch the three ways to raise a tailings dam, and work out the fill each one needs and where its crest ends up;
  • explain why an upstream raise can fail with no earthquake, years after the last raise was built;
  • estimate how fast a tailings deposit rises, and name the levers that keep it safe (rate of rise, a wide beach, a pond kept away from the crest) and the alternatives to a wet deposit.

This chapter adds a raise stepped onto the crest

3 figures · about 20 min to read · Film 8.1, 9 min 6 s

On 30 September 2020 Brazil changed its national law on dam safety. Most laws about building say what a structure must achieve: how strong, how safe, how often inspected. This one did something rarer. It named a way of building and forbade it: no mining dam in Brazil may be built or raised by the upstream method, a montante in Portuguese. Then, so that nobody could argue about what the words meant, the next paragraph defined the method, in translation: a way of building a dam "in which the containment dykes rest on the tailings themselves, or on sediment previously discharged and deposited."Lei 14.066 (2020), Art. 3, adding Art. 2-A to Law 12.334 of 2010. §1 reads: "Entende-se por alteamento a montante a metodologia construtiva de barragem em que os diques de contenção se apoiam sobre o próprio rejeito ou sedimento previamente lançado e depositado." The translation is ours.

The law gave every mine with such a dam until 25 February 2022 to take it out of service as a dam.The Portuguese word is descaracterização, "decharacterization": draining, reshaping or removing the deposit until it no longer works, or fails, as a dam. The next paragraph lets the regulator extend the deadline where the work cannot technically be finished in time. It was not the first word on the subject. Less than a month after the collapse at Brumadinho in January 2019, Brazil's mining agency had already banned the method by resolution, with the same definition.The deadline: Lei 14.066 (2020), Art. 2-A §2. The resolution: ANM Resolution 4 of February 2019, as summarized by Freire (2019). Chile had turned against it half a century earlier.

A lawmaker does not usually care whether a wall steps one way or the other as it grows. So why would a country write the word "upstream" into its laws? The answer is in what the wall stands on, and to see it we have to watch one grow.

8.1 A dam that grows with the mine

A water dam is finished the day it is built. A tailings dam never is while the mine runs. The mill sends out more ground rock and water every day, so the dam has to rise with the deposit behind it. It begins as a starter dam of soil and rock dug from pits nearby, and the tailings are piped out over its crest as a slurry. As Chapter 6 showed, the slurry sorts itself on the way: the coarse sand settles near the pipes and builds a gently sloping beach, while the fine grains and the water run on to a pond. When the deposit nears the top, the dam is raised, and then raised again. Each raise can step toward the pond, away from it, or straight up, and that direction names the method:

  • Upstream: the crest steps toward the pond. Each raise is a small dyke built on the tailings beach, often from the beach's own sand.
  • Downstream: the crest steps away from the pond. Each raise is built over the previous outer slope, on compacted fill and natural ground.
  • Centreline: the crest rises straight up. Each raise straddles the top of the beach and the outer slope.

Below, three dams are raised side by side from the same starter dam, 20 m tall, in four raises of 12 m each, to the same final height. Press Play, or drag the Stage slider:

Notice two things. The upstream crest walks a long way toward the pond, −112 m by the end, while the downstream crest walks 96 m the other way. And notice what the fill costs: the downstream dam's numbers climb faster with every raise. You can work out that bill from the shapes alone. A dam section h metres tall with an 8 m crest and faces at 2:1 is a band 8 m wide down the middle and a triangle on each side, each ½ × h × 2h = h². So its area, which is also its volume of fill per metre length of dam, is

A = 8h + 2h² (8.1)

A area of the section, m² (m³ of fill per metre of dam) · h height, m · the 8 is the crest width in metres, and the 2 comes from the two 2:1 faces

The first term grows in step with the height; the second with its square. That square is the whole story of the next example:

Example 8.1

The fill bill

Given
The dams of Fig. 8.1: a starter 20 m tall, four raises of 12 m to 68 m, a crest 8 m wide, every face at 2:1.
Find
The fill in each finished dam, per metre of its length, and how fast the downstream bill grows with height.
The idea
Every piece of fill is a whole dam section or a part of one, so Eq. 8.1 prices each piece.
  1. Starter: 8 × 20 + 2 × 20² = 960 m³Eq. 8.1 with h = 20 m; every number here is per metre of dam
  2. One upstream dyke: 8 × 12 + 2 × 12² = 384 m³a dyke is a small dam of the same shape, 12 m tall
  3. Upstream: 960 + 4 × 384 = 2,496 m³the starter and four dykes
  4. Downstream: 8 × 68 + 2 × 68² = 9,792 m³each raise covers the old outer face, so the finished dam is one whole section 68 m tall
  5. Centreline: 68² + 8 × 68 + 20² + 4 × 144 = 6,144 m³the outer triangle and the crest band full height; on the pond side, the starter's own triangle and four wedges on the beach, each ½ × 24 × 12
  6. Last downstream raise: 8 × 56 + 2 × 56² = 6,720, and 9,792 − 6,720 = 3,072 m³the dam at 68 m less the dam at 56 m
  7. 3,072 ÷ 384 = 8 dykesthat raise alone, counted in upstream dykes
  8. At half the height: 8 × 34 + 2 × 34² = 2,584, and 9,792 ÷ 2,584 = 3.79a downstream dam twice as tall

Upstream 2,496, centreline 6,144, downstream 9,792 m³ per metre of dam. The last downstream raise takes as much fill as 8 upstream dykes, and doubling the height of a downstream dam multiplies its fill by 3.79.

Check. Raising a downstream dam by a little adds a strip of fill as wide as the whole base, because the outer face moves out from top to bottom. Halfway up the last raise, at 62 m, the base is 8 + 4 × 62 = 256 m wide, and 256 × 12 = 3,072 m³, the same as step 6.

What it means. Fill means trucks, time and money, and a downstream dam pays for each new metre across its whole width while an upstream dam pays for one small dyke. That is the pull toward upstream, and it grows as the dam does.

The cheap dam has a price of its own, and it shows in where each crest ends up and in what each raise stands on:

Example 8.2

Where the crest goes, and what it stands on

Given
The finished dams of Fig. 8.1. Each upstream dyke is 384 m³ per metre, all of it on tailings; each centreline raise puts a wedge of 144 m³ on the beach.
Find
How far each crest moves, and what share of each dam's fill rests on tailings.
The idea
Each upstream dyke stands with its outer foot on the middle of the crest below, and leans back toward the pond at 2:1.
  1. Upstream, per raise: 2 × 12 + 4 = 28 ma 2:1 face climbing 12 m runs 24 m back; the foot on the middle of the old crest adds half the crest
  2. Four raises: 4 × 28 = 112 m toward the pondthe readout's −112
  3. Downstream: 2 × 48 = 96 m away from itthe crest moves 2 m out for every metre of the four raises
  4. Upstream on tailings: 4 × 384 = 1,536 m³, and 1,536 ÷ 2,496 = 0.615four dykes, out of the whole dam
  5. Centreline on the beach: 4 × 144 = 576 m³, and 576 ÷ 6,144 = 0.094four wedges, out of the whole dam

The upstream crest ends 112 m toward the pond with 62% of the dam on tailings; the centreline crest stays put with 9% on the beach; the downstream crest moves 96 m away with none.

Check. The starter's base reaches 2 × 20 + 4 = 44 m upstream of its crest, so the final upstream crest stands 112 − 44 = 68 m out beyond the starter's inner toe. The whole top of that dam has nothing under it but tailings.

What it means. Of the three, only the upstream dam has to trust the tailings to carry it. Whether it holds is a question about the beach, and no amount of care with the dykes can answer it.

8.2 What the wall stands on

Most people say a dam fails when its wall breaks, so the way to make it safe is to build the wall strong. For an upstream dam that answer looks in the wrong place. Each dyke is compacted fill, small and sound. Under it lies the beach, and the beach was never built at all. It was laid down from a slurry, grain by grain, the way a wave lays down the loose sand at the water's edge in Chapter 1, and nobody rolled it afterward. Near its surface, in the sun and wind, it drains and can look as firm as the damp sand of a castle. A few metres down it sits below the water table of the deposit, the phreatic surface, and there every gap is full of water.

How high that water stands under the dykes is not fixed. It depends on where the pond is. Here is one upstream dam drawn twice, with the pond kept far from the crest and with the pond close to it:

Notice that the only difference between the two panels is the water. The dykes, the beach and the tailings are the same. In B the dykes stand on loose grains with water in every gap, and as Chapter 5 showed, that is a material whose strength depends on what happens to that water when something pushes on it.

Something always does. Each new dyke adds its weight to the beach beneath it. The weight of the sloping dam presses the tailings under it outward, toward its open face. Nobody needs to shake anything. So the question to settle is what loose, soaked grains do under a push that is slow and steady:

A new dyke is placed, slowly, on a beach of loose tailings with water in every gap. The water can only leave slowly. What happens to the grains under the dyke?

The water takes over. Pushed, loose grains try to shuffle into the gaps between them and pack tighter. To do that, the water in those gaps must get out of the way, and here it can't leave fast enough. So the grains cannot move closer, and the weight they were carrying passes to the water. The water pressure rises, the grains press on one another less, and their grip goes with the press, as Chapter 5 showed in the sandbox. Nothing has to break, and nothing has to shake.

The film Dams that are never finished puts the same push on a box of grains, then follows it out into the world:

8.3 A slow push is enough

Put the box back into the dam. Below the phreatic surface, the beach under an upstream raise is loose sand and silt with water in every gap; it is contractive, so a push makes it try to pack tighter. Whether the water can get out of the way in time depends on how far it has to go and how easily it moves, and Chapter 5 put a clock on that: the time grows with the square of the distance (Eq. 5.2). A sample in a box drains in seconds. A deposit tens of metres thick, laced with fine silt from the pond, does not drain in the seconds or minutes it takes a slope to start moving. For that moment the tailings are undrained, the water takes the load, and the grains stop gripping. The deposit flows as a heavy liquid, and the dykes on it go with it. That is static liquefaction: liquefaction with no earthquake at all.

The trigger can be small, and it can come late. Dam I at the Córrego do Feijão mine near Brumadinho was raised upstream in ten raises over 37 years, to 86 m. Its last raise was built in 2013, and tailings stopped arriving in July 2016. On 25 January 2019, with no sign of trouble on any of its instruments, its slope collapsed in under ten seconds, and about three quarters of its tailings flowed out within five minutes. The expert panel found flow liquefaction of the tailings inside the dam itself. They were loose, saturated and brittle, and the water level in them had stayed high near the toe after deposition stopped. What tipped them was a combination of slow creep and the loss of suction in the drier tailings above the water table after heavy rain at the end of 2018.Robertson et al. (2019), Executive summary, pp. i–ii, and p. 16 (raises, height, dates). The toll is in Chapter 6. The growing had stopped. The loose, soaked tailings were still there.

An earthquake is a faster push of the same kind, and Chile, where the ground shakes often, learned it first. After the El Cobre tailings dams failed in an earthquake in 1965 and buried the village below, Chile wrote its first rules for tailings dams, in 1970. They covered dams with people living within reach downstream; among other things they kept the pond as far from the sand wall as possible and had the wall's sand raised outward, over the crest, and they have been read ever since as shutting out the upstream method for those dams. Chile's rules of 2007 say it in one line, which translates as "the use of the upstream method is prohibited."El Cobre in 1965: Dobry & Alvarez (1967). The rules: Chile DS 86 (1970), Arts. 30, 31 and 44; Chile DS 248 (2007), Art. 14(h). Stava, in Italy, failed with no earthquake at all.On 19 July 1985 the upper of two tailings dams above the village of Stava, in the Italian Alps, burst. Its mud poured into the lower basin and on down the valley, about 180,000 m³ of it, and 268 people died. The upper dam was still being raised, by the upstream method. Luino and De Graff put first among the causes the mistaken assumption that the tailings would consolidate fairly quickly.

That answers the question this chapter opened with. A country writes "upstream" into its law because no rule about the wall can make an upstream dam safe. The danger is in what the wall stands on: loose, saturated tailings that a slow push can turn to liquid, and that stay that way after the raising stops. So the law names the one thing it can name, the place the wall is allowed to stand.

Check yourself A mine proposes to build its upstream dykes of crushed rock instead of beach sand, so that the dykes themselves are strong. Does that make the dam safe?

No. Stronger dykes still stand on the same loose, soaked beach. If the tailings under them liquefy, rock dykes go down with them as surely as sand ones.

8.4 How fast it may rise

Upstream dams are still built where the law allows them; most South African tailings dams, for one, are raised this way. The ones that stand are kept standing by keeping the tailings under them drained. A long beach keeps the pond, and with it the high water, away from the crest, as in panel A of Fig. 8.2. The pond itself is kept small: its water is drawn off to a separate dam as soon as it can be, not stored against the tailings.SANCOLD (2020), §4.8, p. 18. The third lever is time: the rate of rise, how many metres a year the surface of the deposit climbs.

Time matters because every metre of new tailings is a load on the tailings below. Below the phreatic surface that load is carried at first by the water, and it passes to the grains only as the water seeps away and the grains settle closer, the slow process Chapter 5 called consolidation. Rise slowly and each metre has drained and settled before the next arrives. Rise fast and the water pressure builds up from one season to the next, the tailings stay loose, and the phreatic surface climbs with them.

So the deposit runs a race between two clocks. One is the time it takes to add a metre. The other is the time the water below takes to get out, and by Eq. 5.2 that grows with the square of the distance the water must travel, so it grows as the deposit thickens; the fine, silty tailings laid down toward the pond are the slowest of all. Nobody can work out the second clock exactly for a real deposit, layered as it is, so the industry limits the first one instead. South African guidance puts the limit for most upstream dams at about 2 to 2½ m a year, up to about 6 m a year for dams whose outer wall is built of coarse, free-draining sand, and says plainly that the figure is a judgement based on experience.SANCOLD (2020), §4.6, p. 15. At 2 m a year, each metre has half a year to drain before the next one covers it.

The rate of rise itself is plain arithmetic: the volume the mill sends out in a year, spread over the area of the deposit,

r = M ⁄ (ρd S) (8.2)

r rate of rise, m a year · M dry tailings sent out, tonnes a year · ρd tonnes of solids in each cubic metre of settled deposit · S area of the deposit's surface, m²

A mine of ordinary size shows how fast that can be:

Example 8.3

How fast the deposit climbs

Given
An illustrative mine that sends out 50,000 tonnes of dry tailings a day. Settled in the deposit they hold 1.4 tonnes of solids in each cubic metre (also illustrative). The deposit covers 2 km², and the dam is raised 12 m at a time.
Find
How fast the deposit rises, and how often the dam must be raised.
The idea
Eq. 8.2, one step at a time: tonnes to cubic metres, a day to a year, then spread over the area. A square kilometre is a million square metres, so millions of cubic metres over square kilometres gives metres.
  1. 50,000 ÷ 1.4 = 35,714 m³ a daytonnes over tonnes per cubic metre
  2. 35,714 × 365 ÷ 1,000,000 = 13.04 million m³ a yeara year of days, counted in millions
  3. 13.04 ÷ 2 = 6.52 m a yearmillions of cubic metres over millions of square metres
  4. 12 ÷ 6.52 = 1.84 yearsbetween one 12 m raise and the next
  5. 13.04 ÷ 2.5 = 5.2 km²the area that would hold the rise to 2½ m a year

The deposit climbs 6.5 m a year, a new raise every 1.8 years: two to three times the usual limit for an upstream dam. To stay under 2½ m a year it would need about 5.2 km².

Check. The order of magnitude: 13 million m³ is a block 1 km by 1 km by 13 m, and spread over two such squares it stands 6½ m deep.

What it means. The rate of rise is set by the mine's output and the size of the valley, not by the dam engineer. A mine that grows its output, or a deposit that narrows as it climbs, can outrun its own tailings. The engineer's choices are a bigger footprint, a slower mine, or a dam that does not stand on the tailings at all.

Check yourself The mine of Example 8.3 doubles its output. What happens to the rate of rise, and to the time between raises?

The rate doubles, to 13.04 m a year, and a 12 m raise falls due every 11 months. An upstream dam on that deposit would be far past any rule of thumb.

8.5 Raising away from the water

The other two methods do not ask the tailings to carry the dam. A downstream raise stands on compacted fill and on the ground beyond the old toe. Because each raise covers the whole outer face, a sloping core and drains can be carried up with every lift, as in a water dam, and the downstream panel of Fig. 8.1 draws them. Such a dam can hold back a pond, and it rides out earthquakes best. Its costs are the ones Example 8.1 counted, and land: its toe marches out 4 m for every metre of rise, 192 m over the four raises of the figure, and that ground has to be set aside from the day the mine opens.

A centreline raise splits the difference. Its crest stays put, so pipelines and roads along it never move, and a vertical drain can rise with every lift. A small wedge of each raise rests on the top of the beach, 9% of the fill in the figure, so that part of the beach must be sandy, drained and compacted. It can be built of cyclone sand: the slurry is spun in a hydrocyclone, which flings the coarse grains to its wall and out at the bottom while the fines and most of the water leave at the top.SANCOLD (2020), §4.4.4, p. 12. The coarse sand drains freely and can be compacted, which is what a wall needs.

Check yourself Tailings behind a downstream dam rise 6 m a year. Is that rate a danger to the dam?

Far less than it would be to an upstream dam. The limit exists because each upstream raise stands on the last few years of tailings. A downstream raise stands on compacted fill and the ground beyond the toe, and the tailings behind it only lean on it, as a heavy liquid would; that is a load it is designed to carry. South African guidance says the rate of rise is not relevant behind a fully engineered earthfill or rockfill wall (SANCOLD (2020)). The wall must still be raised fast enough to stay ahead of the tailings.

Between centreline and upstream lies the modified centreline raise. Each raise steps its crest a little toward the pond, so more of it rests on the beach than in a centreline raise, and the core leans slightly upstream, supported on that side by a zone of tailings. Mount Polley, in British Columbia, was designed to be raised this way.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), pp. 8 and 53. The panel adds that as built, one early raise was entirely upstream construction and later ones crept upstream (pp. 55 and 69). Hold that thought; it comes back in Chapter 13.

The table gathers the three methods:

8.6 Less water in the deposit

Every method so far stores the tailings wet and builds a wall to hold them. The other road is to take the water out. Thickened tailings leave the mill with less water and stand on steeper beaches than a thin slurry does (Jewell (2012)). Filtered tailings, sometimes called dry stack, go further: filters take out enough water that the tailings can be carried by truck or conveyor and spread and compacted like earthworks. The review panel that investigated the Mount Polley breach set out the case for them from first principles of soil mechanics: take away the surface water, keep the tailings unsaturated with drainage, and "achieve dilatant conditions throughout the tailings deposit by compaction".Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), §9.3.1–9.3.2, pp. 121–123, which also gives cost as the main reason filtered tailings are not used more widely. Each of those is a way of keeping the grains pressing on one another: no pond to soak them, no water in the gaps to take the load, and grains packed dense enough to swell, not collapse, when they are sheared. Even then the compaction is not optional; a loose, dry stack that later gets wet can flow too. The catch is cost: filtering is more expensive than piping a slurry, and most filtered operations so far have been small.

8.7 A water dam built like a tailings dam

All of this might suggest the trouble is mine waste. Coquitlam Dam, in British Columbia, shows that it is not. It holds water, for BC Hydro's power plants and for about a third of Metro Vancouver's drinking water, and it was built in 1913Drinking water: BC Hydro (2026). The date and the way it was built: BC Hydro (2008); Water Power (2001). by hydraulic fill: soil washed into place with water and left to settle, which leaves it loose and saturated, much like the beach under an upstream raise. Here it is as a case file:

Notice that the old dam is still there, and still holds the lake. The new one stands behind it for the earthquake that might make the old fill flow. Brazil asked the same of its upstream tailings dams in 2019: before taking one out of service, a mine had to reinforce it from downstream or build a new containment structure below it.ANM Resolution 4 of 2019, as summarized by Freire (2019).

What to remember

  • A tailings dam grows with the mine, by upstream, centreline or downstream raises. To the same height, upstream needs the least fill (2,496 m³ per metre in Fig. 8.1, against 9,792 downstream) because it builds each raise on the beach.
  • An upstream raise stands on loose tailings with water in every gap. Pushed, even slowly, the grains try to pack tighter, the water cannot leave in time and takes the load, and the grains stop gripping. No earthquake is needed, and the danger lasts after the raising stops.
  • A slow rate of rise gives the water time to leave the tailings; a long beach and a small pond keep it away from the dykes. How fast the deposit rises is set by the mine's output and the area the deposit covers.
  • Downstream and centreline raises stand on dense, drained fill, so the grains under the dam keep pressing; filtered, compacted tailings take the water out of the deposit itself.
  • What decides the danger is the state of the fill, loose and wet or dense and drained, not what it holds back: Coquitlam is a water dam that needed the same cure.

A downstream raise can carry a core and drains up with it, like a water dam. Most of the world's large dams are built that way from the start: heaps of earth and rock, zone by zone. What is inside a dam like that, and why does each soil sit where it does?
