Chapter 9 · Part III · Inside the embankment

Every zone has one job

Why build a dam out of six different soils?

The voids are the channels of flow for percolating water.

R. R. Proctor, Fundamental principles of soil compaction, 1933

So far. Chapter 8 ended inside a tailings dam raised downstream, which can carry a core and drains up with it, like a dam built to hold water. Part III opens that kind of dam properly: the embankment, a heap of earth and rock, and the different soils it is built from.

After this chapter you can

  • name each zone of an embankment and its job, and say what goes wrong if it is missing;
  • explain why the upstream shell can be soaked and still strong, and what one event makes it dangerous;
  • say how loose earth is made into dense fill, and check a rolled layer with a field test.

This chapter adds a core and a filter inside the heap

2 figures · about 20 min to read · Film 9.1, 6 min 51 s

Between 1964 and 1967, in the canyon of the Peace River in northern British Columbia, crews built a hill one layer at a time. Each layer of its middle was spread no more than 10 inches thick (6 inches from late August 1965), scratched up on top so the next would bond to it, and rolled four times by a 90-ton compactor on rubber tyres. Each layer was meant to come out at least 98 per cent as dense as the same soil packed in a standard laboratory test. When they stopped, the W.A.C. Bennett Dam stood 183 m high and ran 2.0 km across the canyon and the terraces on either side, about 44 million cubic metres of earth and rock.BC Hydro expert panel (2012), pp. 1–3: 600 ft high, 6,700 ft long, 57.5 million cubic yards of fill, built 1964 to 1967; the rules for placing the core are in its table of zones, p. 3.Bennett is far from the tallest dam of its kind. Shuangjiangkou, in China, a rockfill dam built round a core of gravelly soil, is 315 m high. It began storing water in May 2025 and connected its first generator to the grid in June 2026 (International Water Power (2025); China Power News Network (2026)). It is reported as the world's tallest dam, a title it is expected to hold until Rogun, in Tajikistan, reaches its planned 335 m, which was projected for 2033.

From outside, a dam like this is one long slope of earth. Cut it across and it is seven materials. The panel of engineers that reviewed Bennett in 2012 lists them as zones, from the middle outward. Zone 1 is the core, there to hold the reservoir back. Zones 2 and 3, a transition and a filter, are each described as a filter to the core. Zone 4 is a drain. Zone 5 is a bedding layer for the riprap, the armour of large rocks on the upstream face. Zone 6, the random shell, "provides the weight for the stability of the dam". Each went in by its own rules: the core in the thinnest layers at a water content held close to one chosen value, the transition and filter in thicker layers under a vibrating roller, the shell with coarser streaks allowed because they help water out.BC Hydro expert panel (2012), the table of zones, pp. 3–4, quoted for Zone 6.

Keep an eye on Zone 2, the transition. It sits between the core and everything coarser, and of all the zones its job is the hardest to see in a drawing. Chapter 11 is where it earns its keep.

Why go to that trouble? The canyon had plenty of soil. Why not build the whole hill out of the tightest soil in it?

9.1 One soil, or several?

Chapter 3 gave half an answer: a short plug of clay in a pipe of sand takes nearly the whole drop in head. The film at the end of Chapter 7 asked the other half: how can a wall of dirt hold back a lake at all, when water passes through dirt? Most people say the wall must be made watertight. Build it of clay, the tightest soil there is, and the water stays out. Test that before you read on:

The same 24 m dam is built twice on solid rock: once all of silt, and once all of clay, a hundred times tighter. In the silt dam, water seeping through breaks out of the back slope well above the ground. Once the water has had time to soak into the clay dam, where does it stand inside it?

Where it stood in the silt dam. Through any one material the head falls steadily from the lake side to the far side, however tight the material is: that is Darcy's pipe from Chapter 3 with nothing but clay in it. Making the whole dam a hundred times tighter cuts the leak a hundredfold and makes the water take far longer to arrive. Once it has arrived, it stands in the same place, and the back slope is as wet as before. How tight the soil is sets how much water gets through; where the water ends up standing is set by the dam's shape and the lake's level.

The film below runs that experiment, and then a third dam built of both soils.

Its first few minutes retell the race and Darcy's pipe from Chapter 3, as a reminder; then it looks inside a dam:

The film puts its answer in one line: a dam does not have to be watertight; it has to keep the water pressure out of the part that holds it up. Every zone in this chapter serves that idea. Chapter 4 showed that soil holds only as well as its grains press on one another, and that water in the gaps takes part of that press away. The part of an embankment that holds it up against the lake is the downstream half. So the first question about any design is where the water will stand inside it, and only the second is how much of it will get through.

To put numbers on it, take the one dam this book keeps coming back to, our dam: the 24 m embankment with 2:1 faces (the notation of Example 1.2) drawn in Plate 0, whose water the seepage lab computes in Chapter 10 and whose slopes the workbench tests in Chapters 12 and 13. The lab can build it of a single fill or with a clay core between shells of sand and gravel, on a foundation of gravel or of clay. Here it is both ways, on clay:

Example 9.1

The plug inside our dam

Given
Our dam holding water 20.4 m deep, on the seepage lab's clay foundation, built two ways: all of one fill (k = 10⁻⁷ m/s), or with a clay core (10⁻⁹ m/s, 3 m wide at the top and 21.4 m at the base) between shells of sand and gravel (10⁻⁴ m/s). The lab computes where the water stands.
Find
How high the water stands in the downstream half each way, how much of the head the core takes, and how much each version leaks.
The idea
The same flow passes every zone in turn, so the tightest one takes nearly the whole drop in head, as the clay plug did in Darcy's pipe (Fig. 3.2).
  1. One fill: water breaks out of the downstream face 8 m above the groundthe highest point where water seeps out of the face, read from the lab
  2. With the core: the water behind it stands 0.65 m above the groundthe phreatic surface close behind the core
  3. Head the core takes: 20.4 − 0.65 = 19.75 mfrom the lake's level down to the water behind the core
  4. 19.75 ÷ 20.4 = 0.968, so 96.8%the core's share of the drop
  5. Leak: 44.4 L/day per metre with one fill, 37.2 with the corethe lab's Seepage readout, both ways

The core takes 96.8% of the head. The water in the downstream half drops from 8 m up the face to 0.65 m above the ground, while the leak falls by only about a sixth.

Check. Estimate the flow through the core by hand with Darcy's law. Ten metres up, the core is 13.4 m wide, so the water crossing it loses head at about 19.75 ÷ 13.4 = 1.47 metres per metre. At 10⁻⁹ m/s over a wet height of about 20 m, that is about 2.5 litres a day through each metre of dam. The lab with a full cutoff under the core, so that the core is the only way through, gives 2.1: the hand sum is within a fifth of it. The rest of the 37.2 goes under the core, through the clay foundation, where Chapter 10 follows it.

What it means. A core works by where it puts the water, far more than by how much water it stops. The leak changed by a sixth; the water level in the downstream half fell by more than seven metres, and with it the water pressure under the grains that hold the dam up.

9.2 Four jobs

A core alone does not make a dam, because the water it lets through has to go somewhere and the core has to be held in place. Every embankment with a core hands out the same four jobs to different soils.

Hold the water back. That is the core's job: compacted clay, or glacial till, the unsorted mix of clay, silt, sand and stones that a glacier leaves behind. Bennett's core is glacial soil of that kind, a non-plastic mix of silt, sand and gravel.BC Hydro expert panel (2012), p. 31 ("non-plastic silt sand gravel", and a glacial soil tested as similar to it) and p. 48 (the moraine materials used in the core). Where the ground beneath is gravel or cracked rock, the barrier has to go down into it too. A cutoff trench carries the core down through loose river deposits to rock, and under the trench a grout curtain, lines of holes drilled into the rock and pumped full of cement grout, closes the rock's cracks.Rock is tested for grouting by pumping water into a section of a drill hole. One Lugeon is an inflow of one litre a minute into each metre of hole at a pressure of 1,000 kPa, equivalent to a rock permeability of about 1.3 × 10⁻⁷ m/s (BC Hydro expert panel (2012), p. 5).

Let the water out. Whatever gets through the core must leave the dam without building up pressure in the part that holds it up. Drains of clean sand and gravel do that: a chimney drain standing against the downstream side of the core, a blanket along the base, and a toe drain that carries the water out to where it can be measured.

Stop the soil. But water leaving fine grains for coarse ones carries the fine grains with it, so a drain laid straight against a core would slowly wash the core away. Filters and transitions sit between them and step the grain size up gradually, each zone fine enough that the grains of the zone inside it cannot wash into its gaps, and coarse enough to let the water through. This is the thinnest zone in the dam, and its job is the subtlest; Chapter 11 is about it.

Add weight. The shells of rockfill or sand and gravel are most of the dam. They hold the core in place against the push of the reservoir and hold themselves up by friction, which is to say by the press of their grains on one another. Over the upstream shell goes riprap, against waves and ice; along the top, the crest carries a road and stands high enough above the highest flood to leave some freeboard.

Read a cored dam from the middle outward and you meet the jobs in the same order every time: tight in the centre, coarser and freer-draining toward the faces. Each zone is coarser than the one inside it, so the water can get out, and fine enough to hold that zone's grains in. Engineers number the zones in that order too. Zone 1 is the barrier, Zone 2 the filters and transitions under or beside it, Zone 3 the main rockfill, though each dam adapts the scheme: Bennett's run from 1 to 6, core outward.The convention, as Cooke and Sherard set it out and Cruz quotes it: Cruz (2008), p. 57.

Check yourself Rockfill drains freely and is strong. Why not pile it directly against the core?

Water leaving the core would carry its fine grains into the big gaps between the rocks, and the core would wash away from the inside. The filter and the transition step the grain size up so that no zone can wash into the next.

Below, a 60 m earth–rockfill dam is drawn to scale with all its zones in place, beside three other kinds of dam. Click a zone, or its chip, to read what it is made of, how easily water passes through it, its job, and what happens if it fails. Build shows the order in which the dam goes up, and Explode pulls the zones apart:

Notice that the phreatic surface stays at the reservoir's level all the way through the upstream shell and only drops inside the core: the upstream shell is soaked. Notice too how thin the filters and transitions are, a few metres wide in a dam more than 250 m across at its base, and that Build places them in the same stage as the core, layer by layer, since they could never be slipped in later. The cards are easier to compare side by side, so here they are for the earth–rockfill section:

Tailings dams can be zoned the same way. Mount Polley's, in British Columbia, was: the review panel's section through it shows a core of till, a filter and a transition downstream of the core, rockfill supporting them, and a zone of tailings or rockfill on the pond side. The panel found the filter thin and much of it more poorly graded than a filter should be, and still found no evidence that the breach was caused by water eroding the core.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), pp. 7–8 (the zones and their duties) and pp. 11–12 (the filter, and the finding on erosion of the core). Its zones are not where its answer lies.

9.3 Two shells, one soaked

The two shells look alike in a drawing, and they lead different lives. The downstream shell is the part the core protects. Behind our dam's core the water stood 0.65 m deep, so above that the gaps in the downstream shell hold air, the water pressure in them is zero, and the grains press on one another with their whole weight.

The upstream shell gets no such protection. It sits under the reservoir, and every gap in it is full of water at whatever pressure the lake's depth puts there. One could assume that a soaked shell must be a weak one, since water in the gaps takes part of the grains' press away. It does take part of it, and the grains grip one another less for that; but as long as the water is still, the shell is no less safe. Buoyancy lightens each grain's press on the grains below it, and it lightens the pull that tries to slide the grains down the slope by exactly the same share. Chapter 4 showed the result for a heap of sand: under still water it stands as steeply as it does dry. Here are the numbers for the shells of Fig. 9.1, made of the workbench's rockfill:

Example 9.2

Soaked, and still the safer face

Given
Rockfill weighing 22 kN/m³ soaked and 20 kN/m³ moist, friction angle φ′ = 42°, no cohesion; water 9.81 kN/m³. The upstream face slopes at 2.2:1, the downstream face at 1.9:1. The upstream shell lies under still water; the downstream one is dry.
Find
How hard the grains press 20 m below the surface of each shell, and the factor of safety of each face treated as a long, straight slope; then the upstream face's if the water in it were trapped and seeping out.
The idea
Under still water the grains press with their buoyant weight, soaked weight less water. For a long slope of cohesionless grains, FS = tan φ′ ÷ tan β, the same dry or under still water; with water seeping out parallel to the face it falls in the ratio of buoyant to soaked weight (Chapter 4).
  1. Buoyant weight: 22 − 9.81 = 12.19 kN/m³each cubic metre's weight less the water it pushes aside
  2. Upstream, 20 m down: 12.19 × 20 = 243.8 kPathe press of the grains on the grains below
  3. Downstream, 20 m down: 20 × 20 = 400 kPano water in the gaps, so the whole weight presses
  4. 243.8 ÷ 400 = 0.61the soaked grains press 61% as hard
  5. Upstream face: tan 42° × 2.2 = 0.9004 × 2.2 = 1.98tan β = 1 ÷ 2.2; the still water lightens the press and the pull alike
  6. Downstream face: 0.9004 × 1.9 = 1.71steeper, at tan β = 1 ÷ 1.9
  7. Upstream, water trapped: 1.98 × 12.19 ÷ 22 = 1.10water seeping out through the face, as at the foot of a beach at low tide

Soaked, the upstream shell's grains press only 0.61 times as hard as the dry shell's, and yet its face is the safer of the two, 1.98 against 1.71, as long as its water is still. Trap the water and the upstream face falls to 1.10.

Check. The two faces are the same rockfill at different slopes, so their factors should differ only by the ratio of the slopes: 1.98 × 1.9 ÷ 2.2 = 1.71. And at a 1:1 face, 45°, the dry rockfill would have FS = tan 42° = 0.90: no heap of this rockfill stands that steep.

What it means. A soaked shell is safe while its water can come and go with the lake. Rockfill, at 10⁻¹ to 10⁻³ m/s, drains as fast as any reservoir can be lowered; a shell of fine fill would not, and its face would fall toward the trapped case. These are long, straight slopes; real slips are curved and run deeper, and Chapter 12 checks them on our dam.

That trapped case has a name. Lowering a reservoir faster than its water can leave the upstream shell is rapid drawdown: the water that pressed on the face from outside is gone, the water inside is still there, and it pushes outward through the slope. It is the one event that turns a soaked shell from safe to dangerous. It is why designers prize an upstream shell that drains freely, and one reason the earth–rockfill section's upstream face is the flatter of the two.

9.4 Where the rule breaks

"Tight in the middle, coarse outside" is the rule for a dam with a core. The other three tabs of Fig. 9.1 break it, each for a reason.

The concrete-face rockfill dam has no core. Its barrier is a slab of reinforced concrete laid over the upstream face, joined to the rock around its edges by a concrete plinth, with the grout curtain drilled from the plinth. Behind the slab the whole dam is rockfill, rolled hard so that it settles little and the slab does not crack. Its finest zones are directly under the slab, not in the middle: a cushion of crushed rock and sand gives the slab a firm, smooth bed and limits the leak if a crack opens. Water that passes the slab drops through the rockfill to the base and runs out, and the rockfill needs no filter against the slab because it has no fine grains to lose. The leaks it can take are large. At two big dams of this kind in Brazil, Barra Grande and Campos Novos, leaks of 1,000 to 3,000 litres a second were measured with no sign of trouble in the downstream slope.Cruz (2008), pp. 60–61, reviewing Cooke & Sherard (1987).

The concrete gravity dam has zones only in a looser sense: a richer, frost-resistant concrete on its faces, a lean mass concrete inside so that the heat of setting stays low, and drains and a gallery near the upstream face. None of them is there to stop water carrying grains away, because concrete has no loose grains. Its danger, as Chapter 7 showed, is the water underneath it.

The tailings dam is built of its own waste. In the centreline dam on the last tab, sand split from the tailings by cyclones is spread and compacted on the downstream slope, a chimney drain keeps that sand from filling with water, and the finest waste settles out by the pond, on the upstream side, as far from the slope as it can be (Chapter 8 showed how such a dam rises). The materials are the mine's, and the aim is the cored dam's: keep the water away from the part that holds the dam up.

So "tight in the middle" is one way of doing something every dam on the four tabs does. Each decides where the water will stand, and keeps it out of the part that carries the load.

Check yourself A crack opens in a concrete-face rockfill dam's slab and the leak through the dam rises tenfold. Why would its engineers worry less than about a crack in a clay core?

The water that passes the slab falls into rockfill with no fine grains to lose, and drains out at the base without raising the water pressure in the dam. Water through a crack in a core can carry the core itself away, which is why a core needs filters and a slab does not.

9.5 How a heap becomes fill

So far every zone has been described by what it is made of. How it is put in place matters as much. Soil dug from a borrow pit and tipped into a heap is loose, the loose sand of Chapter 5: wide gaps, ready to settle when it is wetted or shaken, and inclined to shrink when it is sheared, handing its load to the water in its gaps. A dam of loose soil would settle unevenly and crack, and a soaked shell of it could lose its grip altogether. So every zone goes in as thin layers, each squeezed dense by rollers before the next is spread. That squeezing is compaction, and it is why Bennett's core went in no more than 10 inches at a time.

How dense can a soil be made? In 1933 R. R. Proctor, a field engineer with the water department of Los Angeles, published a way to find out.Proctor's first article (Proctor (1933)) rested on laboratory tests of more than 200 soils, checked in the field on four dams his bureau had built in the two years before. He explained the dry side much as this chapter does below: in a very dry soil, films of water where the grains touch draw them firmly together, and a little more water releases that pull. Past that point he wrote of the water as having "an effect similar to that of lubrication". Pack a sample of the soil into a mould with a set number of blows from a standard hammer. Weigh it, dry it in an oven, and weigh it again. Then add a little water to the soil and repeat. A cubic metre of the packed sample weighs its bulk unit weight γ, grains and water together; its water content w is the weight of the water as a fraction of the weight of the grains. Take the water out and what is left is the weight of grain in each cubic metre, the dry unit weight:

γd = γ / (1 + w)(9.1)

γd dry unit weight, the grains in each cubic metre (kN/m³) · γ bulk unit weight, grains and water (kN/m³) · w water content, weight of water ÷ weight of grains

The more grain packed into each cubic metre, the denser the fill. Plotted against the water content, Proctor's dry unit weights climb, reach a peak and fall again, here for an illustrative soil:

Notice that the curve has a single peak and falls away on both sides. On the dry side, the castle's grip from Chapter 1 works against the roller: rings of water where the grains touch bind them into crumbs that resist being pushed into one another's gaps, and a little more water weakens the rings and lets the grains pack closer. On the wet side, water fills nearly every gap, and in the moment a roller takes to pass it cannot get out: the water carries the roller's press, as it carried the load in the undrained tests of Chapter 5, and the grains are pushed no closer. The peak is the optimum water content, and the peak's weight is the most this effort can achieve with this soil. A heavier roller, or more blows, gives a higher peak at a little less water.

A specification asks for a share of that peak. Its relative compaction is the dry unit weight reached on site divided by the laboratory maximum:

RC = γd / γd,max(9.2)

RC relative compaction, usually given as a percentage · γd,max the peak of the laboratory curve for the same soil (kN/m³)

Bennett's core had to reach 98 per cent, at a water content between 2 per cent below the optimum and 1 per cent above it.BC Hydro expert panel (2012), the table of zones, p. 3 (the specification) and p. 9 (permeability against the water content at placing). The water content matters for more than density. The panel found that the same core soil, placed drier, with less of its gaps filled with water, let water through 60 to 140 times more easily once soaked than when it was placed wetter. The core's card in Fig. 9.1 gives a second reason to keep a core near its optimum or a little wet of it: there the soil bends as the dam settles, where a drier, stiffer one would crack.

On site an inspector checks each layer: dig a small hole, weigh what comes out, measure the hole's volume (by filling it with sand of known density, for instance), and dry a sample for its water content. Those two numbers give γ and w, and with them the gaps. A cubic metre of solid grain would weigh Gs γw, where Gs, about 2.65 for quartz sand, is how many times denser the grain is than water (Chapter 5). So the volume that one unit of grain takes up, gaps included, is Gs γw / γd, and the gaps alone, the void ratio, are that less one:

e = Gs · γw / γd − 1(9.3)

e void ratio, volume of gaps ÷ volume of grains · Gs specific gravity of the grains · γw unit weight of water, 9.81 kN/m³

Example 9.3

Does the layer pass?

Given
An illustrative field test on a freshly rolled layer: bulk unit weight 20.6 kN/m³, water content 12%. The laboratory peak for this soil is 19.0 kN/m³, and its grains have Gs = 2.65. The specification asks for 98%, as Bennett's did.
Find
The dry unit weight, the relative compaction, the void ratio and the gap fraction; and whether the layer passes.
The idea
Take out the water's weight (Eq. 9.1), compare with the laboratory peak (Eq. 9.2), then count the gaps from the room the grains take (Eq. 9.3).
  1. γd = 20.6 ÷ 1.12 = 18.393 kN/m³1 + w = 1.12: each kilonewton of grain carries 0.12 kN of water
  2. RC = 18.393 ÷ 19.0 = 0.968, so 96.8%the share of the laboratory's best
  3. 2.65 × 9.81 ÷ 18.393 = 1.413room taken by one unit of grain, gaps included
  4. e = 1.413 − 1 = 0.413the gaps alone
  5. 0.413 ÷ 1.413 = 0.29gaps as a share of the whole volume

The layer reaches 96.8% of the laboratory peak, with a void ratio of 0.413. It is dense, and it fails a 98% specification: it falls short of what Bennett's core was meant to reach.

Check. The water must fit in the gaps. The share of the gaps it fills is w × Gs ÷ e = 0.12 × 2.65 ÷ 0.413 = 0.77, less than 1, so air fills the rest. The open circle in Fig. 9.2 must then sit below the zero-air-voids line at 12%, which is 2.65 × 9.81 ÷ 1.318 = 19.72; at 18.393, it does.

What it means. Gaps that fill 0.29 of the volume are fewer than the third of the volume that Chapter 3 allowed soaked soil. Sand packed this dense swells when it is sheared and draws water in (Chapter 5), so it holds. Compaction turns a loose heap that would hand its load to the water into fill that keeps it on the grains.

Check yourself A layer tests at 95% and well wet of the optimum. The contractor offers to roll it a few more times. Will that help much?

Not much. Wet of the optimum the gaps are nearly full of water, which cannot get out while a roller passes, so the water takes the extra press and the grains move little closer. Drying the soil toward the optimum, or digging the layer out, does more.

Each zone, then, is a soil chosen for one job, packed by rules written for that job, and set where its designers expected the water to be. The core expects the water to stop at it, the filter expects to meet whatever gets through, and the drain expects to carry it off.

What to remember

  • A dam need not be watertight. It has to keep the water pressure out of the part that holds it up, so that the grains there press on one another with nearly their whole weight. In our dam a clay core takes 96.8% of the head and the leak barely changes.
  • Four jobs, middle outward: hold the water back (core, cutoff, grout curtain), let it out (drains), stop the soil moving with it (filters and transitions), and add weight (shells). Each zone is coarser than the one inside it.
  • The downstream shell is kept nearly dry. The upstream shell is soaked and still strong, because still water lightens the grains' press and the pull on them alike, and rockfill drains as fast as the lake falls. Rapid drawdown of a shell that drains slowly is its danger.
  • "Tight in the middle" is the cored dam's way. A concrete-face rockfill dam puts its barrier on the face, a gravity dam is its own barrier, and a tailings dam builds itself from its waste, all to keep water away from what carries the load.
  • Compaction packs loose fill dense, so that it keeps its load on its grains. Each soil packs densest at its optimum water content, and relative compaction measures a layer against that laboratory best.

Questions

  1. 9.1

    Why can the upstream shell be soaked and still strong, and what one event makes it dangerous?

    Hint

    Compare what still water does to the press of a grain on the grains below it and to the pull that tries to slide it downhill. Then ask what happens if the water cannot leave.

    Answer

  2. 9.2

    A concrete-face rockfill dam has no core. Where is its barrier, and why does its main rockfill need no filter against the slab?

    Hint

    Ask what a filter is for, and whether the rockfill has anything a leak could carry away.

    Answer

  3. 9.3

    Press Build on each tab of Fig. 9.1. Which dam puts its watertight element in only after the body of the dam is built, and what does that mean for inspecting it?

    Hint

    Watch the stage in which the barrier appears, and whether anything is built over it afterwards.

    Answer

  4. 9.4

    The earth–rockfill dam has filters on both sides of its core. Why does the downstream one matter more?

    Hint

    Which way does the water cross the core, most of the time?

    Answer

  5. 9.5

    An illustrative field test on a rolled layer gives a bulk unit weight of 21.0 kN/m³ at 14% water. The laboratory peak for the soil is 18.9 kN/m³. What is the relative compaction, and does the layer pass a 98% specification?

    Hint

    Take the water out first with Eq. 9.1, then divide by the peak.

    Answer

  6. 9.6

    Bennett's core had to reach 98% of the laboratory peak and be placed between 2% below and 1% above its optimum water content (BC Hydro expert panel (2012), p. 3). Why specify the water content as well as the density?

    Hint

    Two layers with the same density can still differ in how they behave once the reservoir soaks them.

    Answer

Every zone in this chapter was placed on a guess about where the water would go: the core to take the head, the filter to catch whatever gets through, the drain to carry it off. Water does not read drawings. Where does it actually go, and how much of it?

10

Chapter 10 · Part III · Inside the embankment

Where the water goes

If every dam leaks, what makes a leak safe?

So far. Chapter 9 built our dam, a 24 m embankment with slopes of 2:1 (two across for every one up, as in Example 1.2), and in its zoned form a clay core between free-draining shells. Every zone went where it did on a guess about where the water would go. This chapter follows the water itself: where it gets in, which way it goes, and where it comes out.

After this chapter you can

  • trace the five ways water gets past a dam, and read a flow net to work out how much flows and how steeply the head falls where it leaves;
  • estimate a dam's leak by hand with Darcy's law, and check the estimate against the seepage lab's solution;
  • explain why a drain makes a dam leak more and yet makes it safer, and choose a defence from a picture of the seepage.

This chapter adds two flow lines and three equipotentials

4 figures · about 25 min to read

Walk along the downstream toe of an earth dam and sooner or later you come to a small concrete box set into the ground. Across one end stands a steel plate with a V cut into its top edge, and through the V slides a thin, clear sheet of water. It drops a few centimetres into a channel and runs off toward the river. On a regular round someone comes by, reads how deep the water stands behind the plate, and writes it down. That depth says how many litres a second are coming out.

The water in the box is the dam's leak, its seepage. It went into the ground on the floor of the reservoir, or soaked into the dam's upstream face, and crept through to this side. Nobody is alarmed by it. The US Army Corps of Engineers' manual on seepage states it as a fact before it says anything else: "All earth and rock-fill dams are subject to seepage through the embankment, foundation, and abutments."USACE EM 1110-2-1901, para. 1-5, and again in para. 8-1; para. 13-3 describes the V-notch weirs. Every dam leaks. The useful question is what makes a leak safe, and here is a first test of your feel for leaks:

Our dam stands on 15 m of sand and gravel, with nothing under it to stop water passing beneath, and it is built of one kind of earth fill. Build it again with a narrow core of clay, a hundred times tighter than that fill, between shells of free-draining sand and gravel. The ground underneath stays as it was. What happens to the leak?

It rises, from 2,366 to 5,434 litres a day under each metre of dam, more than twice as much. The water was never going through the dam; almost all of it goes under. The free-draining upstream shell lets it reach the gravel close to the core, so it only has to get under the core's 21.4 m base instead of the whole 102 m. Example 10.3 works it through.

To decide, follow the water: where it enters, which way it goes and how far, and where it comes out. That takes a map of the ways past a dam, a way of drawing the water's paths, and in the end a solver.

10.1 Five ways past a dam

You met the rule in Chapter 3: water flows from high head to low, as fast as the soil lets it, and Darcy's law, Eq. 3.2, says how fast. The race in Fig. 3.3 showed how wide the range of permeability is: gravel, at 10⁻² m/s, passes water ten million times as easily as compacted clay, at 10⁻⁹ m/s. Zoning depends on that spread. A clay core much narrower than the dam can take almost the whole drop in head while the free-draining shells beside it take almost none.

A dam is more than one pipe, though. Water has five main ways past it, and the drawing numbers them:

Notice that the core and its cutoff, which take most of the drawing's care, stand in the way of path 1 and of path 2 only as far down as the cutoff reaches. Paths 2, 3 and 5 run through ground that was there before the dam. Its designers chose neither its permeability nor its layering; they could only find them out, and the water uses whatever they missed.

10.2 Drawing the water: the flow net

To say how much water takes path 2, and how hard it pushes where it comes out, you need the head everywhere in the ground. Fig. 3.2 found it for a pipe, where the water has one way to go and the head falls along a straight line. Under a dam the water spreads out and bends. The rule in every small piece of ground is still the same, though: in steady flow nothing piles up, so each piece passes on exactly the water it receives, and it passes it toward lower head by Darcy's law.In symbols the two facts are one equation, ∇·(k∇h) = 0. Read it from the inside out: ∇h is the slope of the head, k∇h the flow it drives by Darcy's law, and ∇· (the divergence) asks how much more flows out of a tiny box than flows in. Zero means nothing piles up and nothing runs dry. In uniform soil k comes outside and it becomes Laplace's equation, the same one that governs the steady flow of heat through a metal plate. Those two facts fix the head everywhere once you know it along the edges: the reservoir floor, the ground beyond the toe, the underside of the structure.

For most of the twentieth century engineers drew the answer by hand, as a flow net: two families of lines. Flow lines are the paths the water follows. Equipotentials join points of equal total head: push one of the straws of Fig. 3.1 into the ground anywhere along one, and the water in it rises to the same level. In soil that passes water equally well in every direction, the water crosses every equipotential at right angles, because straight across them is the way the head falls fastest.Philipp Forchheimer, an Austrian engineer, recognized that steady groundwater flow obeys Laplace's equation and drew some of the first flow nets (Houben et al. (2025)). Arthur Casagrande, at Harvard, made the net a working tool for dam designers in a paper of 1937, with rules for beginners that still hold: start with four or five flow channels, and adjust the whole net before any of its details (Casagrande (1937)).

What makes a net useful is a choice of spacing. Space the flow lines so that each neighbouring pair carries the same share of the flow; the strip between them is a flow channel. Space the equipotentials so that the head falls by the same amount, Δh, between each pair; that is a head drop. Now look at one cell of the net, b wide across the flow and l long along it. By Darcy's law the flow through it, per metre of dam, is k × (Δh/l) × b. Draw the net so that every cell is a square, b = l, and the flow through each cell is k·Δh, whatever its size. With Nd drops sharing the total head H, Δh = H/Nd, and Nf channels each carrying k·Δh give the whole flow:

q = k · H · Nf / Nd(10.1)

q flow per metre length of dam (m³/s per m) · k permeability (m/s) · H head lost between where the water enters and where it leaves (m) · Nf number of flow channels · Nd number of head drops

The ratio Nf/Nd depends only on the shape of the ground and the structure. The rules for sketching a net are short: lines cross at right angles, every cell looks square, an edge that passes no water (a concrete base, a rock surface) is itself a flow line, and ground under still water is an equipotential. Getting every cell square at once takes practice and an eraser. Here is a finished net under a small concrete weir (a low dam across a river, not the measuring weir of the toe), an illustrative example sunk into a bed of sand:

Notice that the squares are big where the water has room, out under the reservoir and deep under the weir, and small where it is squeezed, around the weir's buried corners. A small square means the same drop in head over a short distance: a steep gradient, and fast water. Crowding in a flow net is a picture of the gradient. Notice too where the smallest square is: at the exit, where the water turns upward beside the weir and leaves the sand. That is where the water pushes hardest on the grains it is leaving.

Example 10.1

Reading the weir's net

Given
The net of Fig. 10.2 (illustrative): Nf = 4 channels, Nd = 12 drops, head H = 10 m, sand with k = 10⁻⁴ m/s. The smallest square, at the exit, is 1.4 m deep along the weir's downstream face.
Find
The flow under each metre of weir, and the gradient where the water leaves.
The idea
Every square passes k·Δh, so the flow is a count (Eq. 10.1). In the last square the water loses one drop of head over the square's length.
  1. Δh = 10 ÷ 12 = 0.833 mthe head lost in each drop
  2. Each channel: 10⁻⁴ × 0.833 = 8.3 × 10⁻⁵ m³/sa square passes permeability times its drop in head
  3. q = 4 × 8.33 × 10⁻⁵ = 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ m³/sfour channels, each carrying the same
  4. In a day: 0.000333 × 86,400 = 28.8 m³86,400 seconds in a day
  5. i at the exit = 0.833 ÷ 1.4 = 0.595the last drop, spent over the depth of the last square

About 29 m³ of water a day passes under each metre of the weir, and it leaves the sand beside the weir at a gradient of 0.60.

Check. Make the sand ten times as permeable. The squares are the same squares, because nothing in the drawing knows about k, so the flow rises tenfold, to 3.3 × 10⁻³ m³/s, and the exit gradient stays 0.60. A gradient is a drop in head over a distance, and both come from the drawing alone.

What it means. The exit gradient of 0.60 is below the 1 at which upward-flowing water floats sand (Chapter 4), but not by much, and it sits exactly where the net is most crowded. The weir's weak spot is a square metre or two of sand beside its downstream face.

The Check holds a lesson for every seepage calculation. The permeability of a natural sand is rarely known to better than a factor of a few, so the flow from a net is only as good as that guess; the pattern of heads, and with it every gradient and every water pressure, comes from the geometry, which the engineer can draw. That is why engineers sketch nets carefully where they want pressures and roughly where they want quantities."For calculation of seepage quantity only a crude flow net is required. Accurate flow nets are required to determine pressure distribution": USACE EM 1110-2-1901, para. 4-6. Real ground adds a complication the drawing leaves out: soil laid down in layers passes water more easily along its layers than across them, a property called anisotropy.Casagrande warned that where layering is visible the permeability along the layers "may easily be ten times greater" than across them, and much more in distinctly layered soils; even a rolled earth dam, compacted layer by layer, keeps some of it (Casagrande (1937), pp. 151–152). Engineers draw the net on a section stretched by the square root of the ratio, then squash it back (USACE EM 1110-2-1901, para. 4-7). A net drawn for uniform soil is the start of the analysis, not the end.

Check yourself The water upstream of the weir rises from 10 m to 15 m above the sand. Which lines of the net move?

None of them. The net is fixed by the shape of the weir and the sand. Every drop in head, the flow and the exit gradient grow by half again, in proportion to H.

10.3 Seepage lab

A net through a whole earth dam is harder to sketch than one under a weir, because the top of the wet part of the dam is unknown until the net is finished. So the page computes it instead. Everything in the next drawing is calculated. The page divides our 24 m embankment and the 15 m of ground beneath it into 1 m cells, applies Darcy's law between every pair of neighbours, and solves for the head in all of them at once (the steady seepage equation, ∇·(k ∇h) = 0). Along the way it finds the phreatic surface, the water table inside the dam, using the same saturated–unsaturated approach as commercial seepage software. Lines of equal head are drawn every 10% of the reservoir head. Flow lines are drawn in two sets: four start on the dam's upstream face and five on the reservoir floor. Within each set, each neighbouring pair carries the same flow, as in a hand-drawn flow net. Between the sets it differs: on the starting settings a gap between two foundation lines carries about 8 times the flow of a gap between two dam lines, so compare line spacing only within a set. The lab's lines are therefore no square net, and Eq. 10.1 can't count them: read the heads from its equipotentials and the flow from its readout.

It opens on our dam built of one fill, 10⁻⁷ m/s, standing on sand and gravel a hundred times more permeable, 10⁻⁵ m/s, with no drain and no cutoff, and the reservoir 20.4 m deep:

Notice that the equipotentials under the dam stand almost upright and nearly evenly spaced, like the head along the pipe of Fig. 3.2. The gravel passes water 100 times as easily as the fill, so to the water the dam is nearly a lid and the gravel a pipe 15 m deep and as long as the dam's base. Notice too how little goes in through the dam's own face: 221 of the 2,366 litres a day. That picture can be checked by hand.

Example 10.2

Our dam's leak, by hand

Given
The lab on its starting settings: reservoir 20.4 m deep, tailwater at the ground; sand and gravel 15 m deep with k = 10⁻⁵ m/s; the dam's base, toe to toe, 102 m.
Find
The leak under each metre of dam, in litres a day, and how it compares with the lab's.
The idea
Treat the gravel as the pipe of Fig. 3.2: the whole head lost along the base, through an area 15 m deep for each metre of dam (Eq. 3.2).
  1. i = 20.4 ÷ 102 = 0.200head lost per metre of path
  2. q = 0.00001 × 0.200 × 15 = 0.00003 m³/sDarcy's law through 15 m² for each metre of dam
  3. 0.00003 × 86,400 × 1,000 = 2,592 L/dayseconds in a day, litres in a cubic metre
  4. 2,592 ÷ 2,366 = 1.096the hand number against the lab's
  5. A kilometre of dam: 2,366 × 1,000 ÷ 86,400 = 27.4 L/sa thousand metres of dam, litres a day turned into litres a second

About 2,600 litres a day under each metre of dam by hand, 10% more than the lab's 2,366. A kilometre of this dam would leak about 27 litres a second.

Check. Should the hand number be high or low? Darcy's pipe sends the water straight along 102 m. The real water has to dive into the gravel at the upstream toe and climb out again beyond the downstream one, and the lab's flow lines bow downward to do it. A longer path passes less, so the straight pipe should be a little high, and it is. The pipe also ignores the water that goes through the fill, but that is small: 99% of the lab's leak crosses the dam's centre line under the dam.

What it means. Ten per cent is better than the permeability deserves. A natural gravel's k is rarely known within a factor of a few, and the Bureau of Reclamation, which teaches this very calculation, says its result should be read only as the order of magnitude of the seepage (USBR (1987), sec. 6.9(b)).

10.4 What the lab knows that intuition doesn't

A hand estimate is only as good as the picture of the flow behind it, and the lab earns its place where that picture is wrong. The first case is the question this chapter opened with. Give our dam a clay core a hundred times tighter than its fill, 10⁻⁹ m/s, between shells of sand and gravel, 10⁻⁴ m/s, ten times more permeable than the gravel beneath them:

Example 10.3

The core that leaks more

Given
Both dams on the sand and gravel, no drain, no cutoff, reservoir 20.4 m. The dam of one fill leaks 2,366 L/day per metre; the cored dam, 5,434. The core is 21.4 m wide at its base.
Find
Why the cored dam leaks more, and what a full cutoff under its core does.
The idea
Almost all the water goes under both dams. What changes is how much of the base the water must get under, which the head the solver finds at the top of the gravel shows.
  1. 5,434 ÷ 2,366 = 2.30the core more than doubles the leak
  2. In through the upstream shell: 5,343; through the reservoir floor: 91 L/daythe shell is the easy way in, so the water reaches the gravel beside the core
  3. Head at the top of the gravel, 12 m upstream of the centre line: 19.1 m (94%); with no core, 12.6 m (62%)the shell spends almost none of the head, so the water arrives at the core with nearly all of it
  4. Length to get under: 102 ÷ 21.4 = 4.77the whole base under a dam of fill, which is a lid to the gravel; only the core's base under the cored dam
  5. Full cutoff under the core: 5,434 ÷ 2.177 = 2,496a wall from the core's base to the rock: the leak falls to 2.2 L/day

The core more than doubles the leak, because the shells deliver the water to the gravel right beside it and the water only has to pass under the core's 21.4 m base. Taken down to rock with a cutoff, the same core cuts the leak about 2,500 times.

Check. If the length under the dam were the whole story, a length 4.8 times shorter would pass 4.8 times the water; the lab gives 2.3. The rest of the trip does not shrink with the core: the water still has to climb out of the gravel and cross some 40 m of it to the toe, and 6.0 m of head is still left at the top of the gravel a metre downstream of the core. So the factor should fall short of the ratio of lengths, and it does.

What it means. A barrier works only if the water can't go round it. A core that stops on top of a pervious foundation is a wall with a gap under it, and its shells hurry the water to the gap. The same core joined to rock by a cutoff makes the dam almost dry.

Check yourself A full cutoff cuts the cored dam's leak about 2,500 times. Would it do as much for the dam of one fill?

No: 2,366 falls only to 166, about 14 times less. With the gravel cut off, the water goes through the fill instead, and the fill passes water a hundred times more easily than the core.

The second surprise runs the other way. A drain inside a dam is a strip of clean sand and gravel, graded so that the soil around it cannot follow the water in (Chapter 11 explains how), and open to the air at its outlet, so the water in it is at zero pressure. Every bit of water in the dam or the ground that can reach it heads for it. The Corps of Engineers' manual notes the consequence for a horizontal drain under the downstream half of a dam: it lowers the pressure under the dam and increases the quantity of seepage.USACE EM 1110-2-1901, para. 9-3 and its Figure 9-1. The lab shows by how much:

Example 10.4

A drain that leaks more and is safer

Given
The dam of one fill on the sand and gravel, reservoir 20.4 m: 2,366 L/day per metre and a safety against piping of 1.27. The chimney drain stands 4 m downstream of the centre line, and its blanket runs from there along the base to the toe. The toe drain fills the dam's toe.
Find
The leak and the safety against piping with each drain, and why the chimney raises the leak.
The idea
A drain holds everything it touches at zero pressure. It ends the water's trip early, and it gives the water a way out that holds the soil back.
  1. Chimney and blanket: 4,052 ÷ 2,366 = 1.7171% more water
  2. Path under the dam: 55 m instead of 102; 102 ÷ 55 = 1.85the gravel's water now leaves through the blanket, which starts 4 m past the centre line, 55 m from the upstream toe
  3. Steepest exit not covered by the drain: i = 0.0029; safety 343the water leaves through the drain, not through bare ground or the face
  4. Toe drain: 2,647 L/day, 12% more; safety 12.8a shorter cut at the end of the trip

The chimney drain makes our dam leak 71% more and raises its safety against piping from 1.27 to over 300. The toe drain costs 12% more water and raises the safety to 12.8.

Check. Darcy's law predicts a path 1.85 times shorter should pass 1.85 times the water; the lab gives 1.71, a little less, because the water still has to dive into the gravel and rise into the blanket. In the gravel immediately under the blanket's start the solver finds a head of 0.54 m: the drain has taken almost all of the 20.4 m by the time the water reaches it.

What it means. The extra water costs nothing but water. In return the drain takes the water pressure out of the downstream half of the dam, so the grains there press on one another with nearly their full weight and grip accordingly, which is what Chapter 5 meant by drains putting strength back. And it gives the water an exit that holds the soil back.

Check yourself Where would you put a piezometer to show that the chimney drain works, and what should it read?

In the fill a few metres downstream of the chimney, near the base. With the drain working, the water in it should stand barely above its tip, because the fill there is drained to about zero pressure; a reading well above that means the drain is clogged or cut off.

10.5 A dam on clay

Now take the gravel away. Switch the foundation to Clay, 5 × 10⁻⁸ m/s, half as permeable as the fill. The leak collapses to 44.4 L/day per metre, and something else appears. On gravel the phreatic surface reached the downstream slope only 2 m up; on clay it meets the slope 8 m up, and 65% of the water leaves through the slope's face. With no easy way underneath, the water comes through the dam, and that needs a different hand estimate: one for water moving through the fill with a free surface on top.

The estimate engineers use is due to the French engineer Jules Dupuit, in 1863.Dupuit (1863). The entry correction: Casagrande (1937), p. 150. Pretend the water moves level. Cut the dam into upright slices. In a slice where the saturated fill is h deep, the water flows through h square metres for each metre of dam, and the gradient is the slope of the water table there, Δh over Δx. By Darcy's law q = k × (Δh/Δx) × h, and the same q passes every slice, so where the wet part is thin the water table must be steep. Rearranged, q · Δx = k · h · Δh. Add up the slices from the downstream end to the reservoir. On the left the Δx add up to the length L. On the right the products h · Δh, as h rises from nothing to H, add up to the area of a triangle with height H and base H, ½H², the same sum that gave the push of water in Eq. 2.2:

q = k · H² / (2L)(10.2)

q flow through the dam per metre length (m³/s per m) · k permeability of the fill (m/s) · H depth of the reservoir (m) · L length the water travels, from where it enters to the downstream toe (m)

Where does the water enter? The upstream wedge of the dam stands in the reservoir and its water is at nearly the reservoir's head, so measuring from the upstream toe would make the trip too long. Arthur Casagrande showed in 1937 that a simple rule does well: start the trip upstream of where the water surface meets the face, by 0.3 times the horizontal run of the wetted face.

Example 10.5

Our dam on clay, by hand

Given
The dam of one fill, k = 10⁻⁷ m/s, slopes 2:1, toes 102 m apart, on 15 m of clay with k = 5 × 10⁻⁸ m/s; reservoir H = 20.4 m, meeting the upstream face 10.2 m upstream of the centre line. A flow of 10⁻⁷ m³/s is 8.64 litres a day.
Find
The leak by hand, through the fill and under it, and where the water breaks out on the downstream slope.
The idea
Two flows side by side: through the fill by Eq. 10.2, and under it through the clay by Darcy's pipe, as in Example 10.2.
  1. Run of the wetted upstream face: 2 × 20.4 = 40.8 mtwo across for every one up
  2. Entry correction: 0.3 × 40.8 = 12.24 mCasagrande's rule
  3. L = 12.24 + 10.2 + 51 = 73.44 mfrom the entry point to the centre line, then half the base to the downstream toe
  4. H² ÷ 2L: 416.16 ÷ 146.88 = 2.833 m20.4² = 416.16, and 2 × 73.44 = 146.88
  5. Through the fill: 2.833 × 8.64 = 24.48 L/dayEq. 10.2, with k = 10⁻⁷ m/s turned into litres a day
  6. Under it: 4.32 × 0.200 × 15 = 12.96 L/dayDarcy's pipe through the clay, its k in litres a day
  7. Total: 24.48 + 12.96 = 37.44 L/daythe lab: 44.4
  8. Break-out: a = √(L² + H²) − √(L² − 4H²) = 15.16 m up the slopeCasagrande's construction for a slope this gentle; 4H² because the slope runs 2 across for 1 up
  9. Its height: 15.16 × 0.447 = 6.78 m0.447 is the sine of the 2:1 slope's angle, 1 ÷ √5

By hand, about 37 L/day per metre, 16% below the lab's 44.4, with the water breaking out about 6.8 m up the downstream slope against the lab's 8 m.

Check. The lab can also say where its water crosses the dam's centre line: 31.8 L/day inside the fill, 12.5 in the clay beneath. Darcy's pipe gets the clay's share almost exactly; Dupuit's slices come out low, because the hand sum keeps the fill's water and the clay's in separate pipes and the solver lets them trade. The Bureau of Reclamation's rule of thumb for a dam of one fill puts the break-out at roughly a third of the reservoir's depth (USBR (1987), sec. 6.3(c)): 20.4 ÷ 3 = 6.8 m. The lab resolves its face only to its 1 m cells.

What it means. A clay foundation half as permeable as the fill is far from watertight: more than a quarter of the water still goes under it. Under the cored dam of Example 9.1 it is most of the water: a cutoff beneath its core takes its leak on clay from 37.2 to 2.1 litres a day. Every hand method here gets the flow within a factor of two and the break-out within a couple of metres, enough to tell a sound design from a poor one. What the break-out does to the slope it softens is Chapter 12's question.

10.6 Five ways to manage seepage, and one to watch it

The chapter's question now has an answer. How much a dam leaks matters to whoever pays for the water, and to the neighbours of a tailings pond; on its own it seldom threatens the dam. A leak is safe when it leaves where the designer meant it to, through a drain and not out of a slope; when it leaves gently, at a gradient well below the one that floats grains, through a filter that holds them back; and when it leaves the downstream part of the dam at low water pressure, so that the grains there press on one another with their full weight. Engineers have six kinds of defence for it, drawn here at one scale on our dam:

Notice that only the first panel stops the water. The other five accept that it will arrive and manage the arrival. Lengthening the path is the oldest of them. Before flow nets were in everyday use, weirs on sandy riverbeds were sized by a rule of thumb: make the water's path along the underside of the structure long enough for the soil.The rule of thumb was W. G. Bligh's "line of creep": the head a structure could hold grew with the length of its contact with the soil. E. W. Lane, at the Bureau of Reclamation, proposed counting the level parts of that path at a third of the steep ones. A Bureau study of 1934, which checked the rules against pressures measured under real dams, recommended his weighting over Bligh's (Hebert (1934)), and Lane published it in 1935 (Lane (1935)). The lab's half-depth cutoff is a lesson in that rule's limits: it adds 15 m to a 102 m path, and the leak barely moves.

Watching is the defence that says whether the others work. Piezometers are the straws of Fig. 3.1 made permanent: a tube, or a pressure sensor, sealed at a point inside the dam or its foundation, reporting the head there. Read against the reservoir level for years, their trend shows whether the drains are clear and whether the pressure in the downstream slope is where the design put it. The leak itself is measured at weirs like the one this chapter began with.A 90° V-notch converts depth into flow. The Bureau of Reclamation's form of Cone's formula, Q = 2.49 h2.48 with Q in cubic feet a second and h in feet, becomes Q = 1.342 h2.48 in cubic metres a second and metres (USBR Water Measurement Manual, eq. 7-6). Because the flow grows faster than the depth's square, a weir reads small flows finely. Engineers judge the leak against the reservoir. A leak that rises and falls with the reservoir is the ground obeying Darcy's law. A leak that grows while the reservoir does not, or water that comes out cloudy, is a warning: turbidity means soil is moving, and even clear seepage is sampled, because it can carry fine soil the eye can't see.USACE EM 1110-2-1901, paras. 13-3 and 13-4.

The Prologue's dam had such a system: a pond below it caught what came through, and the first sign of trouble that night was the water in that pond rising. So it is fair to ask whether the leak brought it down, and the review panel asked. Piping and cracking, water opening a path through a dam and carrying soil out along it, is one of the commonest ways earth dams fail, and the panel found details that worried it. But apart from one brief spike in the flow, in April 2013, the records showed no abnormal seepage, and the panel found no evidence that piping or cracking caused the breach. Mount Polley's seepage was not what failed it.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), section 4.3.3, pp. 11–12; the pond that night, p. 10. What did fail it is the business of the last chapter.

What to remember

  • Every dam leaks. A leak is safe when the water leaves where the designer chose, gently and through a filter, and leaves the downstream slope at low water pressure, so its grains keep pressing on one another.
  • A flow net of squares turns Darcy's law into counting, q = k·H·Nf/Nd. Crowded squares mean a steep gradient; the smallest sit at exits and corners, where the water pushes hardest on the grains it leaves.
  • Head over path, times k, times depth, estimates the leak under our dam to within 10%, and Dupuit's slices estimate the leak through it. A hand estimate is an order-of-magnitude tool, because k is rarely known better than that.
  • A barrier works only if it reaches something tight. A core that stops on gravel can leak more than no core at all; joined to rock by a cutoff, it cuts the leak about 2,500 times.
  • A drain makes a dam leak more and stand safer: it takes the water pressure out of the downstream half, so the grains there grip with their full weight, and it lets the water out through a filter.

Questions

    A flow net sketched under a steel sheet-pile wall has 4 flow channels and 8 head drops. The water stands 6 m higher on one side of the wall than the other, and the sand passes 2 × 10⁻⁵ m/s. How much water passes under each metre of wall in a day? How much head is lost in each drop?

    Use Eq. 10.1; there are 86,400 seconds in a day.

    Suppose our dam on gravel, as the lab opens, were 400 m long, and all its leak were collected at one 90° V-notch weir. How many litres a second would reach the weir, and how deep would the water stand over the notch? For the weir use Q = 1.342 h2.48, with Q in m³/s and h in metres.

Free from the Bureau of Reclamation.

Switch the foundation to Clay and the water breaks out of our dam's downstream face 8 m up. The dam still stands. But where water leaves the ground it pushes on the grains it passes, and where it left our dam of one fill on gravel it pushed with a gradient of 0.79. What if it pushes hard enough to carry them away?
