11

Chapter 11 · Part III · Inside the embankment

When water carries soil

Bennett and Teton both leaked through their cores. Why does one of them still stand?

The Panel considers that too much was expected of the grout curtain, and that the design should have provided measures to render the inevitable leakage harmless.

Independent Panel to Review Cause of Teton Dam Failure, Report on Failure of Teton Dam, 1976

So far. Every dam leaks, and Chapter 10 followed the water through ours: where it gets in, which way it goes, where it comes out, and how drains and cutoffs decide all three. At the toe of our dam on sand and gravel, the water left the ground with a gradient of 0.79. This chapter asks what that water does to the grains it leaves behind.

After this chapter you can

  • explain a sand boil as the block of Chapter 4 floating, and judge an exit gradient against the margin engineers want;
  • name the four ways water carries soil out of a dam, place a real failure in one of them, and say why a pipe, once started, speeds up;
  • size a sand filter for a sand, and say why a clay core needs a different rule.

This chapter adds a filter and drain at the toe

7 figures · about 20 min to read · Film 11.1, 9 min

On the morning of Saturday, 5 June 1976, the reservoir behind Teton Dam in eastern Idaho was nearly full for the first time. The dam was new: an earth embankment 93 m high (305 ft above the riverbed) across a canyon of hard volcanic rock, finished the November before and filling since October. Two days earlier, springs of clear water had appeared in the rock of the canyon wall, about 400 m downstream. The engineer in charge took them for a good sign: the ground around the reservoir was filling up as it should.Teton Panel (1976): the dam, p. v and p. 1-1; the springs of 3 June, 1,300 and 1,500 ft downstream, p. 12-1, and the project engineer's testimony, p. 2-1.

Shortly after seven o'clock, the first people to arrive for work found muddy water running out of the rubble at the foot of the right abutment, where the dam met the canyon wall, at 20 to 30 cubic feet a second (0.57 to 0.85 m³ a second), and a trickle of cloudy water higher up the same junction. Both grew all morning. At about half past ten, with a loud burst, a large new leak broke out of the downstream face, from a tunnel about 1.8 m across, and the water began cutting a gully back up the face. At eleven a whirlpool opened in the reservoir, above the upstream slope. At 11:55 the crest began to fall in between the whirlpool and the head of the gully, and the reservoir went through. Eleven people died in the flood, by the count of the Bureau of Reclamation, which built the dam; the panel that investigated the failure associated fourteen deaths with it, directly or indirectly.The morning: Teton Panel (1976), p. 12-1, pieced together by the panel from sworn testimony and photographs (pp. 2-1 to 2-15). Eleven deaths: Stene (1996), p. 1. Fourteen: Teton Panel (1976), p. v and p. 1-1.

Teton leaked through its core. So, twenty years later, did the W.A.C. Bennett Dam on the Peace River in British Columbia, the dam whose zones opened Chapter 9. In June 1996 a hole opened in its crest, and the investigation that followed, reviewed by a panel of experts in 2012, found that seepage had carried part of its core away. Bennett is still holding back its reservoir. In both dams water found a way through the core and picked up soil on the way. The difference lay in where it could take that soil, and that difference is what this chapter is about.

11.1 Sand that floats

Start at the beach. Chapter 1 met the soft sand at the water's edge as loose sand that a wiggle shakes into soup. As the tide goes out there is a second reason for it. The water held in the beach seeps back out at the foot of the face, and where it flows upward through the sand it takes part of the grains' press away. Push it up harder and it takes all of it.

Chapter 4 put numbers on that. Water that loses i metres of head for every metre it travels drags on the grains in each cubic metre with i × 9.81 kN, in the direction it flows. A cubic metre of soaked sand presses down on the grains below it with its buoyant weight, about one water's worth. Turn the flow upward, raise the gradient, and the drag eats into that press until, at the critical gradient, the two cancel. The grains still touch, but they no longer press on one another, the effective stress is zero, and the sand has no grip at all. It is the block on the ramp of Fig. 4.1 with so much water under it that it floats. For a typical quartz sand, grains 2.65 times as heavy as water with 0.65 m³ of gap for every cubic metre of grain, Example 4.4 worked it out from the grains: (2.65 − 1) ÷ (1 + 0.65) = 1.00.

That is easy to see in a tube. Fill it with a metre of that sand, feed it water from below out of a tank, and let the water spill out of a spout at the top of the sand. Then raise the tank:

Notice that nothing about the sand changes from one tube to the next. The grains, the gaps and the water in them are the same; only the tank moves. In A the water stands still and the grains carry their whole weight under water. In B the water climbs through the sand, losing half a metre of head over its metre, and its drag takes half the grains' press. In C the drag matches the grains' weight, and the top of the bed lifts and churns. That is a sand boil, and it is what an engineer fears to find beyond the toe of a dam, where water that has passed under it rises out of the ground.

Check yourself A looser sand of the same grains has 0.8 m³ of gap for each cubic metre of grain. Does it boil at a lower or a higher gradient?

Lower. Its critical gradient is (2.65 − 1) ÷ (1 + 0.8) = 0.92: more of each cubic metre is water, so the grains weigh less under it and take less drag to float.

The gradient where seepage leaves the ground is the exit gradient, and engineers judge it against the critical gradient by a ratio, their margin against heave:

FSheave = ic / iexit (11.1)

ic critical gradient, about 1 for sand · iexit the upward gradient where seepage leaves the ground

A slope in Chapter 4 was judged at a factor of safety of 1.5. For an exit, the Bureau of Reclamation's design standard asks for at least 3 at an unfiltered exit of an existing dam, and 4 for a new dam or a repair, or about 2 to 2.5 where the soil and the water pressures are well measured.USBR DS-13 ch. 8, section 8.2.2.2, pp. 8-5 to 8-7, which also gives the warning about internal erosion quoted in the next paragraph. The margin is high because the number it divides by is shaky. Right at the toe the gradient has no settled value: the closer you look, the steeper it gets, so a computed exit gradient depends on how finely the ground was divided.Water flowing under a dam's base turns a sharp corner to come up beside the toe, and in the mathematics of a flow net the gradient at such a corner grows without limit. A grid of cells smooths the corner over one cell, so its answer depends on the cell's size. The seepage lab reads its exit gradient over the last half metre of ground. Natural ground is never as even as a model of it, and a lens of fine sand can sit where the model has gravel. And in fine sand under a roof, grains can be carried along at far gentler gradients than the one that floats them, as the next section shows.

The standard also says what the ratio does not measure: it flags sand boils, not every kind of internal erosion. Its own words are that it "is not a factor of safety against the initiation of internal erosion". A dam can boil without failing, and fail with no boil at all, as Teton did. For now, here is the ratio at work on our dam:

Example 11.1

The margin at our dam's toe

Given
Our dam of one fill on sand and gravel, as the seepage lab of Fig. 10.3 opens: reservoir 20.4 m deep, no drain, no cutoff. The lab's largest exit gradient is 0.786, in the ground right beyond the toe, and it takes ic = 1.0, a round value for sand.
Find
The margin against heave at the toe; the exit gradient a new dam would need; what a cutoff halfway down the gravel does.
The idea
Divide the critical gradient by the exit gradient (Eq. 11.1), and turn the target margin round to find the gradient it allows.
  1. FS = 1.0 ÷ 0.786 = 1.27the margin as the lab opens; its readout says the same
  2. For a margin of 3: iexit ≤ 1.0 ÷ 3 = 0.33the most an existing dam's exit may have
  3. For a margin of 4: iexit ≤ 1.0 ÷ 4 = 0.25the most a new dam's exit may have
  4. 0.786 ÷ 0.25 = 3.1how many times gentler the exit would have to become
  5. Half-depth cutoff: FS = 1.0 ÷ 0.682 = 1.47the lab's exit gradient with the wall in place

The toe has a margin of 1.27 against heave. A new dam would need its exit gradient cut about 3.1 times, to 0.25; a cutoff halfway down the gravel takes the margin only to 1.47.

Check. The margin times the exit gradient should give back the critical gradient: 1.27 × 0.786 = 1.0. And the answer sits where Fig. 11.1 says it should: an exit gradient of 0.79 leaves the grains at the toe about a fifth of their press, 21%, against the half that tube B keeps.

What it means. The sand at our toe is not boiling, but its margin is a third of what a designer would accept. Stopping the water is hard: the wall halfway down barely helped, because the water goes under it. The defences of Fig. 10.4 offer another way, at the exit itself, and the rest of this chapter comes to it.

11.2 A pipe that feeds itself

A boil is a warning, and grains are only part of what it carries. Each grain that comes up with the water leaves a hole the size of a grain behind it. The question is what that hole does next. Make a guess before you read on:

Water rising beyond the toe of a dam on sand has started to carry grains out, and a small hollow has opened under the edge of the dam. As the hollow works its way back under the dam, does it get easier or harder for the water to carry more sand away?

Easier. The water in an open hollow flows almost freely and loses almost none of its head there, so all the head between the reservoir and the toe has to be lost in the sand still ahead of the hollow. The longer the hollow, the shorter that stretch of sand, the steeper the gradient across it, and the harder the water pulls grains from its tip. The hollow becomes a pipe that feeds itself, and nothing in the sand slows it down.

To decide, count the head the water has to lose, and the distance it has to lose it over. Under the intact dam the water loses its whole head along the full path from the reservoir floor to the toe. What happens next depends on what holds the hollow open. The dam above it holds up its roof, so it stays open; water in it moves freely, and the hollow can grow back toward the reservoir, against the flow. Engineers call this backward erosion piping: it starts at the exit and travels upstream. The figure plays it from the first boil to the breach:

Notice which way the pipe grows. The water flows from the reservoir to the toe, and the pipe grows from the toe to the reservoir. It does its damage out of sight, under the dam, and the only sign above ground is at the exit: a boil, a cone of sand round a spring, water that runs cloudy. By the time the pipe reaches the reservoir, the water has a tunnel straight through, and the tunnel widens until its roof falls in. The arithmetic of a pipe that feeds itself is short:

Example 11.2

A head budget for a growing pipe

Given
Our dam on sand and gravel: 20.4 m of head between the reservoir and the toe, spent along a path 102 m long under the dam's base. The lab's exit gradient at the toe, 0.786. An open pipe that loses no head along its length (illustrative: a real pipe loses a little).
Find
The average gradient on the path the water has left to cross, before the pipe and as it grows; and roughly what the water does at the pipe's tip.
The idea
The head is fixed by the reservoir. Whatever length of sand is left has to lose all of it (gradient = head lost ÷ distance, as in Chapter 3).
  1. i = 20.4 ÷ 102 = 0.20the average gradient under the intact dam
  2. 0.786 ÷ 0.20 = 3.9how much steeper the water runs where its paths crowd together at the exit
  3. Pipe 50 m back: 20.4 ÷ 52 = 0.39the same head over the sand that is left
  4. At its tip: 0.39 × 3.9 = 1.5if the water crowds into the tip as it crowded into the toe: past the critical gradient
  5. Pipe 90 m back: 20.4 ÷ 12 = 1.7now even the average floats the sand

Halfway under the dam the average gradient has doubled, to 0.39, and the push at the pipe's tip is past the critical gradient. With 12 m of sand left, the average alone is 1.7.

Check. The average gradient reaches 1 when the sand left is as long as the head is high, 20.4 m: a pipe 81.6 m back, four fifths of the way under. Roughly halving the path roughly doubles the gradient, as step 3 found.

What it means. These numbers sketch a head budget and leave out how fast sand erodes, but the direction is certain: every grain that leaves makes it easier for the next one to leave. A pipe that has started will not stop by itself. The place to stop it is the exit, before it starts.

Check yourself A pipe has eaten 70 m back under our dam. What average gradient is the water spending on the sand that is left?

20.4 ÷ 32 = 0.64, more than three times the 0.20 under the intact dam.

How fast this happens depends on the sand. Fine, uniform sand pipes most easily: in laboratory tests on fine sands under a roof, grains began to move at average gradients as low as 0.08.Schmertmann's tests, and a gradient of about 0.08 back-calculated from piping at A. V. Watkins Dam: FEMA (2011), pp. 109–110. A well-graded sand, with a spread of sizes, resists, because its larger grains hold the smaller ones back. The figure's scale note says hours to decades, and both ends are real.Teton went from the first muddy water to the breach in about five hours. At the other end, the panel that reviewed Bennett Dam notes that a sinkhole forming over erosion deep in a dam is often slow, and may take years to show at the crest (BC Hydro expert panel (2012), p. 62).

11.3 Four ways water carries soil

A boil at the toe is one way in. Teton showed nothing at its toe until its last morning; its trouble started deep inside, in the core. Engineers now sort the ways that erosion inside a dam can begin into four. The International Commission on Large Dams names them, and the panel that reviewed Bennett used the same four: concentrated leak, backward erosion, suffusion and contact erosion.ICOLD Bulletin 164; the four, with their definitions, in the terminology of BC Hydro expert panel (2012), pp. 60–62. Here they are, each drawn on our dam at one scale:

Notice that only one of the four needs an exit at the ground surface. A concentrated leak (A) is water running through an opening that is already there: a crack, a gap beside a pipe through the dam, a loose layer, or open joints in the rock under a core. Its walls are scoured from the inside, and the opening widens. Backward erosion (B) is the pipe of the last section. Suffusion (C) happens in a soil whose grain sizes have a gap, coarse grains and fine ones with few in between: the coarse grains carry the load, the fine ones sit loose in their gaps, and seepage can wash the fine ones out and leave the skeleton standing. Contact erosion (D) happens where a fine soil lies against a coarse one and water runs along the boundary, as in a dam built on a layer of silt over open gravel.

A concentrated leak needs a crack, and a core is compacted precisely so that it has none. But a crack can open after the core is built. A core that settles more over a deep part of the valley than over a shallow one stretches, and the stretched part can crack. And water can open one by itself. Where something holds part of the core up, as the steep walls of a narrow trench can, the soil below is pressed together less than its depth would suggest. Teton's core was carried down into the rock of its abutments in such a trench, a key trench. If the water pressure in the soil rises above the least of those presses, the water can split the soil apart, the way a wedge splits wood. That is hydraulic fracture, and the panels that investigated both Teton and Bennett found it a likely way their cores first opened.

All four end the same way if nothing stops them: soil carried out of the dam, and a channel that grows. The statistics count them together, under an older name. Engineers often call every kind of internal erosion piping, though strictly the word means the backward erosion of the last section. Foster, Fell and Spannagle's 2000 study of 124 embankment-dam failures up to 1986 counted every kind as piping, through the embankment, through the foundation, or from one into the other.Foster, Fell & Spannagle (2000), their table 3: failures to 1986, excluding failures during construction. Internal erosion of all kinds caused about as many failures as overtopping: 47% against 48% once spillway and gate failures are counted with overtopping. That is more than overtopping alone (34%). Some failures had more than one cause, so the shares add up to a little over 100%. Water pouring over the top of a dam is the other half of the story, the one Chapter 6 told. The rest of this chapter is about the half that starts inside.Most clays resist erosion far better than sand, because their tiny flakes cling together: in laboratory tests a sand moves at an upward gradient of about 1, a clay often not until tens or hundreds (USBR DS-13 ch. 8, p. 8-6). A few clays come apart into separate flakes in fresh water instead (FEMA (2011), p. 78), and such a dispersive clay loses that defence. The pinhole test finds them: water is forced through a fine hole punched through a sample, and a dispersive clay turns it cloudy (Sherard et al. (1976)).

11.4 Why a filter works

The first cure anyone reaches for is to stop the water. Example 11.1 showed how hard that is under our dam, and Teton's designers tried it with a grout curtain, cement grout pumped into the joints of the rock under the core. Karl Terzaghi had proposed the opposite half a century earlier: let the water out, and keep the soil in.Teaching in Istanbul in the early 1920s, Terzaghi showed in simple laboratory tests that a layer of coarser sand with weight on top of it stops a fine sand from boiling, and patented the idea. He wrote about piping under dams and how to prevent it in 1922 (Terzaghi (1922)). The grain-size rules grew out of his consulting on small weirs in Europe; Fannin (2008) traces the story. A layer of the right sand where the water leaves the soil passes the water and holds the grains. A filter stops soil, not water.

How can anything let water through and not sand? The figure shows it at the scale of grains: on the left the grains of a core meet rockfill, on the right a filter of sand:

Notice that the filter does not need gaps smaller than every grain of the core. It needs gaps smaller than the core's coarsest grains. Those lodge in the filter's face, their own gaps are smaller still and catch the next size down, and so on: the soil builds its own filter against the real one, and the water goes on through.Three equal balls touching leave a gap through which a ball only 0.155 of their diameter can pass, about a sixth. A real filter has grains of many sizes, the small ones sit in the gaps of the large, and laboratory tests by Sherard and his colleagues found it acts like a sieve whose openings are about 0.11 times its 15% size (FEMA (2011), pp. 275–276). A filter that does this is designed by grain size, and grain size is read off a curve.

Pour a soil through a stack of sieves, finest at the bottom, and weigh what each sieve holds. The grain-size curve plots, for each size, the share of the soil by weight that is finer. Engineers then name the soil by points on that curve: D15 is the size that 15% of the soil is finer than, D85 the size that 85% is finer than. D85 stands for the coarse grains that have to stop at the filter's face; D15, for the fine grains that decide how easily water passes. Here are a fine sand and a filter for it:

Notice that the filter's curve lies almost wholly to the right of the sand's: nearly all its grains are coarser than nearly all of the sand. That looks as if the sand could slip through, and it would, if the filter's openings were as wide as its grains. They are about a ninth of its D15. Terzaghi's two rules put the filter in its band:

D15F ≤ 4 · D85B and D15F ≥ 4 · D15B (11.2)

D15F the filter's 15% size · D85B, D15B the base soil's 85% and 15% sizes (mm); the base is the soil the filter protects

The first rule keeps the soil in. A filter whose D15 is at most four times the sand's D85 has openings at most 0.11 × 4 = 0.44 of the sand's D85, so at least the coarsest 15% of the sand cannot get in, and the layer those grains build holds back the rest. The second rule lets the water out. Water passes a sand roughly in proportion to the square of its fine grains' size (its D15), so a filter whose fine grains are several times coarser passes water many times more easily, and the water leaves the soil without building up pressure in the filter. The agencies that design dams use these rules for sands and gravels, with 4 in the first and 3 to 5 in the second.FEMA (2011), table 5-2 (p. 84) for the retention rule by soil category; p. 84 for the permeability rule as the Bureau of Reclamation, the Corps of Engineers and the Natural Resources Conservation Service each write it; p. 88 for the square of D15.

Example 11.3

A filter for a fine sand

Given
The sand of Fig. 11.5 (illustrative): D15 = 0.20 mm, D85 = 0.45 mm. A graded filter's openings are about 0.11 of its D15.
Find
The range of D15 a filter may have; how its openings compare with the sand's coarse grains; how much more easily it passes water.
The idea
Apply both rules of Eq. 11.2, choose inside the band, then check the openings against the grains they must stop.
  1. Largest D15F: 4 × 0.45 = 1.8 mmkeep the soil in
  2. Smallest D15F: 4 × 0.20 = 0.8 mmlet the water out
  3. Choose D15F = 1.2 mminside the band, clear of both ends, since no pit delivers a curve exactly
  4. Openings: 0.11 × 1.2 = 0.13 mmthe smallest particle the filter stops
  5. 0.13 ÷ 0.45 = 0.29openings against the sand's coarse grains
  6. 1.2 ÷ 0.20 = 6the filter's fine grains against the sand's
  7. 6 × 6 = 36water passes a sand roughly as the square of its fine grains' size

Any filter with D15 between 0.8 and 1.8 mm will do. One at 1.2 mm has openings under a third of the sand's coarse grains and passes water about 36 times as easily as the sand.

Check. Even at the coarse end of the band the openings are 0.11 × 1.8 = 0.20 mm, under half the sand's 0.45 mm: the rule keeps a margin. And the band is 1.8 ÷ 0.8 = 2.25 times wide, which is the sand's own D85 over its D15: a sand with a wider spread of sizes leaves a wider choice, and a uniform sand a narrow one.

What it means. A filter works by grain size alone. Nothing in it is tight, and water passes it more easily than the soil it protects; it holds the grains because its coarse grains bridge the gaps and the soil's own coarse grains bridge the rest. Where water leaves a soil through such a layer, the grains at the exit keep pressing on one another.

Check yourself Would rockfill with a D15 of 30 mm hold the sand of Example 11.3?

No. Its openings are about 0.11 × 30 = 3.3 mm, 7.3 times the sand's coarse grains, so the sand washes straight in: the left-hand panel of Fig. 11.4. A dam steps the size up through a sand filter and a coarser transition before the rockfill.

A clay core needs a different rule. Its D85 may be a few hundredths of a millimetre, and four times that would ask for a filter of very fine sand or silt, which would drain poorly. But clay does not wash out grain by grain from a sound core; it erodes from the walls of a crack, and what the filter must do is catch what comes out of the crack and seal it. James Sherard and Lorn Dunnigan tested filters in the laboratory against many core soils with a leak forced through them, in the 1980s, and found that ordinary filters of clean sand reliably stop erosion from concentrated leaks in fine silts and clays, while broadly graded glacial soils need a relatively fine one.Sherard & Dunnigan (1989); the rules as the agencies now write them in FEMA (2011), table 5-2, p. 84, and the cake on the filter's face, pp. 275–276. The rules the agencies use today come from that work, sorted by how much of the core is finer than 0.075 mm: for a core more than 85% that fine, the filter's D15 may be up to nine times the core's D85; for one 40 to 85% that fine, it must be no more than 0.7 mm whatever the core. The eroded clay builds a thin cake on the face of such a filter, finer as it builds, and the crack stops leaking soil.

11.5 Two cores, two endings

Now Teton and Bennett can be set side by side. Here is Teton's core where it failed, on the right abutment, drawn to scale from the review panel's own section:

Notice how little stands between the core and the rock. The silt of Zone 1 lies straight against the walls and floor of the trench, and the rock there is full of open joints, gaps wide enough to take silt. The panel called this choice of material a major factor in the failure: wind-deposited silt, it found, is highly erodible, and putting it against heavily jointed rock gave the water both something to carry and somewhere to carry it.Teton Panel (1976), pp. viii–ix, conclusions 3, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 13. Its closing judgment is the epigraph of this chapter: too much was expected of the grout curtain, and the design should have made the inevitable leakage harmless. A filter between the silt and the rock would have done that.

Here is Bennett, at its highest, drawn to scale from the dimensions its designers published:

Notice the transition, the zone Chapter 9 asked you to keep an eye on. It is many times wider than the filter and sits right against the core. The panel that reviewed Bennett in 2012 concluded that the settling of loosely packed core around the casing, as it got wet, could not by itself explain how far the first sinkhole had sunk: some of the core must have been carried away. The likeliest route was concentrated leaks through cracks opened by hydraulic fracture, where the casing and the nearby canyon wall left the core weakly pressed. The eroded core went into the transition, and the erosion probably went on only for a short time before the transition stopped it. The panel judged the transition, filter and drain together a good filter system, one that might let a little core erode at their boundary but would prevent ongoing erosion.BC Hydro expert panel (2012), pp. 35–37 (the two mechanisms and the cracks), 47 (the sinkholes) and 48 (the filter system). The holes were filled by compaction grouting, and the dam went on working.

That answers this chapter's question. Teton and Bennett both leaked through their cores, and in both the water carried core soil with it. At Teton the soil went into open joints in the rock, nothing stopped it, and in five hours the tunnel had taken the dam. At Bennett the soil went into a transition graded to hold it, and the leak sealed itself against the transition's grains. The water at Bennett went on through, as water in every dam does; the soil stopped, and the grains of the core went on pressing on one another.

The film The sand that boils retells the chapter, from the tube of sand to Bennett:

What to remember

  • Water rising through sand drags its grains upward. At the critical gradient, about 1, the drag matches the grains' weight under water, they stop pressing on one another, and the sand boils. Designers want an unfiltered exit at a third or a quarter of that.
  • Grains washed out at an exit leave a hollow that works back toward the reservoir, and every metre it gains shortens the path and steepens the push at its tip: a pipe feeds itself.
  • Water starts carrying soil out of a dam in four ways: a concentrated leak through a crack, backward erosion from an exit, suffusion of fine grains through coarse ones, and contact erosion along a boundary between soils.
  • A filter stops soil, not water. Its 15% size is at most four times the protected soil's 85% size, so the coarsest grains lodge at its face and hold back the rest, and at least about four times the soil's 15% size, so water leaves freely. Clay cores need the finer, tested rules of Sherard and Dunnigan.
  • Teton's leak met open rock and Bennett's met a transition. In both the water went on through; only at Bennett did the soil stay, and the grains of the core keep pressing on one another.

Questions

Teton and Bennett were stories of water that moved too hard through the soil and tried to take it along. A dam can lose its grip without losing a grain. With all that water inside it, carrying part of the load its grains would otherwise carry between them, will its slope stand?

Chapter 12 · Part IV · Will it stand?

Will the slope stand?

This dam is standing, with water breaking out of its face. How close is it to sliding?

So far. Chapter 4 gave a block on a ramp a score, the factor of safety, and showed that water seeping out of a sand face roughly halves the steepest slope it can hold, measured as rise over run. Chapter 10 followed the water through our dam, and Chapter 11 what it does where it comes out. One question is left to ask of any dam with water inside it: will its slope stand, and by how much?

After this chapter you can

  • work out the factor of safety of a long, straight slope, dry and with water seeping out of it;
  • work one slice of Bishop's method by hand, say why the method has to go round in a loop, and add up a whole slip circle;
  • explain why emptying a reservoir quickly can bring down its upstream slope, and say what a factor of safety of 1.5 does and does not promise.

This chapter adds a slip circle through the downstream slope

3 figures · about 25 min to read · Film 12.1, 6 min 4 s

An earth dam rarely announces that it is in trouble. The first sign is often a strip of its downstream face that stays green through a dry summer, or a band of dark, soft ground a few metres up the slope where water seeps out into the light. Walk our dam, the 24 m embankment of the last three chapters, built all of one compacted soil on clay ground, and you would find that band 8 m up its downstream face, exactly where the seepage lab of Chapter 10 said the water would come out. Nothing is moving, and the crest road is level.

The engineer who checks the slope gets a single number back, a factor of safety of 1.12. Above 1 the slope stands, so this one stands, with 12% to spare. The owner has money for one fix. Make a choice before you read on:

A dam made all of compacted fill has a factor of safety of 1.12, with water breaking out 8 m up its downstream slope. Which change helps it most?

The drain does the most: the factor of safety goes from 1.12 to about 1.6. The flatter slope reaches only about 1.27, and the cutoff about 1.14. The fill is strong enough when it is dry. Its trouble is the water in it: on the critical slip surface, water pressure carries about a third of the soil's weight (0.35 of it), so the grains press together with only two-thirds of it. A drain lets that water out before it reaches the downstream slope. You'll paint that drain yourself in Chapter 13.

Whatever you chose, the choice rests on a number, and a number is only worth what you know about how it was made. To judge the fixes we need to make that number ourselves, starting where Chapter 4 left off: with a slope so long and even that one small piece of it stands for the whole.

12.1 The long slope, scored

Chapter 4 found the steepest face a sand can hold by treating one patch of the face as the block on its ramp. A designer doesn't build at the steepest face; she builds flatter and asks how much flatter. So ask the same patch a different question: how much grip does it have, against how much it needs? That ratio is the factor of safety, and for a long, even slope of grains with no glue between them, the slope Chapter 4 called an infinite slope, it takes one line.

On a dry slope at angle β, a slab of soil parallel to the face presses into the slope below it with its weight times cos β, and is pulled down it by its weight times sin β. Friction offers tan φ′ times the press. The weight cancels, as it did for the block:

FS = tan φ′ ÷ tan β(12.1)

φ′ the soil's friction angle · β the slope's angle; a slope of n:1 has tan β = 1/n, so FS = n · tan φ′. It holds dry, and it holds under still water, where buoyancy lightens the press and the pull alike.

The formula hides a pleasant fact: the factor of safety grows in proportion to how flat the slope is. Make a 2:1 slope into a 3:1 slope and its safety rises by half. But the water has its own say. Where water seeps out of the face, parallel to it, its drag adds to the pull and nothing to the press, and Example 4.5 showed what that costs: the grip falls in the ratio of the soil's weight in water, its buoyant unit weight γ′, to its soaked weight γsat:

FS = (γ′ ÷ γsat) · tan φ′ ÷ tan β(12.2)

γ′ = γsat − γw, the soaked weight less the water's, 9.81 kN/m³. For most soils γ′/γsat is close to one half.

Here are both rules drawn for two materials of the workbench in Chapter 13, the tailings sand and the rockfill, with two results from the full slope check marked beside them:

Notice that the seeping line is the dry line pressed down to half its height, everywhere: γ′/γsat does not depend on the slope. Notice too the two rings. The workbench knows nothing about long slopes. It searches thousands of curved surfaces through a whole section, with the water pressures its seepage solver computes, and for these two dams it lands within about 1% of a one-line formula. The example says why:

Example 12.1

A tailings-sand slope, dry and seeping

Given
The workbench's tailings sand: φ′ = 33°, no cohesion, soaked γsat = 19.5 kN/m³; rockfill φ′ = 42°; water 9.81 kN/m³. Both slopes at 2:1, so tan β = 0.5.
Find
The factor of safety of a long slope of tailings sand, dry and with water seeping out parallel to its face, and of a long dry slope of rockfill.
The idea
One slab parallel to the face stands for the whole slope (Eq. 12.1); seeping water adds a pull and no press (Eq. 12.2).
  1. Dry sand: tan 33° ÷ 0.5 = 0.6494 ÷ 0.5 = 1.299grip over pull for one slab; the weight cancels
  2. γ′ = 19.5 − 9.81 = 9.69 kN/m³the sand's weight in water
  3. 9.69 ÷ 19.5 = 0.4969the share of the pull that comes with a press
  4. Seeping sand: 1.299 × 0.4969 = 0.645the drag of the leaving water adds pull and no press
  5. Dry rockfill: tan 42° ÷ 0.5 = 0.9004 ÷ 0.5 = 1.801rougher, more angular grains, the same rule

Dry, a 2:1 slope of tailings sand scores 1.30; with water seeping out of it, 0.645, and it slides. Dry rockfill at 2:1 scores 1.80.

Check. The workbench's whole dam of tailings sand on clay scores 0.637, and its worst surface is a skin 2.0 m deep, the shallowest the check counts: nearly a slab parallel to the face, the very thing the formula assumes. Its rockfill dam, right after its reservoir has been emptied, scores 1.814 on a skin 2.0 m deep. The ratio of the two sand answers, 0.645 ÷ 1.299 = 0.497, is γ′/γsat and nothing else.

What it means. Water seeping out of a face halves its safety. A slope that grips well enough dry can slide with water coming out of it, without a grain changing; only the water moved.

Check yourself A long dry rockfill slope is built at 1.5:1, steeper than our dam's. What is its factor of safety?

1.5 × tan 42° = 1.5 × 0.9004 = 1.351: it stands, with a third to spare, as long as it stays dry. Rockfill dams are often built that steep.

12.2 Slopes slide on curves

One could assume that every slope fails the way the long-slope rule pictures it, a thin skin peeling off its face like snow off a roof. Clean sand and rockfill do fail that way, which is why the rule and the solver agreed. Our dam's fill does not. It has a little cohesion, c′ = 10 kPa, a grip that doesn't depend on how hard its grains are pressed, and a thin skin has too little weight for its friction to matter and plenty of cohesion for its size. A deep slip is the cheaper failure: it has more weight pulling, through soil that is wetter and so presses less.

The shape engineers give a deep slip comes from Sweden. In March 1916, a year after it was built, the Stigberg Quay in Gothenburg harbour slid, and a committee was set up to find out why.Petterson told the story himself in English, nearly forty years later (Petterson (1955)). Wolmar Fellenius, who chaired Sweden's state geotechnical commission, extended the method to soils with both friction and cohesion in the 1920s and defined the factor of safety for a slope as the ratio of the moments holding it to those turning it (Massarsch & Fellenius (2012)). The commission's final report of 1922 is the first publication known to use the word "geotechnical". The committee's analysis used a method worked out by Knut Petterson, an engineer with the harbour, and Sven Hultin, a professor at Chalmers: take the surface the ground slides on to be an arc of a circle. A circle has a convenient property: a mass sliding on one turns about the circle's centre as a solid piece, so its balance can be checked with one sum of turning effects. The Swedish engineers cut the sliding mass into upright slices and added them up. Most checks of an embankment slope still start there.

Look at one slice and you have met it before. It is Chapter 4's block on a ramp, except that its ramp is a short stretch of the circle, tilted at an angle α that changes from slice to slice: steep under the crest, nearly level near the bottom of the circle, tilted the other way where the circle climbs back out beyond the toe. Each slice's weight W pulls it down its stretch with W sin α; the soil under it grips back with cohesion over the length of the base, l, plus friction from the grains' press on it, N′. This is the method of slices. The slip surface's factor of safety is the grip of all the slices over the pull of all of them:

FS = Σ (c′·l + N′·tan φ′) ÷ Σ W·sin α(12.3)

Σ the sum over every slice · c′·l + N′·tan φ′ the grip on a slice's base (kN per metre of dam) · W·sin α its pull. The ratio comes from balancing turning effects about the circle's centre: each slice's weight acts at a lever arm of R sin α from it, each grip at R, the presses on the bases point at the centre and turn nothing, and the radius cancels.

The pull is easy: weights and angles, measured off the drawing. All the difficulty is in N′, how hard the grains on each base press, and that is where the water comes in.

12.3 One slice by hand

The water in the gaps pushes on the base of a slice with its pressure u over the base's length, u·l, and whatever part of the slice's load the water carries, the grains don't. The earliest method of slices took the press on the base to be the part of the weight at right angles to it, less the water: N′ = W cos α − u·l. That treats each slice as if its neighbours weren't there. But they are, and they push on it.

Alan Bishop's step, published in 1955, was to let them push, but only sideways, and to balance each slice up and down.Bishop, at Imperial College London, published the method in Bishop (1955). Taking the slices' pushes on each other as horizontal is why it is called his "simplified" method; his paper also gave a fuller version that keeps their upright parts, which matter little on a circle. E. Spencer's method of 1967 (Spencer (1967)) balances the forces and the turning effects together, taking the pushes as parallel, and works on surfaces of any shape. Sideways pushes have no upright part, so they drop out of that balance. What holds the slice up is then the water and the grains pressing on its base, both at right angles to it, and the grip along the base, which at the point of balance is the grip available divided by the factor of safety. Solve that balance for N′ and you get Bishop's method:

N′ = (W − u·b − c′·b·tan α ÷ FS) ÷ mα,  mα = cos α + sin α · tan φ′ ÷ FS(12.4)

b the slice's width (m) · u·b the upright part of the water's push on the base · c′·b·tan α ÷ FS the upright part of the cohesion's share of the grip · mα the factor that turns what is left into a press at right angles to the base.

Look where FS is: on the right-hand side. To know how hard each slice presses, you must already know the factor of safety, and to know the factor of safety you must know how hard every slice presses. The way out is to guess, work every slice with the guess, add them up with Eq. 12.3, and use the answer as the next guess. Here is the critical circle of our dam, the worst of the 2,000 or so the workbench tried, with one of its slices drawn large:

Notice that the circle goes deep: about 12 m below the face, far below any skin, and out 6 m beyond the toe. Notice also that most of it runs below the dashed line, in soaked fill. Now take slice 13, the thirteenth from the top, and work it the way the solver does, with the factor of safety the loop ends on:

Example 12.2

Slice 13 of 40, by hand

Given
From the solver, per metre length of dam: width b = 1.359 m, weight W = 319.0 kN, water pressure on its base u = 76.40 kPa, base tilted at α = 31.94° (sin 0.5291, cos 0.8486, tan 0.6235). The fill: c′ = 10 kPa, φ′ = 32°, tan φ′ = 0.6249. The loop's answer, FS = 1.116.
Find
The grains' press on the base, N′; the grip on the base; the pull along it.
The idea
Balance the slice up and down (Eq. 12.4), then grip = cohesion along the base plus friction from the press (Eq. 12.3).
  1. u·b = 76.40 × 1.359 = 103.8 kNthe water's push up on the base
  2. W − u·b = 319.0 − 103.8 = 215.2 kNthe weight the water leaves for the grains
  3. c′·b·tan α ÷ FS = 10 × 1.359 × 0.6235 ÷ 1.116 = 7.59 kNthe cohesion along the tilted base also holds the slice up a little
  4. mα = 0.8486 + 0.5291 × 0.6249 ÷ 1.116 = 1.1449the factor that turns an upright load into a press at right angles to the base
  5. N′ = (215.2 − 7.59) ÷ 1.1449 = 207.6 ÷ 1.1449 = 181.3 kNthe grains' press on the base, Eq. 12.4
  6. l = 1.359 ÷ 0.8486 = 1.601 mthe tilted base is longer than the slice is wide
  7. Grip: 10 × 1.601 + 181.3 × 0.6249 = 129.3 kNcohesion over the base's length, plus friction from the press
  8. Pull: 319.0 × 0.5291 = 168.8 kNthe part of the weight along the base, W sin α

The grains press on slice 13's base with 181.3 kN, giving a grip of 129.3 kN against a pull of 168.8 kN.

Check. The water carries 103.8 of the slice's 319.0 kN, about a third, close to the share it carries on the whole circle (0.35). The solver, which carries every digit, gets 181.38 and 129.35 kN: the rounding on this page costs less than a tenth of a kilonewton.

What it means. On its own, slice 13 would slide: its grip is 0.77 of its pull. A slip circle stands or falls as a whole, and a third of this slice's weight is carried by water, not grains.

then press Test in the workbench

Do the same for all forty slices and add up. The grips come to 3,473.6 kN and the pulls to 3,111.8 kN, and 3,473.6 ÷ 3,111.8 = 1.1163, the readout's 1.12. The sum gives back the factor of safety the slices were worked with, which is how you know the loop has finished. Start it where the solver does, at 1.5, and the forty slices return 1.181; feed that back and they return 1.129, then 1.119, 1.117 and 1.116, and after that the third decimal stops moving.

The slices that save slice 13 are the ones near the bottom of the circle. Where the circle climbs back up toward the toe, a slice's base tilts the other way, and its weight pushes back against the slide instead of driving it; 11 of the forty are like that. Their grip counts in full, and their pull is negative: it takes away from the total. The older method that ignored the neighbours scores this same circle at 0.978: it says the dam should already have slid. It errs on the safe side, by a lot when the water pressure is high, and that is what Bishop's sideways pushes fixed.

Check yourself If you started Bishop's loop at a guess of 1.0 instead of 1.5, would it end somewhere else?

No. The guess only sets the starting point; the loop keeps going until the slices return the number they were worked with, and only one number does that, 1.116. From 1.0 it climbs to it instead of falling.

12.4 What the water costs

Slice 13 lost about a third of its weight to the water. So did the whole circle, and that is the number that explains the fixes. Bishop and Morgenstern, writing in 1960, put a slope's water into a single ratio, the pore-pressure ratio ru, the share of the soil's weight that the water pressure carries.In Bishop & Morgenstern (1960) ru is the pore pressure at a point divided by the weight of soil above it, and the paper's charts give a slope's factor of safety as a straight line falling with ru. The workbench reports one value for a whole surface, the slices' Σ u·b ÷ Σ W. The paper's second author, Norbert Morgenstern, is the engineer the Prologue met at the head of a review panel. Work it out for our circle and then take the water away:

Example 12.3

The same circle without its water, and the three fixes

Given
The critical circle of Fig. 12.2, FS = 1.116; its slices weigh 8,375.9 kN in all, and the water pushes up on their bases with Σ u·b = 2,955.1 kN. The dam is 1,296 cells of 1 m² in section. The workbench's results for each fix.
Find
How much of the weight the water carries, what the circle would score without it, and what each fix buys for what it costs.
The idea
A fix works by adding grip, adding weight where it resists, or taking the water away. Compare them on one scale.
  1. ru = 2,955.1 ÷ 8,375.9 = 0.3528the share of the weight the water carries
  2. With u = 0 on the same circle: FS = 1.741the same slices, weights and angles, the water pressure set to zero
  3. 1.741 ÷ 1.116 = 1.560the water costs the circle more than a third of its score
  4. Flatter, 2.5:1: 1,440 ÷ 1,296 = 1.111; FS = 1.27311.1% more fill
  5. Flatter, 3:1: 1,596 ÷ 1,296 = 1.231; FS = 1.41823.1% more fill, still short of 1.5
  6. Cutoff wall under the dam: FS = 1.142the leak falls from 44.4 to 40.4 L/day per metre
  7. Drain: 126 ÷ 1,296 = 0.097; FS = 1.628filter sand in place of 9.7% of the fill, no soil added

The water carries 0.35 of the circle's weight. Without it, the same circle would score 1.74. The drain reaches 1.63 without adding any soil; the flatter slopes reach 1.27 and 1.42 for 11% and 23% more fill; the cutoff barely moves it.

Check. Why does flattening help so little? The water still breaks out 8 m up the face at 3:1, as at 2:1, and the share of weight it carries on the critical circle grows, to 0.380 at 2.5:1 and 0.412 at 3:1: the extra fill sits in the wet part of the slope. The US Bureau of Reclamation's design manual says it plainly: in a dam of one soil, seepage will reach the downstream slope "regardless of its flatness".USBR (1987), p. 190, on the homogeneous section, which it says has been replaced in practice by one with "small amounts of carefully placed pervious materials" to control the seepage.

What it means. The fill was strong enough all along; its water was taking the grip. A fix that removes the water does more than one that adds soil, and the cutoff, which stops a little water going under the dam, leaves the water in the dam where it was.

then press Test in the workbench

Notice what the drain does to the leak: the drained dam lets through 109.7 L/day per metre, 2.47 times as much as without it. It is safer because it leaks more, through a path the engineer chose, the trade Example 10.4 found for piping. A slope feels the water's pressure; how much water passes never enters its sum.

12.5 Emptying the reservoir

So far the reservoir has been full and the danger on the downstream side, where the water comes out. The upstream face lives the other way round. A full reservoir is good for it: Example 2.5 showed that water standing on a sloping face presses it down harder than it pushes it across, and under still water the grains of the upstream shell lose their press and their pull in the same proportion. The danger comes when the reservoir is let down fast, to reach a damaged outlet, to take the load off a dam in trouble, or because the water is needed downstream.

Emptying a reservoir takes days or weeks. Draining the water out of compacted fill takes far longer: at 10⁻⁷ m/s, the fill passes water a hundred times more slowly than the tailings sand and ten thousand times more slowly than the filter sand of a drain, and Chapter 5 showed that the time a layer takes to drain grows with the square of its thickness. So the fill's water stays in while the reservoir's water goes. The water inside still has pressure, now with nothing outside to balance it; it seeps out through the face, and its drag pulls the face's grains downhill, exactly as on the beach face of Fig. 4.4. Here is the upstream half of our dam before and after:

Notice that the water inside the dam is the same in both panels, below the same line. Its pressure has fallen only by the weight of the water taken off above it, while the reservoir that pressed on the face from outside has gone altogether. In Chapter 4's terms, the upstream slope went from a heap under still water to a heap with water seeping out of its face. Engineers call this rapid drawdown, and the workbench checks it the classic way: water pressure on each slice comes straight from the seepage solution; the free-draining materials (anything that passes water at 10⁻⁵ m/s or faster: rockfill, filter sand, tailings sand and the sand & gravel foundation) drain with the reservoir, while clay and fill keep their water pressure, less only the weight of the water taken off above them. The reservoir is taken all the way down at once, and the fill is given no time at all to drain: a deliberately pessimistic picture of a drawdown that in life takes days or weeks.

Example 12.4

Four dams, emptied fast

Given
Our dam's section with its 20.4 m reservoir emptied at once to the original ground, four ways of building it: all compacted fill on clay; the same with the downstream drain; a clay core between rockfill shells, on clay; all rockfill, on sand and gravel. The workbench's upstream check for each.
Find
Which upstream slopes stand, and why.
The idea
Only material that can drain as fast as the reservoir falls gets its grip back as the water goes. Compare each result with the long-slope rule.
  1. All fill: FS = 0.940, ru = 0.441the trapped water carries more of the weight than at full reservoir downstream (0.353)
  2. Same circle, water pressure set to zero: 1.705the soil itself is strong enough
  3. With the downstream drain: FS = 1.045a drain on the far side does little for this face
  4. Clay core, rockfill shells: FS = 1.094this core is wide, and the circle still cuts its clay
  5. All rockfill: FS = 1.814, against the long-slope 1.801the rockfill drains as the reservoir falls: a dry slope

The fill slope slides at 0.94; the drain and the core leave it near 1.0 to 1.1; all rockfill stands at 1.81, the score of a dry slope.

Check. The rockfill dam's worst surface is a skin 2.0 m deep, a long slope in all but name, and its 1.814 is within 1% of tan 42° × 2 = 1.801. The fill dam's surface is a circle 9.3 m deep: its cohesion pushes the slip deep, into the water.

What it means. A dam that must be emptied quickly needs a free-draining upstream shell, thick enough that the slip cannot run behind it through wet fill. Example 9.2 made the same point with a long slope; the workbench's "Empty it fast" mission in Chapter 13 asks you to design one.

then press Test in the workbench

Real reservoirs have done this. San Luis Dam, a large earth dam in California whose reservoir is filled and drawn down as water is stored and released, was found on 14 September 1981 to have slid along its upstream slope, after an unprecedented drawdown of its reservoir, by about 55 m in 120 days.Stark (1987), abstract: the slide's discovery on 14 September 1981, the drawdown of about 55 m (180 ft) in 120 days, and seven earlier drawdown cycles. US Bureau of Reclamation measurements at Alcova Dam, Wyoming, lowered 120 ft in 40 days, showed "appreciable pore water pressures" left in the embankment afterwards: USBR (1987), p. 242. It had been drawn down seven times before, some of them nearly as far. The investigation found clayey soil under the slope that had softened over fourteen years of the reservoir rising and falling, so the grip the slope had on the day was less than the grip it had been built with.

Check yourself A reservoir is lowered by the same 20 m over a year instead of a week. Is the upstream fill slope in the same danger?

Much less. The fill's water has time to leave as the level falls, so its pressure follows the reservoir down, and the slope passes through a series of nearly steady states. Rapid drawdown is a matter of time, like drained and undrained loading in Chapter 5.

12.6 What the check does, and what it leaves out

For circular slip surfaces the workbench uses Bishop's simplified method, the standard hand-and-computer method since 1955. It cuts the sliding mass into 40 vertical slices, works out how hard each slice presses on its base after taking away the water pressure there, and balances the turning effect of the whole mass about the circle's centre. It tries more than two thousand circles, from many entry and exit points and radii, then searches around the worst few, and keeps the lowest score.It ignores any slip shallower than 2 m. On a face of clean sand or rockfill the long-slope rule gives every depth the same score, so a search left to itself drifts to the thinnest skin it may, a few grains deep. Grains rolling off a face are called ravelling, and mending them is a maintenance job; the dam itself has not moved. On the weak-layer foundation it also tries sliding blocks with a flat base along the layer, using Spencer's method, which balances forces and turning effects together and so works on surfaces that are not circles.

Suction above the water level is ignored, as is usual practice, because it can vanish in a wet spell. Each set of conditions a slope is checked for is a load case, and the workbench checks two: the downstream slope with the reservoir full and the seepage steady, and the upstream slope after a rapid drawdown. It leaves out the others a designer must run: the end of construction, when the fill has only now been placed and the water squeezed into it by the weight of the layers above has not yet drained; an earthquake; a flood that raises the reservoir above its normal level. The workbench in Chapter 13 fixes the upstream slope at 2:1, which is steep for an earth dam; real ones are often flatter because of rapid drawdown.

12.7 What 1.5 means

Each load case comes with a target. The US Army Corps of Engineers, whose manual on slope stability is a common reference, asks a new earth or rockfill dam for 1.5 under long-term steady seepage, 1.3 at the end of construction, and 1.1 to 1.3 right after a rapid drawdown.USACE EM 1110-2-1902, p. 3-2, its table of minimum factors of safety for new earth and rock-fill dams; 1.1 for drawdown from the maximum surcharge pool, 1.3 from the maximum storage pool. The manual says on p. 3-1 that the values "continue to be based on experience". The workbench's missions use 1.5 and, for the drawdown, 1.2.

A factor of safety of 1.5 means the grip available on the worst surface is one and a half times the grip needed to hold it. Turned round, the soil could lose a third of its strength before that surface moved. Nobody derived 1.5 from physics, and it says nothing about the chance of a failure. It is a margin chosen by experience to cover what nobody can measure exactly: the strength of soil that was sampled in a few places and tested in a few small pieces, water pressures that piezometers read at a few points, and a model that is only a model. Designers accept less for the short-lived cases partly because they last days or weeks rather than the life of the dam, and partly because the way they are checked is already pessimistic, as the workbench's instant, total drawdown is.

The margin covers ordinary uncertainty. It cannot cover a wrong input. The pull in Eq. 12.3 is weights and angles, and those are hard to get badly wrong. The grip depends on the strength you feed it, c′ and φ′, and a factor of safety is only as good as that strength. Chapter 5 showed that strength depends on how fast the soil is loaded: given time, the water in a soil leaves as the load comes on and the grains take the press; loaded fast, the water cannot leave, and in a soil whose grains want to pack closer it takes part of the press itself. A calculation fed the slow strength scores a slow loading. It says nothing about a fast one.

The film Every dam leaks retells the opening question of this chapter, from the dam at 1.12 to the drain:

What to remember

  • A slope's factor of safety is its grip over its pull. For a long slope of clean grains it is n · tan φ′ for an n:1 slope, and water seeping out of the face multiplies it by γ′/γsat, about a half: the water adds pull and no press.
  • Real embankments slide on deep curves. Cut the mass into slices, each a block on a curved ramp, and add up their grips and pulls. Bishop's method balances each slice up and down, so the factor of safety sits on both sides of the sum and must be found by going round a loop.
  • On our dam's worst circle the water carries 0.35 of the slices' weight, and costs the slope a third of its score. A drain that takes the water away does more than a quarter more fill.
  • Rapid drawdown takes the reservoir's help away from the upstream face and leaves the fill's water in it. Only a free-draining shell gets its grip back as fast as the water falls.
  • 1.5 is a margin chosen by experience for what nobody can measure exactly. The number is only as good as the strength fed to it, and a soil's strength depends on how fast it is loaded.
