Chapter 13 · Part IV · Will it stand?

Build your own dam

Can you design a dam that passes every check, and what can the checks not see?

Effect of minor geologic details on the safety of dams

The title of a paper by Karl Terzaghi, 1929

So far. Part I was the ground: grains that grip only as hard as they press, and water in their gaps that takes part of that press away, in seconds in sand and over years in clay. Part II set the dam that holds by its weight beside the dam that holds by friction, and the tailings dam that is never finished. Part III gave the embankment its zones and followed the water through them and out at the toe. Chapter 12 turned all of it into one number for a slope. Now you design the dam.

After this chapter you can

  • design a section that passes the leak, piping and slope checks, on both of its faces;
  • weigh what each fix costs, in fill, clay or water, against the safety it buys;
  • say what the slope check leaves out, and why a dam can pass it and still fail.

This chapter adds the 1 m grid of the workbench over the section

4 figures · about 20 min to read · Film 13.1, 8 min 46 s

When the review panel opened Mount Polley's design files, it found that the side of the dam that later failed had been checked the way Chapter 12 checks a slope. Trial slip surfaces were drawn through it, the grip the ground could offer along each was set against the weight trying to slide it, and the weakest surface gave a factor of safety. During the raise of 2007 to 2011 that number was 1.7, where the designers required 1.3. The Chief Inspector of Mines found that, on the engineers' understanding of the ground, the calculated factor of safety of that embankment was 1.5 or more.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), p. 64 (1.7 against 1.3); Chief Inspector of Mines (2015), p. 2 (1.5 or greater). By the rules of the trade the dam was safe, and on the night of 4 August 2014 it gave way (the Prologue).

Before finding out what that number missed, design a dam yourself and run the same kind of check on it. This chapter hands you a workbench wired to the tools of the last four chapters, and five missions, each a brief of the kind engineers are given. The last is Mount Polley, rebuilt, and your check will pass it too.

13.1 A workbench with three checks

The workbench is our dam, the 24 m embankment of Plate 0, drawn on a grid of 1 m cells. You paint the cells with five materials, choose the ground it sits on, and set the reservoir. Then the page tests your design with two calculations.

The first is the seepage solver of the lab in Fig. 10.3. It finds where the water inside your dam settles, how much leaks through, and how hard it pushes on the soil where it comes out.

The second asks whether the downstream slope would slide. It tries more than two thousand curved surfaces through the slope (1,960 on a grid, then a few hundred more homing in on the weakest), each a possible slip surface, and on a foundation with a weak layer it also tries flat-bottomed blocks that slide along the layer. On each it adds up, slice by slice as in Chapter 12, the grip the soil can offer (friction, plus the cohesion of a clayey fill) against the pull of the soil's weight trying to slide it downhill. Friction depends on how hard the grains press together, so wherever the seepage solution puts water pressure on a surface, the grip there drops.

Grip divided by pull is the factor of safety, the number of the block on the ramp in Chapter 4 and of the slices in Chapter 12. Below 1 the slope slides. With the reservoir full, dam engineers usually want 1.5 or more, to cover what they can't know about the soil.USACE EM 1110-2-1902, table 3-1, p. 3-2: 1.5 for long-term steady seepage in a new earth or rockfill dam; 1.1 to 1.3 after a rapid drawdown. A third verdict, the upstream slope after the reservoir is emptied fast, waits for the fourth mission. The page reports the three checks in the language of the chapters that built them:

Leaks

Seepage in litres per day for each metre of dam, the flow of Chapter 10. Some is normal. A lot means lost water, or polluted water for a tailings dam.

Pipes

Where water leaves unprotected soil, it pushes on the grains, as in Chapter 11. Rising out of level ground it lifts them; out of a slope it drags them along the face, and the same number is a guide to how hard. Safety against piping is the push that would float sand away divided by the push it gets. For water rising out of level ground the US Bureau of Reclamation wants at least 3 for an existing dam and 4 for a new one (about 2 to 2.5 where the soil is well measured); the missions here ask for 3 at every exit.USBR DS-13 ch. 8, section 8.2.2.2, p. 8-7. The number warns of sand boils; it can't see every kind of internal erosion.

Slides

The lowest factor of safety of any slip surface at least 2 m deep, as in Chapter 12. Shallower slips are surface damage that maintenance fixes.

Here is the workbench. It opens on a dam of compacted fill, untested; the tabs above the drawing hold the five missions, each with a brief, targets and hints:

Notice that the slip surface and the water belong together. Test the dam of fill and the blue bars stand tallest where the surface runs lowest under the dashed line; that is where the water carries most of the soil's weight, and where the grip is thinnest. Every mission below is, one way or another, about putting the water where it can do no harm.

13.2 Mission 1: dry the slope

The first brief is the dam that opened Chapter 12: compacted fill on clay, standing at 1.12 with water breaking out 8 m up its downstream face. There you chose a fix on paper. Here you paint it. Before you do, it is worth asking whether you could have known where the water would come out without any solver at all. Dam designers had a rule of thumb for it long before computers:USBR (1987), section 6.3(c), p. 190, after Justin, Hinds and Creager: in a completely homogeneous dam, seepage "will emerge on the downstream slope regardless of its flatness", to "roughly one-third the depth of the reservoir pool". in a dam of one material, water held long enough behind it will break out on the downstream slope at about a third of the reservoir's depth, however flat that slope is.

hout ≈ H / 3 (13.1)

hout height above the base at which water breaks out on the downstream face of a homogeneous dam (m) · H depth of the reservoir (m)

Example 13.1

A rule of thumb against the solver

Given
Our dam built of fill alone, with the reservoir 20.4 m deep. The solver's answer: water breaks out 8 m up the downstream slope.
Find
Where the one-third rule puts the breakout, and how well it agrees with the solver at three slopes.
The idea
A third of the depth (Eq. 13.1), whatever the slope.
  1. hout ≈ 20.4 ÷ 3 = 6.8 mthe rule
  2. Solver: 8 ÷ 20.4 = 0.392 of the depththe solver's breakout as a share of the reservoir
  3. At 2.5:1 and 3:1: 8 m and 8 ma flatter face moves the toe out but not the breakout up or down

The rule says 6.8 m and the solver 8 m, at every slope the workbench offers.

Check. The rule is rough in both directions. Lower the reservoir to 60%, 14.4 m: the rule gives 14.4 ÷ 3 = 4.8 m and the solver 3 m. The solver works in 1 m cells, so its breakout is good to about a metre.

What it means. Flattening a dam of one material keeps its face wet; the water comes out at the same height and has further to go to the toe. That is why the Bureau of Reclamation's manual says the fully homogeneous section "should seldom be used" (USBR (1987), p. 190), and why the first fix to try is a drain.

Mission 1 holds the slope at 2:1 and asks for a factor of safety of 1.5 with a piping safety of 3. The question that opened the last chapter already told you which fix wins, and the workbench agrees: paint the drain and the dam scores 1.63. But a designer has to pay for a fix, and the three fixes cost different things. Put them side by side as cubic metres changed against safety gained:

Notice that the two fill lines nearly lie on one another: a flatter slope buys safety at roughly the same, low rate however far you take it, and stops short of 1.5 at 3:1. The drain's line is in a different class. Here is the arithmetic behind the drawing:

Example 13.2

The price of a point of safety

Given
The dam of fill at 2:1, 1,296 m³ per metre, factor of safety 1.1163. Flattened to 2.5:1 it holds 1,440 m³ and scores 1.2726; to 3:1, 1,596 m³ and 1.4184. The drain swaps 126 m³ of fill for filter sand and scores 1.6285.
Find
The safety each fix buys for every 100 m³ of the section it changes.
The idea
Divide what each fix gains by what it changes. Fill added and fill swapped both cost money; the drain's sand must also be graded to the fill, as Chapter 11 requires.
  1. 2.5:1: 1,440 − 1,296 = 144 m³; gain 1.2726 − 1.1163 = 0.1563the extra downstream wedge, and what it buys
  2. 0.1563 ÷ 144 × 100 = 0.1085 per 100 m³the rate for the first flattening
  3. 3:1: 300 m³; 0.3021 ÷ 300 × 100 = 0.1007gain 1.4184 − 1.1163 = 0.3021
  4. Drain: 0.5122 ÷ 126 × 100 = 0.4065gain 1.6285 − 1.1163 = 0.5122, for sand swapped in, not added
  5. 0.4065 ÷ 0.1085 = 3.7the drain's rate over the flatter slope's

Cubic metre for cubic metre the drain buys about 3.7 times as much safety as fill, and it alone passes 1.5.

Check. The flatter slope adds weight on the toe and lengthens the slip, but the water still breaks out 8 m up the face (Example 13.1) and still carries part of the weight on the slip surface. The drain removes that water instead, and on the dam as built the water carried 0.353 of the weight of the soil on the weakest slip.

What it means. No fix is free. The drain's cost is paid in water: it collects what reaches it, so the dam now leaks 2.47 times as much, 110 L/day per metre against 44.4, and leads it away where it can do no harm.

Check yourself You paint a block of filter sand inside the downstream half of the fill, but not joined to the toe. Will it help as a drain does?

Barely. Water that collects in a drain has to leave it; a patch with no way out fills up, and the water in it sits at the same pressure as the fill around it. The workbench treats such a patch as permeable soil, and drains only sand joined to the toe along the base.

13.3 Mission 2: hold the water

The second brief is the opposite problem. A dam of rockfill on sand and gravel stands well but leaks like a sieve: 32,490 L/day for each metre, 93% of it through the dam itself. The brief asks for 100 L/day or less without losing the slope or the piping safety, and with no more than 350 m³ of clay per metre. One could assume that a clay core, the watertight wall of Chapter 9, settles it. Here is what happens when you paint one:

Example 13.3

Where the water goes when you block one path

Given
All rockfill on sand and gravel: 32,490 L/day per metre. Clay passes water at 10⁻⁹ m/s, rockfill at 10⁻⁴ m/s. The preset clay core is 21.4 m wide at the base and 3 m at its top, 23 m up.
Find
The leak with the core, the leak with the core and a full cutoff, and the clay it takes.
The idea
Water takes every path open to it (Chapter 10). A core closes the path through the dam; a cutoff closes the path under it.
  1. Core alone: 5,434 ÷ 32,490 = 0.167the leak falls to a sixth
  2. Core and full cutoff: 2.18 ÷ 5,434 = 0.0004so 99.96% of the core's leak was going under it
  3. Mean core width: (21.4 + 3.0) ÷ 2 = 12.2 mthe core is a trapezoid
  4. Clay: 12.2 × 23 = 280.6 m³ per metremean width times height; the workbench counts whole cells, 286

Core and cutoff together leak 2.18 L/day per metre, with 286 m³ of clay, a factor of safety of 1.81, and every exit far from piping.

Check. The core passes water a hundred thousand times more slowly than the rockfill it replaces (10⁻⁹ against 10⁻⁴ m/s), yet the leak fell only sixfold. A mismatch that large means the water had another way round, and the workbench's verdict names it: of the cored dam's leak, 99.98% passes under the dam, through the gravel.

What it means. Before choosing a fix, find where the water goes. The cutoff is useless on its own (the water would still pour through the rockfill) and nearly everything once the core is in.

13.4 Mission 3: tailings on a budget

The third brief comes from a mine. It wants at least 70% of the dam built of cycloned tailings sand, the coarse part of its own waste (Chapter 8), because that is far cheaper than hauling fill from a borrow pit. Built of tailings sand alone at 2:1 the dam scores 0.64 and slides. The sand has no cohesion, and water seeping out of a slope of it takes about half its grip (Chapter 12). The answer is the first mission's drain with a flatter face: a chimney and blanket drain inside tailings sand at 2.5:1 scores 1.63 with 90% of the dam in sand. Its price is again paid in water, and here it is a large price: the drain collects 7,980 L/day per metre, polluted water that a real mine must catch below the dam and pump back.

13.5 Mission 4: empty it fast

Every brief so far tested the downstream slope with the reservoir full. The fourth tests the other face. A reservoir sometimes has to be emptied in a hurry, to reach a damaged outlet or to take the load off a dam in trouble, and Chapter 12 showed what that does: while the water stands against the upstream face it presses the slope in place, and when it goes, the water trapped in fill and clay stays, pushing out with nothing pushing back. This is rapid drawdown, and for such a short-lived event engineers accept a lower factor of safety, 1.1 to 1.3 depending on the case;USACE EM 1110-2-1902, table 3-1, p. 3-2: 1.1 from maximum surcharge pool, 1.3 from maximum storage pool. the mission asks for 1.2. Empty the dam of fill and its upstream slope scores 0.94.

The obvious remedy is a coat of rockfill on the face, since rockfill drains as fast as the reservoir falls. Paint a skin 5 m thick and test: the factor of safety goes down, to 0.89. The weakest slip runs deeper instead, behind the skin, through fill that still holds its water. A free-draining zone helps only if the slip cannot get round it. Rockfill over the whole upstream part of the dam, from the face in to 3 m short of the crest, scores 1.24; carried in to the crest's edge it scores 1.32; stopped 7 m short, 1.14, not enough. All rockfill drains best of all, 1.41, and leaks 29,621 L/day per metre, which is why the brief caps the leak at 1,000.

Now flip the view back to the downstream slope. The upstream shell has made it worse, 1.03 against 1.12: the reservoir's water now crosses the rockfill without losing head and reaches the fill with nearly all of it. So the shell solves one problem by handing the next zone a harder one. Combine it with the first mission's drain (start from Fill + drain, then paint the upstream shell) and the dam passes everything at once: downstream 1.63, upstream after a fast drawdown 1.30, a leak of 240 L/day per metre and a piping safety over 50. A free-draining shell upstream, a fill that holds the water in the middle, a drain that catches it downstream: you have rebuilt the zoned dam of Chapter 9 from its jobs.

Check yourself The downstream drain does almost nothing for the upstream slope after a drawdown (1.05 against 0.94). Why?

A drawdown's danger is the water trapped in the upstream fill once the reservoir has gone. A drain under the downstream half lowers the water there, far from the upstream slip, which still runs through fill that holds its water.

13.6 Mission 5: Mount Polley

The last brief is the dam of the Prologue, scaled to the workbench: a clay core between rockfill shells, on clay, with a weak layer in the ground below. In the real foundation the weak layer lay 8 to 10 m under a dam almost 40 m high, about a fifth of its height down;Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), p. 135 (the layer) and p. 75 (the height). the workbench's lies 4 to 6 m under a 24 m dam. The layer has no cohesion and a friction angle of 19°, against 28° for the clay around it. The brief asks for a downstream factor of safety of 1.5. The dam starts at 1.21. Decide first how you would spend your money:

In Chapter 12 a drain was the best of three fixes. This dam stands on a weak layer at 1.21. Which change lifts it most?

The flatter slope: 1.21 becomes 1.56. The drains move it to 1.215, almost nothing, and the cutoff to 1.28. The layer is weak because of what it is, not because of water a drain could reach: it lies sealed in clay below the dam. What holds the sliding block back is weight bearing on the layer beyond the toe, and a longer stretch of layer to shear, and a flatter slope supplies both.

To see why one answer differs from the others, start with the shape of the slide the check finds. Choose tab 5 and test the dam as it stands.

Example 13.4

A block on a weak layer

Given
The Mount Polley mission: clay core and rockfill at 2:1, on clay (c′ = 10 kPa, φ′ = 28°) with a layer 4 to 6 m down (c′ = 0, φ′ = 19°).
Find
How much weaker the layer is, what shape of slide it allows, and what it takes to reach 1.5.
The idea
Friction is press times tan φ′ (Eq. 4.3), so a smaller angle on a flat, continuous layer offers a flat, weak path.
  1. tan 19° = 0.3443; tan 28° = 0.5317grip per kilopascal of press, layer and clay
  2. 0.3443 ÷ 0.5317 = 0.648the layer grips about 35% less for the same press
  3. Weakest circle 1.313; weakest block 1.209a block that drops at the crest, slides along the layer and rises beyond the toe; it governs
  4. Filters and drains throughout: 1.215the drains never reach the layer
  5. 2.5:1: 1.390; 3:1: 1.559weight on the layer beyond the old toe, and a longer path along it

At 3:1, for 23% more fill, the section scores 1.56 and passes.

Check. Take the layer away: the same 2:1 dam on plain clay scores 1.553. Flattening to 3:1 buys back about what the layer cost, and no more.

What it means. By the workbench's rules this is a dam you could build, and the real panel's verdict points the same way: had the downstream slope been flattened as the original design proposed, it found, the failure would have been avoided. Hold on to the passing number all the same, and ask which strength it used.

13.7 What the number can't see

Most people would stop here, with a passing number. The workbench gave the layer a drained strength, the grip σ′ tan φ′ of a soil whose water keeps pace with the load and leaves as the grains are squeezed. Mount Polley's designers did the same for the clays they knew of under the dam: silts and clays laid down on the bed of a lake fed by melting glaciers, which engineers call glaciolacustrine. After a field program in 2011, their checks gave these soils a peak friction angle of 28°, the same angle the workbench gives its clay foundation. The layer that failed, a higher one, was not in the checks of the side that failed at all.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), p. 69 (the 28° peak angle after the 2011 field program) and p. 76 (only the lower of two such units was in the Perimeter Embankment's stability analysis). The workbench's 19° stands in for the layer's weakness. Neither is the strength the layer had on the night it failed.

The dam had pressed that clay harder than anything in its past. A clay in that state is loose for its load, like the loose sand of Chapter 5, and when it is sheared it tries to contract. Over the years of raising, the load came on slowly enough for its water to seep away, and the panel found the loading had been essentially drained. A slide is fast. In Chapter 3 water took 11 years to cross a single metre of clay; sheared in minutes, the clay's water could not leave; its pressure rose, the press between the grains fell, and the grip fell with it. That grip is the clay's undrained strength, and Eq. 5.4 gave its rough size for soft clays. The panel's laboratory tests on samples of the layer measured it directly. On average:Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), pp. 76 and 135 (normally consolidated, so contractive, under the dam), p. 101 (a loading path essentially drained), table 5.3.1, p. 49 (peak undrained strength ratio, average 0.24 over all tests), p. 98 (after strain weakening, perhaps 0.13).

su ≈ 0.24 · σ′v against σ′v tan 28° ≈ 0.53 · σ′v (13.2)

su undrained strength of the layer, sheared fast (kPa) · σ′v the vertical effective stress the dam had pressed it to (kPa), which on a level layer is the press across it · 0.24 the panel's average from its tests · tan 28° the drained grip the design gave such clays

Drawn against the press, the two strengths are two straight lines from zero, the strength envelope of Chapter 4 drawn twice:

Notice that the gap grows with the press. The higher the dam, the more strength the drained line promises and the more of it vanishes if the clay is sheared fast. The clay was also strain-softening: in the panel's tests its grip peaked and then fell as it kept moving, so its peak strength held only until it began to move. A slide that starts on such a clay weakens the ground it slides on, which is how a dam that had stood for years could go in a night.Why check drained strength at all? Because it is the right check for loads that last: over years a clay's water does leave, and a slope must stand on the strength it has then. The undrained check is a separate calculation, run with the clay's measured strength ratio and its stress history. The two answer different questions, and a design needs both wherever a clay can be sheared fast.

Your workbench passed the dam at 3:1, and with a flatter slope the real dam would probably have stood. But the number that approved it was computed for a strength the layer did not have when it mattered. The panel was blunt about where the fault lay: "the dominant contribution to the failure resides in the design." Its foundation investigations had not found a continuous layer near the breach, nor recognized that it could fail undrained.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), p. iv and p. 105 (the quotation), p. iv (2H:1V would have avoided the failure).

Check yourself The real layer lay 8 to 10 m under a dam about 40 m high; the workbench's lies 4 to 6 m under 24 m. Is the workbench's at the same share of the height?

Nearly. 8 ÷ 40 = 0.20 and 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25; 4 ÷ 24 = 0.17 and 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25. Scaled to its height, the workbench's layer starts a little higher.

13.8 A layer has to be found first

A calculation can only weigh the ground it is told about. Finding out what that ground is, layer by layer and how strong each is, is the work of site investigation: mapping the geology, drilling boreholes and testing what comes up. A borehole samples a column of ground about a hand's width across. Under the side of Mount Polley that failed, the panel found the critical soil at depths of about 8 m, and only four locations where holes went deeper than 8 m and the soil was tested. None was where the breach occurred.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), pp. 28 and 80. The Chief Inspector counted three deep sampled drillholes along the 2 km of that embankment: Chief Inspector of Mines (2015), p. 2. The layer was there, a few metres thick, and the drilling passed it by.The epigraph is the title of a paper Karl Terzaghi published in 1929, in a collection on geology and dams issued by the American Institute of Mining and Metallurgical Engineers (Terzaghi (1929)). Eighty-five years later, a layer a few metres thick under a 40 m dam was such a detail. After the failure, British Columbia's engineering association wrote guidelines for investigating dam foundations, in answer to one of the panel's recommendations.EGBC (2016), preface: written in response to the panel's Recommendation 6, and applying to all dams in the province.

Then there was the slope on top. The design had called for a downstream slope of 2H:1V, but for years the outer face had been left at the steepest angle tipped rockfill will stand, about 1.3H:1V. (You measured about 1.4 across for 1 up in Fig. P.1, from the crest's edge to the toe; the face itself stood at 1.3H:1V.) The panel put the two causes in one sentence: "If constructing unknowingly on the Upper GLU stratum, and not recognizing the potential undrained failure constituted loading the gun, building with a 1.3H:1V angle of repose slope over this stratum pulled the trigger." Here the Upper GLU is the panel's name for the layer. That night the crest dropped at least 3.3 m, more than the 2.3 m by which it stood above the pond. The pond spilled over the lowered crest and cut the breach.Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), p. 75 (an unbuttressed 1.3H:1V slope, almost 40 m high), p. 108 (the quotation), p. 137 (the crest's drop and the pond 2.3 m below the core). The Chief Inspector of Mines listed among the causes a "misplaced faith in the Factor of Safety".Chief Inspector of Mines (2015), p. 5.

Notice how little of the drawing the layer takes up, and how much of the slide runs along it. Everything above the layer is the dam the checks were written for; the layer is the detail they were never shown.

13.9 What the check leaves out

The workbench is honest about its own blind spots, and so should you be. Material strengths and permeabilities are typical values, not design values. The sandbox does not check earthquakes, the liquefaction of loose saturated sand (Chapter 5), or whether each zone is a proper filter for the one beside it. In a real dam, clay painted straight against rockfill would wash into it, which is why real cores have filters.

Four more limits matter to anyone who would trust its numbers. It checks no clay for its undrained strength, as Mount Polley shows. It skips the end-of-construction case, when a clay core or foundation is still carrying the weight of fresh fill in its water, for which designers want 1.3.USACE EM 1110-2-1902, table 3-1, p. 3-2. Its exit gradients right at the toe depend on the 1 m grid, so the piping safety there is a guide. And it shows one cross-section: a real dam is a kilometre or more of sections, each on its own ground, and the weakest may be the one nobody drew.

The last film of the book tells Mount Polley's story in nine minutes, with the workbench in it:

What to remember

  • A design is a plan for the water: a core and a cutoff to hold it back, a drain to let it out before it reaches the downstream slope, a free-draining shell where the reservoir may fall away. Each keeps water from taking the grains' press where a slip would run.
  • Every fix costs something, in fill, clay or water. A drain buys safety cheapest because it removes water instead of adding weight, and pays for it in leak.
  • A factor of safety is only as good as the strength fed to it. A drained check assumes the water can leave; a clay sheared fast keeps its water, and Mount Polley's gave less than half its drained grip.
  • No calculation weighs ground nobody sampled. The layer had to be found before any strength could be measured.

Questions

  1. 13.1

    The workbench passes the Mount Polley section at 3:1, with a factor of safety of 1.56. Give two reasons the real dam could still have failed at that number.

    Hint

    Ask which strength the check used, and what the check was told about the ground.

  2. 13.2

    Meet Hold the water with the least clay you can. What sets the floor in the workbench, and what would set it in a real dam?

    Hint

    Clay passes water a hundred thousand times more slowly than rockfill, so in the model even a thin wall works if it has no gap. Then think about the gradient across a thin wall.

    Answer

  3. 13.3

    The workbench lets you paint clay straight against rockfill. What would really happen, and which chapter said so?

    Hint

    Compare the size of the clay's particles with the gaps between rocks, and think about water crossing the boundary.

  4. 13.4

    In Empty it fast, start from Leaky (all rockfill) and test. Why does its upstream slope score so much better than the dam of fill, and why does it still not complete the mission?

The executive summary takes two pages; section 5.4 tells the dam's design history raise by raise, and sections 6.2 and 6.5 work the failure through with the undrained strength this chapter quotes.

Every number in this chapter was a calculation, and Mount Polley shows how far a calculation can drift from the ground. Real dams are watched. Once the drawings are done, what do engineers measure, and what can a reading tell them that no check could?

Epilogue

The dam after the drawings

What happens to a dam once the drawings are done?

So far. Every number in this book has been a calculation: a pressure, a leak, a grip, a factor of safety, each worked out for a dam whose soil you chose. Chapter 13 ended on a dam that passed its calculation and failed anyway. Real dams are also watched and governed by law, and some fail in ways no calculation in this book would catch.

The dam, piece by piece complete

2 figures · about 10 min to read

On Friday 11 June 2010 a hiker on Mount Kobau, high above the Okanagan valley south of Oliver, British Columbia, found a small lake full to the brim and running over a dirt road, fast enough to cut a channel across it. He reported it at the tourist booth in Osoyoos. The message passed from the booth to the police, and from the police to the Ministry of Forests, where it ended as a voice mail about a washout on a minor road. Nobody heard it until it was too late.Morhart (2010), p. 10, the province's review by its Deputy Solicitor General.

The road ran along the crest of a dam. Testalinden Dam was a bank of silty sand and glacial till about 2.5 m high, finished in 1937 to store irrigation water, built with horses and a horse-drawn scraper to no engineer's design. That spring a deep snowpack was melting in the year's first hot spell. On the afternoon of Sunday 13 June, the water flowing over the bank cut through it. The lake ran down a steep, narrow gully toward the valley floor 1,500 m below and arrived as a mudflow at least ten times the volume of the water that started it. It destroyed or badly damaged five homes and buried 200 m of Highway 97. Nobody was hurt.The dam, the snowmelt and the mudflow: ASDSO, Testalinden case study, quoting the field investigation in Tannant (2015), which found no rain recorded in the three days before (the province's review, written a month after, spoke of heavy rain). The date, the year built, the toll: Morhart (2010), pp. 7, 11 and 12.

None of it surprised the people whose job was to know. The province's files record water seeping near its outlet pipe as early as 1942. By 1960 a road had been built across it, and its spillway, the channel that lets a flood past (Chapter 6), had been filled with earth and a pipe laid through it. In 1977 an inspector wrote that "the dam is in deplorable condition and should, in my (the inspector) opinion, be breached or rebuilt." In 1988 another inspector added, "No attempt has been made to carry out our instructions." The review found warnings going back to the 1960s, and no sign that the repairs were made or that anyone held the owner to them.Morhart (2010), pp. 3 and 7–9; the quotations are from the inspections of 1977 and 1988.

Every fault on that list is in this book: water seeping along a pipe, a spillway too small for a flood, a freeboard of a foot or less. Nothing in the dam's calculations was wrong, because it never had any. What failed was the arrangement around it: inspections and letters, with nobody made to act on them. That arrangement is part of the dam. Here is the dam, and the fall below it, each drawn to its own scale:The foot of freeboard and the 12-inch spillway pipe: Morhart (2010), p. 8, the letter of 1978.

Notice how close the dashed line sits to the crest: in 1978 the lake already stood within a foot of the road. Notice too the spillway pipe, a circle you could cover with two hands. The lake was small, about 36,000 m³ full to the crest;An acre-foot is the water that would cover an acre, 4,047 m², one foot deep: 1,233.5 m³. Testalinden held about 29 of them (ASDSO, Testalinden case study). Mount Polley released some 600 times as much, at the low estimate. What made it dangerous was the 1,500 m below it.Mount Polley released 21 to 25 million m³: Chief Inspector of Mines (2015), p. 13.

E.1 The other half

Testalinden failed in the commonest way an embankment dam fails: water came over the top. Chapter 6 counted the record. Of the large embankment dams that failed in service up to 1986, about a third failed because water poured over the crest, and about half once the failed spillways and gates are counted in.Foster, Fell & Spannagle (2000), its table 3, failures in operation: overtopping 34.2%, with spillway and gate failures 47.0%. This book has spent its chapters on the other half, and the title page gives it one sentence:

Soil holds only as well as its grains press on one another, and the water between them can take that press away.

It carried us from the beach to the workbench, but it does not reach Testalinden. Water running over a crest does not need to take the grains' press away: it drags them off the surface, and each one it takes uncovers the next. So the sentence needs an honest second half:

And water that pours over the top can wash the whole heap away, however hard its grains press.

Other omissions deserve a line each. Earthquakes do more than liquefy loose sand: shaking can crack a core and settle a crest. The flood a spillway must pass comes from rain and snowmelt records that a changing climate makes harder to trust; one lesson drawn from Testalinden is to recheck the spillways of dams built before those records existed. Arch dams, gates and chutes have mechanics of their own.The lessons on floods and old spillways: ASDSO, Testalinden case study.

E.2 Watching the water you painted

For the half this book does cover, the calculation is where a dam's life starts. A real dam's fill is never quite what was sampled, the ground under it was seen only down a few boreholes, and drains silt up over the decades. So engineers build instruments into a dam, and each measures a quantity you have already computed. Here they are on our dam, the workbench's 24 m section on clay with the chimney and blanket drain that Chapter 12 used to dry it; the water level inside it and the slip circle are the solver's:

Notice that each instrument reads an ingredient of a calculation. A piezometer is the straw of Fig. 3.1 made permanent: it reads the water pressure u at one point, as the bars along the slip surface did in Fig. 13.1. The measuring weir reads the leak of Fig. 10.3. The inclinometer, a grooved tube down which a probe measures the tilt, shows where the ground is moving sideways, and at what depth. No instrument reads the factor of safety: it exists only in the calculation, and the readings are what engineers feed it.

So the question an engineer asks of a rising piezometer is how much safety it costs. For our dam, Chapter 12 has supplied what is needed: on its critical circle the factor of safety is 1.116, the water carries 0.353 of the slices' weight (the ratio engineers call ru), and the same circle without water stands at 1.741. In 1960 Alan Bishop and Norbert Morgenstern showed that for a given slope the factor of safety falls very nearly in a straight line as ru grows:The Morgenstern of that paper (Bishop & Morgenstern (1960)) is Norbert Morgenstern, who fifty-five years later chaired the panel that investigated Mount Polley (Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), p. i).

FS ≈ FS0 − n · ru(E.1)

FS0 the factor of safety with no water pressure · ru the share of the slices' weight the water carries, Σu·b ÷ ΣW · n the safety each unit of ru costs, set by the slope's shape and soilWhy nearly straight: in Bishop's sum the water enters only by taking u·b off each slice's weight before friction acts. If every slice lost the same share of its weight, the grip, and with it the factor of safety, would fall in a straight line as that share grew, except that the factor of safety also sits inside each slice's mα. That small feedback bends the line slightly.

Example E.1

What a rising piezometer costs (illustrative)

Given
Our dam on clay, as Chapter 12 left it: FS = 1.116 with ru = 0.353, and FS0 = 1.741 on the same circle with no water. The slices on that circle weigh, on average, 154.1 kN for each square metre of their bases. A metre of water in a piezometer is 9.81 kPa.
Find
The safety lost for each 0.1 added to ru, and the rise in the piezometers along the slip that adds it.
The idea
Draw the line of Eq. E.1 through the two points. Raising the water pressure on every slice by the same amount adds that amount, divided by the slices' weight per square metre, to ru.
  1. 1.741 − 1.116 = 0.625the safety the water takes, at ru = 0.353
  2. n = 0.625 ÷ 0.353 = 1.77the slope of the line: safety lost per unit of ru
  3. 1.77 × 0.1 = 0.177lost when ru rises by a tenth
  4. Δu = 0.1 × 154.1 = 15.41 kPathe extra water pressure that carries another tenth of the slices' weight
  5. 15.41 ÷ 9.81 = 1.57 mthe same rise as a height of water in a piezometer

A rise of about 1.6 m in the piezometers along the slip costs our dam about 0.18 of its factor of safety.

Check. Do it without the straight line. Rerun Bishop's sum on the same circle with every slice's water pressure 15.41 kPa higher: the solver's slices give 0.943, against 1.116 − 0.177 = 0.939 from the line. The two agree to the second decimal.

What it means. A dam like ours designed to 1.5 holds 0.5 above failure, and a season's rise of a metre and a half in its piezometers would spend more than a third of that. Our dam, at 1.116, would go below 1. So an engineer watches each piezometer's trend against the reservoir, and decides in advance the reading at which something must be done.

Then press Test my dam.

Check yourself Over a summer the reservoir behind our drained dam rises 3 m, and piezometer B stays dry. Good news or bad?

Good news. The drain is carrying the extra water away before it can build pressure in the downstream half. Water appearing in B, and climbing with the reservoir, would mean the drain was not keeping up.

E.3 Peck's bargain

Most people take a dam that has stood for decades as proof that it is safe. Testalinden stood for seventy-three years and Mount Polley for eighteen, and both failed. Instruments let an engineer do better than wait. Ralph Peck, Terzaghi's co-author, set out the approach in his Rankine Lecture of 1969: the observational method. You design for the ground you think most likely, and before you build you decide what you will measure, what readings would mean the ground is worse than you assumed, and what you will do then. It is a bargain with ignorance: you need not know everything about the ground at the start, provided it tells you in time and you have a response ready.Peck (1969); the method as the tailings standard defines it, citing Peck: GISTM (2020), glossary. Peck and Terzaghi wrote Terzaghi, Peck & Mesri (1996) together.

Both conditions failed at Mount Polley, though its designers had invoked the method from the start. Its few instruments stood beyond the toe, because the steep slope could not be reached, and too far apart to cover the place where it broke. More fundamentally, as the panel wrote, "piezometers cannot measure pore pressures induced by undrained shearing because the location of the failure surface on which to measure them cannot be known in advance." Had they warned, there was no way to build a buttress in time. With the undrained failure never recognized, the panel concluded, the method had been reduced to "mere trial and error".Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), p. 77 (the method, the instruments' reach, the quotation, no time to respond), p. 80 (no instruments near the breach) and p. 107 (trial and error).

The lesson is now in the international standard for tailings facilities, published in 2020. It asks for the observational method in full for failures that are not brittle, and adds: "Brittle failure modes are addressed by conservative design criteria." A brittle failure, like that of Mount Polley's clay sheared too fast for its water to get out (Chapter 5), gives little warning: the soil loses strength once it starts to move. Against it, the only defence is margin built in before anyone is watching.GISTM (2020), Requirement 7.2.

Check yourself Why would even a piezometer on the slip surface give little warning of an undrained failure?

The pressure that weakens the soil appears only as it shears. By the time the piezometer reads it, the slip is already under way, and a soil that loses strength as it moves leaves no time to respond.

E.4 The law around the dam

An instrument nobody reads, or a reading nobody acts on, does nothing, and Testalinden had warnings on file for decades. Closing that gap is what regulation is for. In British Columbia a water dam answers to the Dam Safety Regulation, and a dam on a mine to Part 10 of the Health, Safety and Reclamation Code for Mines. Both have been rewritten since these two failures.

In 2010 Testalinden was rated "Low", which meant an audit about once in ten years; within two weeks of the failure the province had assessed 628 dams. The regulation of 2016 sorts dams into the Canadian Dam Association's five consequence classes, from low to extreme, by what a failure would do downstream, to lives, property and the environment. The class, not the dam's height, sets the duties. A dam of high consequence or above is checked on site weekly unless its manual says otherwise, inspected formally at least once a year, run from a written manual with an emergency plan, and given a dam safety review by an engineer every seven or ten years. Under today's scale Testalinden would have been significant, not low.The rating and the 628 dams: Morhart (2010), p. 15. The class today, and the match with the Canadian Dam Association: ASDSO, Testalinden case study. The classes and duties: Dam Safety Regulation (2016), Schedules 1 and 2, ss. 8, 9 and 20.

Mount Polley rewrote the mining code. In July 2016 the province announced limits on the steepness of a tailings dam's downstream slope, a minimum factor of safety, flood and earthquake criteria, and an independent review board for every mine with a tailings facility. Every tailings facility and dam on a mine has an engineer of record, and if that engineer reports a safety problem the mine leaves unfixed, the manager must tell the chief inspector within 72 hours, or the engineer must. Some rules read like the panel's findings turned round. A downstream slope steeper than 2H:1V (two across for every one up) needs the engineer of record's justification and the regulator's approval; Mount Polley's stood at 1.3H:1V, and the panel found that a 2:1 slope would have avoided the failure. The factor of safety in operation must be at least 1.5. And the facility's manual must say what is to be done as readings worsen, where the piezometers of Mount Polley's failed embankment had no trigger levels at all.BC Ministry of Energy and Mines (2016); Mines Code, Part 10, ss. 10.4.1, 10.4.3, 10.4.4, 10.5.8, 10.5.9 and its table 10-5, and 10.6.6. The slope: Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), p. iii; no trigger levels, p. 79.

The same ideas now cross borders. The Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management of August 2020 asks every operator that adopts it for an engineer of record, an accountable executive answering to the chief executive and, where a failure would be very high or extreme in consequence, an independent tailings review board. None of it makes a dam safe by itself. It puts named people and outside reviewers where Testalinden had letters in a file.GISTM (2020), Requirements 8.4, 8.7 and 9.1.

Check yourself Two earth dams are each 10 m high. One holds a farm pond above an empty valley; the other holds the same pond above a town. Which needs the more frequent review?

The one above the town. The consequence class, which sets how often a dam is inspected and reviewed, follows what its failure would do downstream, not its size.

What to remember

  • Grains pressing on one another, and the water between them taking that press away, explain about half the ways embankment dams fail. Water pouring over the top explains most of the other half.
  • Instruments read the ingredients of the calculation: piezometers read u, weirs read q, inclinometers find the slip. Nothing reads the factor of safety itself.
  • For our dam each tenth added to ru, about a metre and a half of water in the piezometers along the slip, costs about 0.18 of the factor of safety.
  • The observational method works when a failure gives warning and there is time to act. An undrained, brittle failure gives neither, so it must be met with margin in the design.
  • Regulation is part of the dam: a class set by what lies downstream, a named engineer, reviews, and readings with actions attached to them.

Questions

  1. E.1

    Inspectors visited Testalinden in 1961, 1977, 1978, 1985, 1988 and 1992. List what they found. Which of those faults would a yearly walk along the crest still have shown in 2010, and what would it have taken to prevent the failure?

    Hint

    The opening pages and the case file name most of the faults. Then ask what the inspections lacked, not what they missed.

    Answer

  2. E.2

    Name three things British Columbia's mining code requires today, and for each say which part of the Mount Polley failure it answers.

    Hint

    Answer

  3. E.3

    The drained version of our dam (Fill + drain in Fig. 13.1) stands at 1.628. Its engineer of record wants an alarm before it falls to 1.5. Using the straight line with our dam's n = 1.77, and the drained circle's average weight of 83.4 kN per square metre of base, how far may the piezometers along its slip rise?

    Hint

    Run Example E.1 backwards: margin, then ru, then kPa, then metres of water.

    Answer

    A wet spring fills our dam's reservoir from 85% to 95% of its height. Set the workbench to the homogeneous dam on clay at 95% and test it. How far up the downstream slope does the water break out, how much does the dam leak, and what is its factor of safety? Which instruments in Fig. E.2 would show the change?

    Hint

    At 85% the water breaks out 8 m up, the dam leaks 44.4 L/day per metre, and its factor of safety is 1.12.

Previous · Chapter 13 · Build your own dam

Go back to the beach where this book began, on an evening when the tide is coming in. The sea covers the firm, dark middle of the beach, and the sand there, already full of water, hardly changes. Then it reaches the castle you built from damp sand, whose walls stood straight up, held by the water clinging where the grains touch (Chapter 1). The first wave fills every gap, the pull is gone, and the walls slump into a low heap. The grains are the same grains; only the water has changed.

Pick up a handful before the next wave comes in: grains pressing on one another, and the water between them. Every earth dam in this book was made of that, and so is the ground under every dam you will ever stand on.

Reference

Answers and hints

Chapter 1 · The beach

1.1 · back to the question

The amount of sand, which in a section is its area. The dry heap's triangle has area ½ × 58.27 × 19.653 = 572.6 cm², the same as the castle's 572.6 cm². The draining heap is lower again, 14.0 cm tall, and wider in proportion.

1.2 · back to the question

Packed densely, the heap holds. Packed loosely, it flows flat and the flag sinks; the readout says the grains packed tighter and the trapped water took their weight. Both heaps were saturated, so saturation alone does not make soup: the sand must also be loose. Chapter 5 explains why the dense heap holds, and with it the pale ring round your foot.

1.3 · back to the question

30 cm: 18 × 0.3 = 5.4 kN on each square metre. 30 m: 18 × 30 = 540 kN on each square metre, a hundred times more. The water rings grip the grains with the same small force in both, so the short wall can stand and the tall one cannot. A kilonewton on a square metre has a name, the kilopascal, which Chapter 2 uses throughout; Chapter 5 compares these numbers with the grip.

1.4 · back to the question

It depends on what you pour, which is the point: the angle is set by the shape and friction of the grains. For example, a heap 6 cm high on a base 18 cm across gives tan β = 12 ÷ 18 = 0.667 and β = 33.7°. Rounder, smoother grains give lower angles. Dry sands usually come out in the low-to-mid thirties of degrees; report what you measured.

1.5 · back to the question

1.5:1 is arctan 0.667 = 33.7°; 2:1 is 26.6°; 3:1 is arctan 0.333 = 18.4°. All three are flatter than 34°, so dry sand stands at each, though at 1.5:1 it has almost nothing to spare.

1.6 · back to the question

Only 3:1, at 18.4°, is flatter than 19.0°, and barely. 2.5:1 is 21.8°, too steep where water comes out. The other choice is to stop the water reaching the face, with a drain, and keep the steeper, cheaper slope. Real fill is not clean beach sand and designers want a margin as well; Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 do the full check.

Chapter 2 · Depth, not size

2.1 · back to the question

From 7.85 MN to 17.66 MN per metre, a factor of (60/40)² = 2.25. Half as deep again more than doubles the push.

2.2 · back to the question

24.0 MN per metre, as heavy as 2,450 tonnes: 1.96 times the push at 50 m, because 70² = 4,900 is nearly twice 50² = 2,500.

2.3 · back to the question

Three metres of water changes the pressure by 29.4 kPa. Thirty metres of sea-level air, at 1.225 kg/m³ (U.S. Standard Atmosphere (1976)), changes it by only 0.36 kPa, because water is about 816 times denser than air. The ears feel the difference.

2.4 · back to the question

16.7 m above the base, a third of the way up. Doubling the depth doubles that height and quadruples the push, so the moment grows 8 times, from 204 to 1,635 MN·m per metre.

2.5 · back to the question

Mostly a help. On a 2:1 face the water presses down 2 times as hard as it pushes across (Example 2.5), and pressing down holds the dam onto its foundation. That is exact for a watertight face; in an earth dam some of the water soaks into the slope (Chapter 10). The sideways part still has to be resisted, and the help disappears when the reservoir is let down quickly, the subject of Chapter 12.

2.6 · back to the question

At the foot of the face 9.81 × 175 = 1,717 kPa, or 1.72 MPa (a megapascal is 1,000 kPa). The push is 150 MN per metre, as heavy as about 15,300 tonnes. Its base is 0.72 times its height, against 0.8 in the example: the same family of shape, a little slimmer. Dimensions from BC Hydro (2013) and BC Hydro (2016).

Chapter 3 · Which way the water goes

3.1 · back to the question

The heads are 25 m at A and 22 m at B, so the water flows from A toward B. But B feels the higher pressure: its tip has 22 − 2 = 20 m of water above it, against 15 m at A, so 9.81 × 20 = 196.2 kPa at B and 9.81 × 15 = 147.2 kPa at A. The water flows from lower pressure to higher, because it flows toward lower head.

3.2 · back to the question

Every point in still water has the same total head. Going deeper trades elevation head for pressure head metre for metre, so a straw anywhere in the lake, or in the soaked bed under it, fills to the lake's surface (Fig. 3.1, panel A). With no difference in head there is no gradient, and Darcy's law gives no flow.

3.3 · back to the question

The share stays at 99.996%, because the resistances haven't changed. The head difference falls from 1.40 m to 0.20 m, so the flow falls by 1.40 ÷ 0.20 = 7 times, from 110 to about 16 litres a year through each square metre.

3.4 · back to the question

0.40 × 2 ÷ 10⁻⁷ = 8.0 × 10⁶ s, which is 93 days: twice the race's 46 days for one metre, because at the same gradient the drop moves at the same speed and has twice as far to go.

3.5 · back to the question

The gradient halves to 3, so the leak halves, to about 7.8 litres a day per metre of dam. The drop moves at half the speed over twice the distance, so it takes four times as long: 4 × 9.24 = 37 years.

Chapter 4 · Grip

4.1 · back to the question

FS = 0.6745 ÷ 0.5774 = 1.17. The water must carry 1 − 0.5774 ÷ 0.6745 = 0.144 of a press of 17.32 kN, and 0.144 × 17.32 = 2.49 kPa: only 14% of the press. In the figure it holds at 2.0 kPa and slides at 2.5. The steeper the ramp, the less margin it has to lose.

4.2 · back to the question

Less likely. The same 5 kPa over the same 1 m² takes 5 kN off each block's press, but the heavier block presses with twice as much, so it loses a smaller share of its grip. With no water the weight cancels out of the factor of safety; water pressure is what makes weight matter.

4.3 · back to the question

σ = 18 × 2 + 20 × 8 = 196 kPa; u = 9.81 × 8 = 78.48 kPa; σ′ = 117.52 kPa, which is 65% of the 180 kPa the grains press with when the water table is below the column.

4.4 · back to the question

No. The extra water adds 9.81 × 20 = 196.2 kPa to the total stress and the same to the pore pressure, so σ′ and the strength are unchanged, as the lake on the column showed. The danger from a deeper reservoir is elsewhere: more head drives more water under the dam, and where it comes up again on the downstream side the upward gradient takes away the press (Eq. 4.4). Chapter 11 follows it there.

4.5 · back to the question

The drag is 0.6 × 9.81 = 5.89 kN per cubic metre against a buoyant weight of 10.19, which leaves 4.30 kN, and 4.30 ÷ 10.19 = 0.422: about 42% of the press, and of the strength, is left. The gradient is under the critical 1.04, but more than half the grip has gone.

4.6 · back to the question

tan β = 0.5095 × 0.5774 = 0.2942, so β = 16.4°. Dry, the same sand would stand at 30°.

Chapter 5 · When the water can't get out

5.1 · back to the question

The firm sand is dense. Sheared by the foot it must swell, and the water it needs is drawn in from the surface, which sinks below the top grains and leaves them dry for a moment; meanwhile the stretched water pulls the grains together and the sand stiffens. The sand at the edge is loose. Wiggled, its grains try to drop into the gaps, the trapped water's pressure rises and takes their weight, they press less and grip less, and the foot sinks.

5.2 · back to the question

With the drain shut no water can get in, so the water already there is stretched, Δu falls below zero and σ′ = σ − Δu rises above the load. With the drain open water flows in as the sample swells, Δu stays near zero, and the grain stress stays near the load. The fall stops at −100 kPa*, the model's stand-in for cavitation: real water lowered to about zero absolute pressure, roughly −100 kPa gauge, breaks into bubbles of vapour and air, so trapped water can only pull so hard. After that, as the result line says, a little swelling gets through.

5.3 · back to the question

Shut, it falls in steps, a little with each shake, as the extra water pressure ratchets up toward the load, until after a few shakes the grains hardly press and the house tips. Open, the displaced water leaves through the drain, Δu stays small and the grains keep pressing; the loose sand still compacts, so the house still settles a little, but it does not sink and tip. Read the trend, not the model's numbers.

5.4 · back to the question

Sand: 3² ÷ 0.20387 = 44.1 s, three times the shaking, so it is undrained while the ground shakes. Clay: 5² ÷ 0.08807 = 283.9 days, and 283.9 ÷ 365.25 = 0.78 years: about as long as the raise itself, so the clay is partly drained as the dam grows, carrying a good part of each raise in its water for months. If it starts to slide, in minutes, it is undrained.

5.5 · back to the question

Its fill was hydraulic fill, sluiced into place with water, like tailings: loose and saturated. Fifteen seconds is shorter than the time water needs to leave even 2 m of sand (about 20 s in Example 5.2), so every shake was undrained, the water pressure in the loose fill ratcheted up, and the fill near the base of the upstream slope liquefied. Coquitlam Dam in British Columbia, a hydraulic fill dam of the same era, is in Chapter 8.

The power goes from 74.2 to 121.8 MW, a factor of 1.64, because H goes from 56 to 92 m. The load goes from 17.7 to 45.2 MN per metre, a factor of 2.56: the depth at the heel goes from 60 to 96 m, 1.6 times, and the load grows with its square, 1.6 × 1.6 = 2.56. The last metres of water earn the least and cost the most.

6.2 · back to the question

Neither. H is measured to the tailwater; the heel is 4 m lower, 88.8 m below the surface, and 9.81 × 88.8 = 871.1 kPa (Example 6.2).

6.3 · back to the question

Merriespruit began as overtopping: water flowed over the crest for one to two hours and washed away the outer wall, and only then did the loose tailings behind it liquefy and flow. Mount Polley was not a liquefaction of the tailings at all; what it was is the subject of Chapter 13. The other four were liquefaction of the tailings, set off by an earthquake at El Cobre, hastened by small ones at Fundão, and with nothing from outside at Stava and Brumadinho.

6.4 · back to the question

It keeps a small residual strength, the grip left between grains that still touch while the deposit flows. That remainder slows the flow and decides where it stops, so it sets how far the tailings run and what they reach.

6.5 · back to the question

Twice the flow, 1,039 m³/s, needs h3/2 = 2 × 5.196 = 10.392, so h = 10.3922/3 = 4.76 m: 1.59 times the design rise, not twice. The lake stands at 29.76 m, only 0.24 m below the crest: almost all of the 5 m between the normal level and the crest is gone.

Both carry part of the weight on water, so the block or the dam presses on what is under it with less, and the friction, which comes from that press, shrinks while the push or pull trying to move it stays the same: W − U in Eq. 7.1 is the "press left over" of Fig. 4.1.

It falls faster near the top because the push grows with the square of the depth while the uplift grows only in proportion to it; at 57 m one more metre of water adds about 559 kN of push, and with the drains working even less than the 235 kN of uplift it would add with them clogged.

The one-third rule amounts to removing 62 per cent here, above the Corps' usual range and close to the 67 per cent it allows only when tests justify it (USACE EM 1110-2-2200, para. 3-3.d(1)(c)). With the result this sensitive, a careful designer would want pressure gauges in the drain holes to show what the drains actually achieve, and would keep watching them.

7.6 · back to the question

It prevents a crack, once open, from being pushed wider by the water in it: if the masonry presses the crack shut harder than the water pushes it open, water is squeezed out instead of forced in. The middle-third rule only keeps the face from being pulled apart by the weight and the push; it allows the face to be pressed with almost nothing, and any crack then fills with the reservoir's full pressure and spreads. At Bouzey's break the Bureau of Reclamation's back-calculation found the upper wall failing even the middle-third rule, with its face in tension (Fig. 7.3).

Chapter 8 · Never finished

8.1 · back to the question

Upstream: 32 × 34 + 320 = 1,408 m³ at 34 m, and 2,496 ÷ 1,408 = 1.77. Centreline: 34² + 20 × 34 + 160 = 1,996 m³, and 6,144 ÷ 1,996 = 3.08. Upstream fill grows roughly in step with height, because each raise is the same small dyke; downstream fill grows nearly with its square, because each raise widens the whole base; centreline is in between, closer to downstream.

8.2 · back to the question

About 10% of the centreline dam's 2,976 m³ per metre is on the beach, against 44% of the upstream dam's 1,728. The centreline wedges are the pond-side edge of each raise; the crest and the whole outer shell, the part that holds the dam up, stand on compacted fill and the starter. If the wedge is sandy, drained and compacted, as it must be, it holds too. The upstream dam's crest has nothing under it but beach.

8.3 · back to the question

Ending the raising stopped adding load, but it did not make the tailings dense or dry. They stayed loose and saturated, the water level near the toe stayed high, and they were brittle, so a very small strain could set off a large loss of strength. Slow creep, and the loss of suction in the drier tailings above the water table after heavy rain, supplied that strain. With the water unable to leave in the time the slope took to move, the tailings were undrained, the water took the load, and the dam liquefied from within (Robertson et al. (2019)).

8.4 · back to the question

With the drain shut the water takes the load and the house sinks: that is an upstream raise standing on soaked beach. With the drain open the water leaves, the sand settles a little and keeps its grip: that is a raise built on drained fill, as downstream and centreline raises are (and they are dense as well, which helps more). The sandbox is a two-dimensional teaching model, so read its numbers as trends only.

8.5 · back to the question

20,000 ÷ 1.4 = 14,286 m³ a day; 14,286 × 365 ÷ 1,000,000 = 5.214 million m³ a year; 5.214 ÷ 1.5 = 3.48 m a year. That is above the 2 to 2½ m a year of SANCOLD (2020). To hold it to 2½ m a year: 5.214 ÷ 2.5 = 2.09 km².

8.6 · back to the question

Because it was built by hydraulic fill, which leaves soil loose and saturated, the same state as the beach under an upstream raise. Loose, saturated, contractive fill can liquefy when it is shaken or pushed, whatever the water behind it is for. The cure was the same too: a dense, drained, compacted dam against its toe that does not depend on the old fill.

Chapter 9 · Every zone has one job

9.1 · back to the question

Under still water, buoyancy lightens the grains' press and the pull down the slope by the same share, so the face is as safe as when dry: 1.98 for the rockfill face of Example 9.2. Rockfill drains as fast as the lake falls, so its water stays still. The danger is rapid drawdown of a shell that drains slowly: the water left inside seeps out through the face, and the same face falls to about 1.10.

9.2 · back to the question

The barrier is the concrete slab on the upstream face, sealed to the rock by the plinth, with a grout curtain drilled from the plinth into the rock below. Water through a crack in the slab enters rockfill that has no fine grains to lose and drains straight out at the base. A cushion of crushed rock and sand under the slab limits the leak, and a fine transition under the joint between slab and plinth catches silt washed into a gap there and seals it (the cards of Fig. 9.1).

9.3 · back to the question

The concrete-face rockfill dam: its slab goes on in the fourth of seven stages, once the rockfill is in place, and it stays on the face, where it can be seen and repaired whenever the reservoir is drawn down. An earth core rises with the shells, layer by layer, and is buried for good; its condition can be read only from instruments inside it and the water that seeps out of the dam.

9.4 · back to the question

Seepage crosses the core from the reservoir side to the downstream side, so the grains it could carry leave through the core's downstream face; the downstream filter keeps them in, and doubles as the chimney drain. The upstream filter matters when the flow turns round, as it can after a fast drawdown, when water in the core flows back toward the lowered reservoir.

9.5 · back to the question

γd = 21.0 ÷ 1.14 = 18.421 kN/m³, and 18.421 ÷ 18.9 = 0.975, a relative compaction of 97.5%. It fails 98%, narrowly; it would pass a 95% specification.

9.6 · back to the question

Because density alone does not decide how a core behaves when soaked. Bennett's panel found that core soil placed drier let water through 60 to 140 times more easily, once soaked, than the same soil placed wetter, and a dry, stiff core cracks more readily as the dam settles. Proctor showed the same thing in 1933: one soil packed to the same density at 6.2% and at 22% water was very hard in the first case and like soft putty in the second, and could become like the second once it soaked up water (Proctor (1933)). Too wet, on the other hand, and the soil cannot be packed dense at all, which is the wet side of Fig. 9.2.

Chapter 10 · Where the water goes

10.1 · back to the question

q = 2 × 10⁻⁵ × 6 × 4 ÷ 8 = 6 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s, which is 0.00006 × 86,400 = 5.184 m³ a day, about five cubic metres. Each drop loses 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75 m of head.

10.2 · back to the question

2,366 × 400 ÷ 86,400 = 10.95 L/s, or 0.01095 m³/s. Then h = (0.01095 ÷ 1.342)1/2.48 = 14.4 cm. Over a year that dam would leak about 350,000 m³, and a regular reading of a 14 cm head is how anyone would know.

10.3 · back to the question

The water goes under it. The cutoff reaches 7.5 m down, so the path grows from 102 m to about 102 + 2 × 7.5 = 117 m, and Darcy's law predicts about 13% less water; the lab gives 9%. The water still reaches the toe with most of its head, so the exit gradient there falls only a little. The Corps of Engineers' manual puts it bluntly: theory and model tests show a cutoff must reach at least 95% of the way through a uniform pervious foundation before seepage falls appreciably (USACE EM 1110-2-1901, para. 9-4).

10.4 · back to the question

Very nearly. The depth goes from 14.4 m to 22.8 m, a ratio of 1.58, and the leak from 1,652 to 2,657 L/day per metre, a ratio of 1.61: a little more, because a fuller reservoir also wets more of the fill. The safety against piping falls from 2.26 to 1.07, since the exit gradient grows with the head too. That is why engineers read piezometers and weirs against the reservoir level.

10.5 · back to the question

The chimney, and the extra 60 litres a day per metre are the price. A fill compacted layer by layer passes water more easily along its layers than across them, and a loose or badly bonded layer can carry water over a toe drain and out of the downstream slope. A chimney cuts across every layer, so whatever comes through the upstream half is caught. The Bureau of Reclamation calls an inclined filter drain with a horizontal blanket almost standard for this reason, citing loose lifts, poor bond between lifts and inadvertently pervious layers (USBR (1987), sec. 6.3(c)). The lab's uniform fill cannot show this, which is a reason to read the lab as a guide and not a guarantee.

Chapter 11 · When water carries soil

11.1 · back to the question

Water in the open pipe loses almost no head, so the whole head between the reservoir and the toe is spent on the sand still ahead of the pipe. As the pipe grows that stretch shortens and the gradient across it steepens: under our dam the average goes from 0.20 with no pipe to 0.39 with half the path eaten and 1.7 with 12 m left (Example 11.2). A steeper push carries grains away faster, which lengthens the pipe faster.

11.2 · back to the question

Retention: D15F ≤ 4 × 0.6 = 2.4 mm. Permeability: D15F ≥ 4 × 0.15 = 0.6 mm. So 0.6 mm ≤ D15F ≤ 2.4 mm; a filter near the middle of the band, about 1.2 mm, leaves room for the variation of a real pit.

11.3 · back to the question

The boil is backward erosion: it begins at the exit beyond the toe and works back. Teton and Bennett were both concentrated leaks: water running through openings inside the core, at Teton along the base of the key trench and into open joints, at Bennett most likely through cracks opened by hydraulic fracture. At Bennett some of the transition was also prone to suffusion, which the panel thought let a little core erode before the transition held.

11.4 · back to the question

Teton's silt leaked into open joints in volcanic rock, gaps far larger than its grains, so nothing stopped the eroded silt and the tunnel grew to a breach in hours (Fig. 11.6). Bennett's core leaked into its transition, a soil graded to act as a filter for the core: the eroded grains lodged in it and the erosion stopped (Fig. 11.7). Both leaked water; only Teton let the soil go.

11.5 · back to the question

It stops the sand and lets the water through: the sequence never gets past steady seepage. The berm's weight presses down on the ground at the exit, so the grains there press on one another harder, and the upward drag of the rising water has more press to overcome before the sand can heave. It is Terzaghi's first filter: sand with weight on top.

Chapter 12 · Will the slope stand?

12.1 · back to the question

The slope check never asks how much water passes; it asks how hard the water presses where the soil might slip. Without the drain the water rises through the downstream half and breaks out 8 m up the face, and on the worst circle it carries 0.35 of the slices' weight. The drain gives it an easy path down and out: it flows faster, 109.7 L/day per metre against 44.4, but it no longer presses in the downstream half, so the grains there press with their full weight. Example 10.4 found the same trade for piping.

12.2 · back to the question

No. FS = 0.6494 × 3 × 0.4969 = 0.968, a little below 1. With water seeping out of it, this sand stands only at about 3.1:1 or flatter, where FS = 1; to reach 1.5 it needs about 4.6:1, or a drain to keep the water from reaching the face.

12.3 · back to the question

W cos α = 319.0 × 0.8486 = 270.7 kN; u·l = 76.40 × 1.601 = 122.3 kN; N′ = 270.7 − 122.3 = 148.4 kN; grip = 10 × 1.601 + 148.4 × 0.6249 = 108.7 kN, against Bishop's 129.3. Less grip: the old method takes the water's push on the whole tilted base off the press, and lets no neighbour help. Over all forty slices it scores the circle 0.978, against Bishop's 1.116.

12.4 · back to the question

A full reservoir with steady seepage is the dam's everyday state for decades, so it gets the full margin. A rapid drawdown lasts days or weeks before the water drains out of the fill, it happens rarely, and the check for it already leans toward the worst: the reservoir falls all the way at once and the fill gets no time to drain. The manual's own range for it is 1.1 to 1.3 (USACE EM 1110-2-1902, in its table of minimum factors).

12.5 · back to the question

Any wrong input. The strength fed to the check may be the wrong one: a slow, drained strength for a soil that is loaded fast (Chapter 5). The water pressures may be higher than the model's, because a drain clogs or the soil is more layered than drawn. The load may be one the check left out, such as an earthquake or a flood over the crest. Or the slip may run where nobody looked. Chapter 13 follows one real case.

12.6 · back to the question

At 3:1 it scores 1.418 for 23.1% more fill, and the water still breaks out 8 m up the face. The drain at 2:1 reaches 1.628 with no fill added, and no water comes out of the face at all.

Chapter 13 · Build your own dam

13.1 · back to the question

First, the check uses a drained strength, and the real layer failed undrained: the panel measured an average undrained strength ratio of 0.24 against the drained tan 28° the designers gave such clays (Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), pp. 49 and 69) = 0.532, so the fast grip was 0.45 of the slow one, and it fell further once the clay moved (strain softening). Second, the check knows only the ground it is given; at Mount Polley the layer had not been found where the breach occurred, so no check, drained or undrained, included it. A third answer is also fair: the workbench's layer angle is a stand-in, and the real layer's properties had never been measured before the failure.

13.2 · back to the question

In the workbench the floor is continuity: a clay wall 2 m wide from the cutoff to above the water, 46 m³ per metre, leaks 9.8 L/day and passes every goal, with a factor of safety of 1.81; any gap, and the water finds it. In a real dam the floor is set by what the model leaves out. The whole head is lost across the wall, a gradient of about 20.4 ÷ 2 = 10.2, which would drive the core's fines into the rockfill without filters on both sides (Chapter 11); a thin core also cracks more easily as the shells settle round it. The panel noted that Mount Polley's core had been cut from 8 m to 5 m wide, making it more vulnerable to cracking (Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), p. 75).

13.3 · back to the question

Water leaving the clay would carry its fine particles into the large gaps of the rockfill, and the core would erode from its downstream side, internal erosion of the kind Chapter 11 describes. Real cores sit between filters and transitions graded so that each zone holds back the one beside it (Chapter 9). At Mount Polley the filter and transition were each about 1 m wide, and the panel found many samples of the filter too coarse; it did not find that piping or cracking caused the breach (Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), pp. ii and 75).

13.4 · back to the question

It scores 1.41 against 0.94. Rockfill drains as fast as the reservoir falls, so no trapped water pushes the slope out after the reservoir's support has gone, and its grains keep their press; fill and clay keep their water. But the dam leaks 29,621 L/day per metre against the mission's cap of 1,000. (On sand and gravel the same dam scores 1.81 upstream; the mission fixes the foundation as clay.)

13.5 · back to the question

The reservoir is 22.8 m deep, so the rule gives 22.8 ÷ 3 = 7.6 m. The workbench says 11 m: the rule is a rough guide, and here it errs low.

13.6 · back to the question

Put them under the planned dam where it will be highest and its slopes steepest, in a line across the footprint from the upstream toe to beyond the downstream toe, because that is where a slip would run along a layer; and space them by the geology, closer where the glacial deposits change from place to place. Take them deeper than any slip the dam could cause, through all the glacial soils to firm ground. Recover undisturbed samples of every fine-grained layer and test them for their stress history and their undrained strength, not only their friction angle. Then run the stability check with that undrained strength as well as the drained one. Four holes cannot cover kilometres of dam; their job is to tell you where the next forty should go.

Epilogue · The dam after the drawings

E.1 · back to the question

A spillway reduced to a 12-inch pipe under a road; water rising to within a foot of the crest, so almost no freeboard; seepage near the outlet pipe; an outlet valve nobody could reach, so the lake could not be let down. A walk along the crest would have shown nearly all of them, as the inspections did. What was missing was action: an owner obliged to repair the dam, lower the lake or breach the bank as the letter of 1978 asked, and a regulator able to make that happen; a rating that matched what lay below; and a sign on the dam, so the hiker's report would have said "dam" and not "road". The review's twelve recommendations included the signs and a stronger regulation (Morhart (2010), pp. 4–5 and 7–8).

E.2 · back to the question

Any three of these. A downstream slope steeper than 2H:1V needs the engineer of record's justification and approval before it is built: Mount Polley's face stood at 1.3H:1V, and the panel found 2:1 would have held. A minimum factor of safety of 1.5 in operation: the design target had been 1.3. An operating manual with trigger levels and the actions they call for: the failed embankment's piezometers had none. An engineer of record who must report unfixed safety problems, reaching the chief inspector within 72 hours. An independent review board, and an independent dam safety review every five years. The guidelines for investigating the ground under tailings dams, published alongside the code changes in 2016, answer the layer nobody found (BC Ministry of Energy and Mines (2016); Mines Code, Part 10; Mount Polley Review Panel (2015), pp. iii, 64 and 79).

E.3 · back to the question

The margin is 1.628 − 1.5 = 0.128. As ru: 0.128 ÷ 1.77 = 0.0723. As water pressure: 0.0723 × 83.4 = 6.03 kPa. As head: 6.03 ÷ 9.81 = 0.61 m. Bishop's full sum on the drained circle gives 0.64 m. The alarm sits about two-thirds of a metre above today's reading. The drained dam's critical circle is shallower than the homogeneous dam's, so the same metre of water carries a larger share of its slices' weight.

E.4 · back to the question

With 22.8 m of water the seepage breaks out 11 m up the slope instead of 8, the leak rises from 44.4 to 58.1 L/day per metre, and the factor of safety falls from 1.12 to 1.02. Piezometers in the downstream half would rise, the weir would read more, and anyone walking the slope would see the wet patch climb. Each change is read against the reservoir gauge, which is how an engineer tells a dam obeying Darcy's law from a dam whose drains are failing.
