Appendix

How the models work

  • The seepage lab solves steady 2D flow per metre of dam on a 1 m finite-volume grid, using a saturated–unsaturated formulation to locate the phreatic surface. It uses no anisotropy, no transient effects and no filter design.

Reference

Errata and changes

  • 2026-10-24 · The permeability race, description and caption. Was: a wet front moves down each column; gravel is soaked through in seconds. Now: each column is already soaked, and the shading follows the first water poured on top, as if it were dyed. The race's times, gap fraction × length ÷ (k × gradient), are how long a drop takes to cross soil that is already full of water. Wetting dry soil from the top is a different process.
  • 2026-10-24 · The permeability race, side note. Was: time = gap fraction × length ÷ (k × push). Now: time = gap fraction × length ÷ (k × gradient). The note used a word, push, that the page never defined; the quantity is the hydraulic gradient.
  • 2026-10-24 · The opening of the chapter. Was: This step explains the three kinds of sand on the beach, and with them almost every way a dam can fail.. Now: What water does instead was worked out by Karl Terzaghi. By the end of this chapter it explains why water can make the castle stronger, why a heap under still water keeps its slope, the 19° face the beach chapter left unexplained, and the number every later chapter uses to say whether a slope will stand.. Overclaim: effective stress does not explain dams that fail by overtopping, which the book treats separately.
  • 2026-10-24 · The paragraph introducing effective stress. Was: When the gaps are full of water, the water pushes on every grain from all sides, like the cushion under the block.. Now: The water in the gaps meets almost all of the surface, and it presses on all of it with its own pore pressure; the water therefore carries u of each square metre's σ, and only the rest is left for the grains to carry.. Pore pressure does not push grains apart or outward; it carries part of the load the grains would otherwise carry between them.
  • 2026-10-24 · Where Part I comes back. Was: Soil is strong because its grains press on each other, and water pressure in the gaps pushes them apart.. Now: Soil holds as well as its grains press on one another, and water in the gaps, pushing or pulling, changes that press.. Water pressure acts equally on every grain round a gap; it takes part of the load the grains carry between them rather than pushing them apart.
  • 2026-10-24 · Grain sandbox, the house experiment. Was: With nothing pressing the grains together, friction between them vanishes. Now: Grains that hardly press can hardly grip. The grains still touch and still press a little; their grip falls with the press, toward zero, rather than vanishing outright.
  • 2026-10-24 · The water dam and tailings dam figure, caption. Was: the head H, the drop from the reservoir to the tailwater, drives the turbines. The load on the dam comes from the water's full depth at the heel, a few metres more than H. Now: the head H drives the turbines; the pressure on the upstream face comes from the full depth of water at the heel, a few metres more than H, as a worked example now shows. Readers who checked the heel readout with H got 0.83 MPa against the figure's 0.87; the example works both and shows the 4 m of tailwater that separates them.
  • 2026-10-24 · Why tailings dams fail differently, the list of failures. Was: a timeline of five failures under the liquefaction paragraph, with no raise method or mechanism for some. Now: a table of six failures giving each dam's ore, raise method, trigger, what happened, toll and volume, with sources. The list implied that every failure in it was a liquefaction of the tailings. Merriespruit began with water over the crest, and Mount Polley was not a liquefaction of the tailings.
  • 2026-10-24 · The paragraph on zones. Was: Read any section from the middle outward and you'll find the same order: tight in the centre, coarser and more free-draining toward the faces.. Now: The order (tight in the centre, coarser toward the faces) is stated for dams with a core; the chapter then shows the concrete-face rockfill, gravity and tailings dams breaking it.. Three of the four sections in the figure right below the sentence contradicted it.
  • 2026-10-24 · Concrete-face rockfill dam, face slab card. Was: Reinforced concrete, about 0.3 m plus 0.002–0.003 × depth … Leakage of hundreds of litres per second has been recorded at large CFRDs.. Now: Reinforced concrete, about 0.3 m thick near the crest and thicker with depth … Leaks of 1,000 to 3,000 litres a second have been measured at large CFRDs, and the rockfill passed them without harm.. The thickness rule could not be checked against a source; the measured leaks at Barra Grande and Campos Novos are reported by Cruz (2008).
  • 2026-10-24 · Film: A wall made of dirt, marks. Was: 2:59 All clay, and no drier, linked to the question about a metre of clay. Now: 2:59 The same dam, all of clay, linked to the question this chapter asks about it. The mark pointed to a question about travel time, and its label gave away the answer to the question placed before the film.
  • 2026-10-24 · Caption of the figure of core grains meeting rockfill and a filter. Was: The pores are too small, the particles jam at the interface, and only water passes.. Now: The filter's gaps are smaller than the core's coarser grains: those stop at the face, and the finer grains pile up behind them, so the water passes. The drawing stops every grain at the face by rule; in a real filter only grains bigger than its openings stop there, and the layer they build holds back the rest.. A filter's gaps are larger than the core's fine grains; it holds them because the coarse grains bridge its openings and build their own filter. The caption also disagreed with the drawing's own label.
  • 2026-10-24 · The filter rules. Was: A filter's pore throats are roughly a fifth of its D15.. Now: A graded filter acts like a sieve with openings about 0.11 times its D15 (FEMA 2011, pp. 275–276, after Sherard and colleagues' tests).. A fifth is an old, rough estimate; the measured effective opening of a graded filter is about a ninth of its D15.
  • 2026-10-24 · The Bennett Dam case. Was: Engineers lowered the reservoir and filled the voids by compaction grouting … R.A. Stewart's 1998 account of the crisis ranks it as the gravest dam safety concern in BC Hydro's history.. Now: Both sinkholes were repaired by compaction grouting (the lowering of the reservoir and the ranking are left out).. Neither the lowering of the reservoir nor the ranking could be found in the sources available; the panel's report and Stewart's abstract support the repair and its dates.
  • 2026-10-24 · The workbench's mission briefs. Was: The briefs of Dry the slope, Hold the water, Tailings on a budget and Mount Polley did not say which slope they check.. Now: Each brief says it checks the downstream slope only; Empty it fast checks the upstream one.. A reader who passed a mission and switched the view to the upstream slope saw a failing verdict with no explanation.
  • 2026-10-24 · Tailings on a budget, the completed mission. Was: The mission could be completed while the dam leaked about 8,000 L/day per metre, and the completion text did not mention it.. Now: The completion text names the leak as the price of the drain, and says what a mine does with that water.. For a tailings dam the leak is polluted water; a passed mission should not hide it.
  • 2026-10-24 · Mount Polley case. Was: A case card: 'released about 25 million m³ of tailings and water'.. Now: A case plate drawn to scale from the Review Panel's section: between 21 and 25 million m³, as the Prologue gives it.. The Chief Inspector of Mines reports the release as a range, 21 to 25 million m³; the book now gives one figure throughout.
